ONE OF HIS LITTLE ONES. !As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you. Isaiah lxvi. 13. 0 dreamy child with the sorrowful eyes, Are you growing so early old and wise? Softly the light of the evening lies On your forehead, child. But it surely is morning still with you; Why will you not play as the others do? See, Pussy looks as if she thought, too, It was time you smiled. As you stand there watching the setting sun. You poor little lonely motherless one, Are you so glad that the long day is gone? Are you tired so soon? Do you wait the touch of a tender hand, And the loving eyes that could understand All the visions your childish fancy planned Morning, night, and noon? From the old church slake comes the evening chime, And up over the clouds the first stars climb; God comforts His little ones all the time As a mother would. His sunshine falls like a kiss on your face, And the sound of the bells, that fills the place, Steals into your heart like a sweet embrace Hardly understood. He who cares for the wounded birds that fall, And clothes all the lilies both great and small, Watches over the children most of all With a mother's love. Be counts the pain of the joys you miss, And for ev'ry gladness you lose in this He will give you some deep and sacred bliss In the life above. • i—Little

SCIENTIFIC NOTES. ....HEUER PIGEONS ix Wen Trim—The central station for the carrier pigeons which are kept by the German Go- vernment for use in the event of war is at Cologne, and the birds are kept in what was formerly the Monastery of St. Pantaleon. The ground floor of this building is used as a residence for the manager and for the offices,while the upper storey is converted into an immense dovecot. The pigeons are kept in training by being sent on regular journeys—over short distances in winter and over larger ones in summer. They are all reared at Cologne, whence they are sent, as they may be wanted, CO the outlying stations at Mayence, Strasburg, and Metz. Ta central station is connected with Berlin by intermediate relays, and all the stations established just now are intended to be used as means for putting the fortresses on the western frontier of the Empire in com- munication with the outer world in the event of a siege. As soon as the Cologne station is completely provided for, ills intended to form similar stations on the Russian fronticr.— Live Stock Journal. PLLICTS FOR WINDOWS.—There is no question more diffi- cult to answer than the best plants for window culture, for so much depends on the skill or experience of the cultiva- tor. Some growers will make things thrive that others, utterly fail with; for some plants require nice care, while others thrive even under neglect. The various classes Of scentedgera nilea, leaved, ivy leaved,chasthemmon Zonales, rose, and other and the common Lady Washing- tons. Some of the hardier kinds of dwarf roses, as Bengals and Bourbons, Chinese primroses, cyclamens, and the vari- . ous kinds of Solanum, as the Jerusalem cherry, for instance, do very well. If there be a chance to trail from the boxes, the Kenilworth ivy, mignonette, and the petunia will thrive, and if the trailing be in partial shade, the parlour ivy, moneywort, spiderwort, or running saxifrage will be found very useful and easily managed. If the boxes are in partial shade, palms, ferns, and some of the variegated leaved begonias will do well. If one become very successful with these easily-grown plants, Mad become ambitious of floral success, there may be choicer plants experimented

Tun ELEcratc EEL.—The experience of observers has varied CIA to the effects of the electric power of this fish, but it seems to be agreed that if it be picked up by the tail sen- sations of an acute and painful character are felt, and do not immediately pass away. It is well known that cats and dogs perform remarkable feats of a gymnastic character after the incautious examination of this animal. It is shunned by the other inhabitants of the river, and dreaded by the Indians, who, nevertheless overcome their scruples when the animal is dead, for the muscles are accounted palatable, though the flavour of the electric organ is un- pleasant. The shock is said to be sufficiently powerful, in the case of large fishes, to paralyse horses and kill small animals, and is much more severe than the shock from the torpedo. The discharge takes place apparently under the action of the will. In South America wild horses have been driven into the rivers by parties travelling, so that the fishes might exhaust their energies on the horses befofe the men ventured in the water. The fish sometimes die from exces- sive exhaustion,but usually regain the electric energy in a few hours. The two ends of the fish are in opposite elec- trical conditioas, so that the most powerful shock is re- ceived when contributed to by the head and tail of the fish. —Cassell's Natural History. WHAT Is rim Nevuraz OF Emelt 7—ln the fint place, we understand ether to be of an exceedingly rare nature, as planets pass through without perceptible resistance, if we except the one instance of the shortening of the path of a comet. Its rarity, also, is proved by the fact that it passes freely through the pores of transparent bodies,such as glass, &c. Again, though ita rarity is so great—so much so that by no }town means can we detect it by weighing, nor can we exclude it from the Inside of any body, as we would pump air cut of a receiver—yet we know, from the nature of light vibrations, it must possess more the nature of a solid than of a gas. From our experiments, also, we see it is highly incompressible, and can sustain great stress, and transmit vibraticns and pressures with immense velocity. Probably, therefore, it possesses a jelly-like structure. An attempt has also been made to connect the cause of gravity with the medium, but the difficulty in this question is, that It requires the medium to be of the nature of a gas, with ,molecules of exceeding minuteness, and moving with im- mense velocity, which does not agree with the evidence de- rived from the study of other phigrot7eAnl in which, un- doubtedly, it plays a priacipai Continued, however, these dliii_ritles May disappear, and this secret of nature also laid open ; in which case, the last, or nearly the last, stronghold of action at a distance will be destroyed, and the universe will be displayed as one con- nected arrangement, one part influencing another by a regu- lar mechanism in which there is no break.-4cience for All. A FLY'S Mount—No part of fly constracture is more wonderful than the mouth. Watch a common fly alight on a piece of sugar. From the under surface of the head, appa- rently, is unfolded a long organ looking very like an addi- tional leg; and with this the fly scrapes the sugar, licks up the cream, spoliates the jam, and effects destruction in other and varied ways. To undentand what the organ in question is, let us briefly glance at the typical structure of the insect mouth. Four sets of of organs or appendages compose the "mouth." There is first an upper lip, then a pair of large jaws, then a pair of lesser jaws—forming a tube or tongue in butterflies—and last of all a lower lip. In a beetle the chief mouth organs are the greater and lesser jaws, whilst in a bee or wasp the jaws are also well developed for the work of the hive but the under lip forms a "tongue" wherewith the bee sucks up honey from the flowers. Now in the fly the mouth parts are of modified nature. Speaking generally the "jaws" are represented by small bristle-like organs, and the upper lip is developed; but it is the labium, or under lip, which comes to the front in the development of the fly's mouth. Here it forms, as in the bees, the chief organ of nutrition. It is the under lip which we see unfolded from beneath the head when the fly attacks the sugar. And when we place this organ beneath the microscope, we can readily discover the secret of its service. The "tongue' as we may term the under lip, consists of a stalk highly movable and muscular, at the end of which a couple of broad leaves ex- pand Outward from the middle to form a sucker-like organ, beautifully adapted for licking up fluids, and for scratching solid matters also. This fan-like end is supported on a firm tubular framework, acting as a set of springs to open and shot the fans, whilst the microscre show VS that this atructure is nearly like a file or rasp in its nature. We can understand,then readily enough how much a muscular organ purposes of fly nourishment. When ' caaftnetbea ususemdmieorr he of flies, the morocco covers of our books and the finely polished surfaces of oar furniture are scratched and eroded, we can readily appreciate the cause of the damage, With this file it wages war even on ourselves, For, as a. famous authority on insects remarks, it is by Its means that the fly ‘4 teases us in the heat of /milliner, when it alights on the band or face to sip the prespiration as it exudes from and is condensed upon the skin."

I refer to the manufacture of barrels from straw, which is first reduced to a pulp as if for paper mak- ing, and then compressed by powerful machinery and kiln- dried until it becomes "as hard and solid," we are told," as the hardest of native wood." One of these so-called" paper barrels" can be made for 22 cents, as against 40 cents for a wooden one. The inventor has also prepared a wash for rendering the inside of barrels impervious to liquids, and one large firm is testing the barrels with a view to using them for oil, while the manufacturer is getting some ready for whisky, wine, cider, vinegar, lard, honey, butter, fruit, kerosene, and hot lime. There are also wash-tubs, baths, pails, and powder kegs of the same material. Probably planks for building will come next, and even a paper fleet ' will not be a mere phantom fleet in the future. We are short of home-grown timber in this country, and if we could lee straw in place of wood there would be a little better Chance than there is at present of making our arable land pay. The patentee of the invention, and of recent im- provements on it, is Mr. G. W. Larroway, of Port Byron, New York. WORKING FARM Hot/sm.—The work of the team in field operations is now so very important that farmers must needs study how to obtain most labour from their horses with least etrain on their constitutional vigour. There are two ways In which this can be done—first, by studious attention to dieting; and secondly', adopting what some term "Scotch hours," or the division of the day into two parts, with an Interval of at least two hours' rest between. As to the first, It stands to reason that working animals must be kept well whenconstantly employed in arduous toil; their food should also be given in the best condition for ready digestion, their pats bruised, beans kibbled or ground, and chaff, if of straw or inferior hay, steamed or fermented. Farmers would also find it advantageous to give a little malt with the other food, and one thing calculated to keep farmers' horses in health is that of allowing them to have a drink of chilled water as soon as they come in from the fields, and before they commence devouring their manger food. On the second point, it may be remarked that the farmer who works his horses from six a.m. until-noon, and after feeding and resting them two hours'gives them a second bout from two p.m. till six p.m., gets two hours labour from them more than his neighbour, who employs them from seven a.m. till three p.m., with much less toil, privation, and injury to the animals in the former instance to what they suffer in the lath r. If you hold a new-laid egg before a candle, shading it with the hand, you will find it illuminated by the flame; then take an egg which has been sat upon, say a week, and you will see that if fertile it will be dark and opaque—all except the top of the large end, which is the air space. We cannot expect them to adopt the French system; but they might keep a large number of hens to supply themselves. Just now in country towns eggs are very cheap, because the farmers are all alike—they send them in on market day, and the rush brings down the local price, while in districts where farmers are few, they are almost doable. The grocer gets the benefit, because he fixes his awn rate, and at the same time is enabled to send his own goods in payment. While he gains in two forms, the farmer loses in two ways. People of this kind are very fearful of breeding pure stock, which, if one would be guided by them, never sells. It is found to be different in London, where the West End auction room is often so crowded that a City firm have thought It worth while to set up an opposition, affording both buyer and seller advan- tages over the old firm. THE Boxst.—A Dutchman and an Englishman in South Africa are two very different people. The Boer will live, , even after he is comparatively rich, in a house of which the floor is the hard-trodden earth, and surrounded with scarcely any of the comforts which the most remote English settler would consider essential to his existence. Yet the Dutch- man is perfectly content, while the Englishman is fall of complaints of the country, the Government, his neighbouts, the climate, the soil, and of everything and everybody save his own disposition and himself. The Englishman is a social personage; he likes society, and gossips of his own race. The Boer cares for no one's smoke in sight of his chimney, and, like the Western American settler who moved when a second stranger had been seen near his cabin "that fall," would almost resent any one taking up a farm in his close vicinity. His pastoral tastes require much land for their development, and nothing troubles him so much as the fear that in time he may find his cattle and sheep too many for the grass which he has to offer them. Hence a Dutchman sees little forbidding in the dreary country north of the Orange River, though to a stranger, even from the least alluring portion of the Cape, the Orange River and Trans- vaal are most depressing.—The Countries of the World," by Dr. Robert Brown. LAND BILL.—At a meeting of the Birmingham Liberal Association, on Tuesday night, held under the chairmanship of Mr. W. 11..4-Eria (president of the associatien), a resolution :yas adopted expressing gratitude to the Government for its large and comprehensive measure of land reform for Ire- land. The association recognise with satisfaction the adop- tion of a principle upon which alone the lust interests of the cultivators of the soil could be secured, and approve of those ortions of the bill whkh provide for the creation of a new proprietary, in the belief that the funds advaiced by the State under the authority of Parliament might be wisely and beneficially applied. The association further expressed satisfaction apdr.lappefulnes in the pr•posed emigration scheme, believing that a well-considered co-eperation between the Home and Colonial GoVeinthents is the wisest that can be adopted, and, regarding the measure as being conceived in the highest interests of the Irish people, the association gladly took hold of Mr. Gladstone's declaration to use all legitimate means to carry the bill. Mr. Bradlaugh on Monday addressed two great meetings in the Free Trade Hall, Manchester, on the subjects of Irish and foreign policy find perpetual pensions. In the afternoon, before proceeding with his address, he made a personal state- ment with regard to his re-election for Northampton. He denied that he had ever refused to take the oath in Partia- meo, or that he had said the oath would not be binding 'uptut him. In order not to wovoke a discussion which might interfere with the debate on the second reading of the Irish Land Sill on the 25th inst.y the day when Parliament re- assembles, he had determined not to present himself in the House for the purpose of taking the oath and his seat until the 26th. He meant to take his seat, and he believed the Liberal majority in the House would vindicate his right to it ; and having taken the oath, as required by law, he in- tended, as soon as the forms of the House permitted him, to more for leave to bring in a bill to substitute affirmation for the oath in the case of any'person who objected to take the •CguliC3l Boasne,--Tlie position of anti-state-church mem- bers of Parliament in regard to this Bill is not a little curious. They are asked to sanction 'it, and, Of course, have the power of altering it. The Roman Catholic, Jewish, and Quaker, members, to say nothing of some others of different, or no religious views, are all invited to have a hand in effecting this revolution in the parochial government of the Church of England. What should be their attitude in regard to it? The Gallios may be simply indifferent, but what of those who insist that if there be a pational Church it should re- main national, both in spirit and in administration, and who at the same time believe that the affairs of teligious commu- nities should be managed by religious men, and by their own members? We think their duty is plain. They ought not to sanction any attempt to change, with a view to improve- ment, a system which is fundamentally unsound and in- capable of radical amendment. They should therefore say to Mr. Grey-You are choosing a will-o'-the-wisp, and trying to combine the incompatible and the irreconcilable. Let the Church be disestablished, and then it may have Church Boards according to its own pattern, and without deferring to the wishes of Parliament. It is too late to re-Construct the Establishment, but when that is out of the ivaf it May be comparatively easy to re-organise the Church.—Liberator. THE MattnraGE Laws.—We (Daily News) stated the other day that, in view of the forthcoming Conference among•it Nonconformists on the subject of the Marriage Laws, the Executive Committee of the Liberation Society regarded as "the change in the law most to be desired" that the legal formalities should in all cases, Episcopalian as well as Nonconformist, be observed at the office ef the registrar; any religious service being superadded elsewhere, according to the wish of the parties. The Executive Committee, how- ever, assume that " in the present state of public opinian this proposal is not likely to receive general sanction." They, therefore, suggest the following bases of a measure by' which, in their,opinion, religious equality would, to a great Went, be secured and departure from sound principles be avoided: (a) Increased facilities shonl4 be afforded for giving notices of marriage, and there should be a simplifich- . tion of die forms to be observed. (b) Marriagee at Non- -conformist places of worship and at tile registrar's office- should be placed on as favourable footing as those at Episeo- pal Churches, in regard to length of notice, licenses (both ordinlry and special), and fees. (c) Marriages (in places of worship registered for marriages) without the presence bt a registrar should be authorised, on the production of the (d) The fact of the celebration of the mar- registrar's certificate that the legal notice has been given, or d a once be certified to the registrar by the roifaga el i csehnosuel. person .ofticiating, who should. be required to post to the registrar the document containing such notification and the signatures of the parties. (el It should be the duty of the registrar to register such marriage, and also to make in- quiry, as to the certificates which he has issued, and which have not been returned to him within a given time. (f) The hours within which marriages should take place (8 to 12) 4hould be extended.

LORD PALMERSTON. In one of the Runnymede Letters written by Lord P Beaconsfield when he was lain Benjthin Disraeli, Lord Palmerston is informed that he is "a nisf hetetrmlle taining himself in power in spite of the contempt o na- tion," "the great Apollo of aspiring und P erstrap erws,"oshows" a want of breeding," reminds one of a "favourite footman in easy terms with his mistress," "a Tory underling whose audacity in accepting the seals of the Foreign Office is only equalled by the imbecility of the Whigs in offering them to such a man." "Your Lordship's career." says this imitator of Junius, "is as insiznificant as your intellect." The epistle to Lord Palmerston ends with an apostrophe to Eno.- land, "0 my Country! fortunate, thrice fortunate Eng- land! with your destinies at such a moment entrusted to the Lord Fanny of Diplomacy. Methinks I see your Lordship the Sporus of Politics cajoling France with an airy com- pliment and menacing Russia with a perfumed cane." And though i,•we are disposed to regard these choice expres- sions as the extravagant utterances of a genius struggling to gain for itself a name, yet we must not forget that there were many in the House and out of it who entertained a very poor opinion of the Whig Foreign Secretary." "A Captain of Shams" was the name applied to him by a pre- sent member of the Cabinet, while Mr. Urquhart styled him "the arch-traitor sold to Russia." In 1850, however, the noble lord had an ample oppor- tunity of vindicating himself and his policy, and as the occasion is one of interest to the general reader, we purpose to occupy the space at our disposal in a description of it. Her Majesty's Speech at the opening of the Session of 1850 was particularly emphatic upon the peaceable state of our relations with Foreign Powers. The Speech from the Throne, however, had scarcely been uttered when intelli- gence arrived from the Mediterranean to the effect that we were actually at war with one of the minor Powers of Eu- rope. Great Britain, one of the three States that guaranteed the independeace and constituted themselves one of the pro- tectors of Greece had suddenly broken off her relations with the Greek Government, her Ambassador had been withdrawn from Athens, her Admiral had declared the Grecian coast in a state of blockade, and we, a great Power, were virtually at war with this little one, 'without ;having consulted our co- protectors of France and Russia, or taken any step to justify our conduct either to them or to Europe. What .was it that nearly brought on a European war and caused a temporary disturbance of the good relations between England and France:? It was this. A Mr. Finlay, a British subject long established in Greece, was in possession of a piece of land in the vicinity of the palace of King Otho. That land was forcibly and illegally seized and converted into gardens for the King's palace without the slightest compensation or offer of compensation having been made to its lawful owner This was the first cause of quarrel, and occurred about four years before. There was also, it appeared, another British subject in Athens, a Jew of Gibraltar, named Don Pacifico, whose house was attacked and plundered suddenly by a mob partly composed of Greek soldiers, and incited to the affair by the son of the Greek Minister of War. Don Pa- cifico demanded and was denied compensation. This was the second cause of quarrel. For these reasons the Foreign Secretary, without any consultation with France and Russia, proceeded to extreme measures. His policy, however, was denounced by a very strong Opposition. "The allied troops who led the attack," says Mr. Evelyn Ashley in his Life of Lord Palmerston," were English Protectionists and foreign Absolutists." This assertion, however, requires foundation, and does not appear consistent with the facts of the ease. Lord Palmerston himself called it "a shot fired by a foreign conspiracy, aided dad abetted by a domestic intrigue.' But Lord Palma ,ton was the Minister attacked, and might be excused for believing that hostile monarchs were giving the fatal wound, and that the attack on him was th e work of a corn`dined treachery of Europe. An his- torian is expected t- t tke a calmer view of things. The truth is Lord Palmerston's proceedings were fairly open to difference of judgment on the part of the most devoted Liberals and the most independent thinkers. It did not seem altogether consistent with our dignity or with com- mon discretion to act the part of a blustering bully and pro- ceed to extremities. A gentleman gains no credit by fight. I ing a costermonger, nor could Great Britain gain any credit I by having bullied or coerced Greece. But in the prolonged and powerful debate which took place in the House upon the subject, the friends of Lord Palmerston and the admirers of his general policy for 20 years refused to narrow it down to such an issue. They felt that ta reprimand the Ministry for his proceedings in Greece was to condemn all he had done between 1830 and 1850, and that the system which he had uniformly endeavoured to carry out was to be judged of as a whole and not to be broken up into fragments and to be reversed by the nation because one of the fragments might happen to be somewhat unshapely when taken by itself. Mr. Finlay and his little strip of garden ground, Don Pa- cifico and his pots and pans, the Greek affair and all that related to it sank to utter insignificance in the presence of this wider topic. It was admitted by the country and re- echoed by the Legislature that, if even an error had been committed,the question in reality to be decided was whether the policy of Lord Palmerston over the whole Continent was to be reversed. The House had solemnly to decide whether the statesman who had managed the foreign affairs if this country in times of unexampled difficulty and peril had or had not managed them in a manner consistent with the high and proud position which Great Britain was en- titled and compelled to hold—with the character of Eng- lishmen and with the interests of peace, civilisation and constitutional freedom in every part of the world. To have decided that in the negative would have been a condemna- tion of the Foreign Secretary and the Ministry of which he formed a part. In a prolonged and powerful debate some of the foremost men on both sides of the House opposed and denounced the policy of the Government, for which, as every one knew, Lord Palmerston was responsible. The discussion eVoked some curious combinations of Parties. In the first class were ranked not only the men who desired to overturn the Government and to step into office, but men who did not seek office and others who had usually supported the Minis- try. The party without statesmen, as it has been called, including Mr. Disraeli as its chief—the statesmen without party, including Sir Robert Peel, Sir James Graham, and Mr. Gladstone—and some of the Free Trade Pasty, including Sir William Molesworth and Mr. Cobden—were alike found among the opponents of the Government. Never did such conflicting principles find themselves associated before. Interference and Non-Interference, War and Peace, Mili- tarism and Quakerism were banded together to oust a Minis- ter whom not one of them accused of incapacity or dis- honour. Among his supporters were found an almost equally heterogeneous assemblage of men. The whole interest of the debate now centres in Lord Pal- merston's defence, which was indeed a masterpiece of Par- liamentary argument and address. It is true, as has been justly observed by the author of "The History of Our Own Times," " it was not one of the grand historical displays of oratory that even when the sound of them is lost send their echoes to 'roll from soul to soul.' It was not like one of Burke's great speeches; or one of Chatham's. It was not one calculated to provoke keen literary controversy like Sheri- dan's celebrated Begum Speech,' which all contemporaries I held to be unrivalled, but which a later generation assumes to have been flashy logic. There are no passages of splendid eloquence in Palmerston's pacific speech. Its great merit was its wonderful power as a contribution to Parliamentary argument, as a masterly appeal to the feelings, the preju- dices and the passions of the House of Commons." It was, in fact, a complete exposition and defence of the whole course of the Foreign Policy which Palmerston had directed, but he did not fail to make special defence of his action towards Greece. He based his vindication of this particular draft of his policy on the ground that the poorest claimant who bore the name of an English citizen should be protected Py the whole strength of England against the oppression of a foreign government. In a peroration of thrilling power, in which he appealed to all the elementary emotions of manhood and citizenship and good fellowship, Lord Pal- merston asked the verdict of the House to decide "whether, as the Roman in days of old held himself free from indignity when he could say, Civis Romanus sum,' so, also, a British 1, subject, in whatever land he may be, shall feel confident I that the watchful eye and the strong arm of England will I protect him against injustice and wrong." When Palmerston closed his speech the overwhelming plaudits of the House foretold the victory he had won. It was indeed a masterpiece of tongue fence. A Conservative I Member walking home that night said to a literary Member of I Parliament—" I have heard Canning, Plunkett, and Brougham in their best days, and I never heard anything to beat that speech." It occupied five hours in delivery. It was spoken, as Mr. Gladstone afterwards said, from the dusk of I one day to the dawn of the next. It was spoken without the help of a single note, full as it was of minute details, names, dates, figures, ref erences of all kinds. Nothing could be more complete than his success. Civis Romanus I settled the question. "It was in vain that Mr. Gladstone, In a speech of singularly argumentative power, pointed out that a Roman citizen was a member of privileged caste of a victorious and conquering nation, of a nation that held all others bound down by the strong arm of power, which bad one law for him and another for the rest of the world, which asserted in his favour principles which it denied to others." It was in vain that Mr. Gladstone asked whether Lord Palmerston thought this was the position which it would become a civilised and Christian nation like England to claim for her citizens. The glory of being a Civis Romanus was far too strong for any mere argument drawn from fact and common sense to combat against it. In vain was the calm, grave, studiously moderate remonstrance of Sir Robert Peel, who, while generously declaring that Palmerston's speech made us all proud of the man who delivered it, yet recorded his firm protest against the style of policy which Palmerston's eloquence had endeavoured to glorify." The victory was all with Palmerston. After a debate of four nights a majority of 46 was given in his favour. The Ministry came out not only absolved but triumphant, and Lord Palmerston, though weighed in the balances was not found wanting. "We are all proud of him," said Sir Robert Peel, and the words were caught up and re-echoed all over the land, for he had, in the words of Shakspere's Rosalind, • • ' well and overthrown more than his enemies."

SIR,—" Old Father Christmas" has come and gone since I last wrote you. How strangely different his aspect in this semi-tropical clime to his wonted appearance in Old England. Instead of the red-faced, capacious figure bewrapped in furs, with frost-pinched nose and beard of icicles trampling through snow into the open porch and waving aloft his bunch of hollyand mistletoe, we here behold a figure draped in long yellow silk coat with sunburnt visage shaded by a white frith helmet, and carrying a bunch of the cabbage tree or of the fern tree: With a blazing sun and a bright blue sky, who but a born Colonial can believe that this is " Old Father Christmas ?" Yet, so it is; Christmas Eve has come; bunting flaps in the breeze; hug grasses and ferns decorate the butchers' shops and the hotels; religious services are announced for the coming day; and although our Englishmen persists in believing it is midsummer, every Colonial conspires to cheat him that it is not, and on every 'hand he hears the good old formula, "A merry Christmas to you." Unfortunately, with the advent of the sacred fes- tal day came bad weather, wind and wet, and this continued more or less through Christmas week, and well into the New Year; indeed, in various parts, north and south, there have been heavy hailstorms, and in some instances the stones fell an inch and a quarter long,•damaging crops, breaking win- dows, stripping trees, and killing fowl. Old residents ex- claim, " We never knew such a Christmas as this !" " Very wintry weather !" They even threatened to light fires in their houses, and complained of chills and colds. So this fruitful topic, the "weather," has occupied much attention of late, for the frequent and heavy rains have injured the fruit crop, and threaten to affect the prospects of the har- vest

From Christmas-eve until the middle of January is the grand holiday time for Colonials. True, the hours of busi- ness throughout the year are not what you would call " 1 ong" (say from 8 o'clock to s—from 9 o'clock to 6), yet they are long enough for the climate, which undoubtedly lessens working capacity and predisposes to laissez-faire. For all that Colonials generally speaking work hard and enjoy a good day's out as much as our begrimed and weary Lon- doners. Thus, it is that at this season excursions by sea and land, boating, races, school treats, and pic-nics replace the toil and humdrum of daily routine. Auckland is a great centre of attraction to "country folk," and the country is equally attractive to the denizens of the city. Hundreds crowd into the one to see friends, go to a ball, or to the theatre, or to spend a few days and many dollars in riotous living; whilst hundreds go into the other to gain healthful change, to visit relatives, or to learn a little more concerning the Maoris and the geography of their adopted country. Here and there, in city and rural retreat, there is plenty of innocent enjoyment. -Go for instance on New Year's-eve to the wharf (the Sunday evening rendezvous and promenade), and look at the gay bunting, watch the fireworks from the shore, and the rockets from the ships; mix with the current of laughing, chattering humanity. Suddenly a brass baud breaks into a lively strain, and as suddenly the buzzing crowd, stirred by a common impulse, moves in concerted step, two by two, bearded men and sprightly girls whirl and sprung with boundless vigour and hilarity, until the hour has come, and 1881 reveals his masked face, and smiles upon the merry scene. Yet this were not an English Colony if it did not present other and very opposite scenes, if it did not reproduce and observe that popular custom of " Watch-night" services. Here (as at " Home ") earnest men and women in various sanctuaries recall the history of the dying year, lament in- dividual sins and follies, summon Golly resolution for the unknown future, await in silent devotion the dawning year, and with its advent renew the old expressions of friendship

and goodwill. I have suggested how great the contrast as to pleasure king; how in " Old England" you prize your Chrispnas and New Year's enjoyments chiefly in-doors; here it is otherwise; excursions are the order of the day, and chiefly by sea. Railway travelling is not popular here (as the re- turns for the past year show), and my one experience in some measure explains this, it is in truth slow and un- pleasant. All Auckland goes to the agricultural show at Ellerslie, some five miles distant, so joining a few friends I took a first-class ticket, but tried in vain to obtain a seat of any kind, and could only secure by courtesy of the crowd just enough standing room on the platform attached to the front of a third-class carriage. So shaky was the ride so zigzag the track, that I had to hold fast by the iron railing, i and the speed could hardly be more than six miles an hour. Whilst in this uncomfortable position I had an interesting chat with an enthusiastic Colonist, who boasted that "they were not behind England in any way!" Not even in Railways! No wonder comfortable steamers and sea trips are preferred. Two or three of these vessels visit Kawan, the island name of Sir George Grey, who kindly throws open his grounds to visi- tors; others visit Waiwera and allow time to bathe in the hot springs; others againdiisit the Island of Mototapu, whilst small ferry steamers pTy every hour to North Shore, or Devenport, as it is usually called. This is the healthiest and by means of these steamers the most accessible suburb of Auckland; it already contains 1,000 residents, and the number is rapidly increasing owing to its salubrity, to its facilities for sea bathing, and its excellent views of the Bay of Rangitoto, with its channel, and of the surrounding coast. Except Rangitoto, which always looks picturesque and solemn the coast outline is not imposing and lacks wooding • bathed in sunshine, however, it is very lovely, and the Climate, though not sufficiently bracing for some constitutions, is simply delicious. Moreover, within the distance of four miles, it has the attraction of a fresh water lake, Lake Takapuna, two and a half miles long and one mile broad, with sweetish and very deep waters, lying in the bed of an extinct volcano. Its banks are ash and therefore flat, and you miss the sumptuous wooding, the nooks and dells and the far-reaching mountain scenery which encase our English lakes. One singular feature, however, it pos- sesses, viz., immediate proximity to the sea. Within a few hundred yards on the one hand lies this placid blue lake; on the other, the green restless waters of the Rangitoto channel, on which a steamer lies at anchor, having landed Its passengers by boat, and now awaiting their return from this inland curiosity. Some of your readers may have heard of Mr. Vesev Stewart's "Special Settlements." The fate of those who trusted to the representations made to induce emigrants to buy these lands should warn others to Fait till their arrival In the colony before embarking in any enterprise of such a nature. Though led to expect comfortable homes, good roads, and a bargain in the land, so far as price is con- cerned, the settlers find on their arrival that the promised houses are yet to be built and the roads to be made while better land can be obtained from the Government at made, the price. There are "Albert-land" settlers in Auckland who recall how similar promises as to roads, tic., were made to them, and how shamelessly broken; how, in fact, the settlers had to fight their way through the bush and to sleep in the open or in tents until they could build better shelter Now, what good is there in thus hoodwinking men and women whose difficulties dispose them to look abroad for happier days? Does it add to the "fair fame" of this colony? Does it make contented and hopeful immigrants? No, it simply makes a profitable investment for a few per- sons. Of course, intending settlers are foolish to be thus misled, and would act far more discreetly if they waited. until, on their arrival here, they could inspect land in various stages of condition, from the virgin "bush" to the fenced and cultivated farm, and purchase as they deemed best. One thing is however, certain viz., that however settlers may buy, hard work and may-he years of hardship are in store for them. This may not, of course, ultimately be a calamity. Even these Te Peke settlers who have come out under the fascination of brilliant prospects may, in the end, be no worse in some respects for their inevitable struggle with difficulty ; they will become more self-reliant, more fertile in expedient, stronger, and in 'every way more capable. They will, at least, be able to live on and from the land; the strongest among them will do more than this; hut what of the weak, who faint in the day of-adversity? This "shady side" of emigration, the unavoidable struggle of the first few years, has not, I think, been disclosed as it should have been. New Zealand is undoubtedly a splendid country, but success like the gold in its beds of quart?, has to be dug and toiled for, and can only be won by persistent and intelligent purpose. Whoever is incapable of this should certainly not become a "settler. Apropos of immigration, a return prepared by the Go- vernment shows that during the year 1880 no fewer than .15,152 persons arrived in this colony (including 2,688 Go- vernment immigrants), while 7,918 left the colony, leaving a balance in its favour of 7,703. The "Lady Jocelyn" party is the third special settle- ment promoted by Mr. V. Steinart. The two former are at Kati-Kati, some thirty miles from Tauranga, and in the 'vicinity of the now famous To Aroha, or " Mother of Gold" IMountain. This proximity must prove of considerable mer- cantile value to Kati-Kati. The Te Ardha is part of a mountain range extending northwards along the Hauraki Gulf, a distance of 130 miles, and it is confidently believed that the whole range is auriferous. The most exciting I event of 1880 has been the discovery of gold at Te Aroha, land the proclamation of that district under the Goldfields Act. Opinions widely differ, and hope alternates with doubt as to the results of this discovery. Some 14 years ago I gold was discovered in this same district of the Thames, and caused a tremendous rush. Tradesmen forsook their coun- ters, clerks their desks, and farmers their fields, to struggle for the precious metal; quartz crushing and mining cora- lpanies were formed. In a few months half a million of money was distributed in dividends; fortunes were made and fortunes were lost; and, in fact, whilst a few became rich, so many suffered from foolish speculations, that in Auckland no such gold fever is again possible, and, al- though there is intense interest in the present discovery, shares are not eagerly bought - in fact, they sell with great difficulty. Te Aroha is 33 miles from Hamilton, and is reached from Auckland either by rail to that town and then by coach, or by steamer to the Thames •, and it is now pro- posed to form a river depot at Kopu, and connect it by rail with Te Aroha. Meantime, with the rapid gathering of miners, store keepers, &c., brings the inevitable School and Church into activity, with all the signs of a busy and civi- lised community. Political circles and the community at large have been startled by the resignation of Mr. Bryce, Minister of Native Affairs. No member of the Cabinet has been ms o highly inrecorrupt- respected, not merely for his abilities, but for his ible character. Mr. Bradlaugh headed the poll at the election for Northampton on Saturday. The votes recorded for him numbered 3,437, and those polkd by Mr. Cobbett (Conser- vative) 3,305._ . . . .

Mr. Alfred Young, of the Oxford Circuit, has been ap- pointed by the Home Secretary to the Recordership of the city of Gloucester, vacant by the death of Mr. Granville Somerset, Q.C. At Great Lever, on Saturday, a tram-car guard was struck in the back, but not dangerously hurt, while he was on the top of his car, by a bullet supposed to have come from a volunteer range a mile away. The Queen has approved the appointment of Lord Car- lingford to the office of Lord Privy Seal, vacated by the resignation of the Duke of Argyll. On Saturday Lord Car- lingford arrived at Downing-street and had a long interview with the Premier. It will be remembered that Lord Carling- ford was one who gave in his adhesion to the minoriiy report of the Richmond Commission on the Irish land question. The new " Democratic Federation" issued a manifesto on Saturday. The leaders put forth a social and political programme which they say they have framed to unite the great body of the people, quite irrespective of party, in favour of principles of justice, freedom, and steady progress, which are now too often set aside to suit the convenience of

factions. The sons of the Emperor of Austria once got into a fierce quarrel. In the height of passion one said to the other, "You are the greatest ass in Vienna." At that moment the , Emperor appeared in the doorway, and, highly offended to , find his children quarrelling, said, "You forget, young gentlemen, that lam present." They all then saw the point that had been unconsciously made, and the quarrel ended in a hearty laugh. There is nothing quite so absurd as a hobby horse, and yet every man has a larger or smaller one in the family stable. One never attemp's to ride it but he makes'himself ridiculous. An illiterate preacher who, among other false- hoods, believed that men are always right and women always wrong, was wont to declare that the five foolish virgins who had no oil in their lamps were all women, while the wise virgins were all men. The steamer Nebo, frem Rio de Janerio, has arrived at New York, and reported that on the Bth inst., in lattitude 33 degrees, longitude 73 ,degrees, she supplied with pro- visions the barque Tiger, 77 days out from Liverpool, for Baltimore. The crew had sustained life for several days on strips of leather, soaked in lamp oil, until the oil gave out, and then fed on the captain's dog. Canibalism or death was imminent when the Nebo sighted her. Mr. Carlyle's will is published. He expresses his gratitude to the friendliness and "actually credible human love" shown him in America, especially in New England, and testifies to the "immensities of worth and capability" he believes and partly knows "to be lodged especially in the silent classes there." In token of this feeling he bequeaths the books used in writing Ids "Cromwell "and " Frederick" to the President and Fellows of Harvard College. The will was proved on the 7th inst., and the personalty swan under £35,000. Mr. Hugh Mason, M.P., in a speech which he made at Ashton, on Stturday, referred to the speech of Lord Cairns on the Transvaal peace. He said he had always associated his Lordship, who was a tip-top Evangelical Christian, with coffee taverns, Christian associations, Bible societies, and works of charity and benevolence, bat no man could go through his recent speech without coming to the conclusion that on this occasion he forgot all his Christianity and all his regard for the poor people of foreign lands, and be- came the champion of a policy bloodthirsty and despot::: in ; the extreme.

The London police have arrested a man who, it is alleged, was one of the five persons convicted in 1866 of a daring burglary at the Stamp Office, Manchester. The man has for some time been carrying on business in Lambeth as an omnibus proprietor under the name of Powell, and he has been sworn to by the police as Charles Leeson, who, after receiving a sentence of 15 years' penal servitude for the burglary in question, was with two of the other prisoners, sent, on their restoring a large quantity of the stolen pro- perty, to serve their time in Australia. It is asserted that Leeson shortly afterwards escaped, and had since elubd detection. The case has been remanded in order that further , evidence may be produced,

"He knew the Government had a bill on the subject upon the stocks, but he did not believe it would pass into law, because it happened to be a bill which had some use and some sense in it, and the Government,

GENOA THE SUPERB

I • • . ! Any account of the Ligirian Republic, how it rose and VI, ought to be particularly interesting to the Englishman- ' , fbr A variety of reasons, but mainly becatise Genoa at one. . , time was 'the most powerful of, mercantile donamunities, occupying for a season a naval and commercial pre7eminence sbmething like that width' We ourselves enjoy among the nations of the earth. In the volume before us Mr. Bent has Olven due prominence to this one feature of Genoese his- he has properly elaborated other points which are culated to lend to the story special attractiveness for the glo-Saxon, and as the book throughout bears the marks ot careful research, and is ably constructed, it should readily ffnd a place in the library, side by side ivith standard Italian records. The Genoese were early brought into close con- nection with the English by the prominent part each played in the Crusades. On the Holy Wars the Italian Republics —Genoa, Pisa, and Venice built all that was great in the commerce of the middle ages. They acted as the carriers for the Crusades, and as such were the only Christians who contrived to gain anything to themselves out of the struggle between the Crescent and the Cross. In this they displayed a good deal of business cunning, if they did not succeed in obtaining credit for much chivalry. The Genoese notably seem to have been remarkably clever in looking after "No. 1" throughout the various expeditions, and the chapter vihich tells of their doings in the Crusades is one of the liveliest in the book: ' The Holy Wars were, indeed, most *portant for Genoa, as the foundation on which were laid centuries of prosperity and wealth. How disastrous to that prosperity were the bitter feuds which long raged between the Italian Republics—fends which terminated for Pisa in her rain at Meloria by Genoa, and ended a hundred years later in the Venetians driving the Ligurians from the Adriatic—we need not stay to inquire. More to our pur- pose and far more agreeable is it to dwell for a moment on the maritime progress Genoa made in the Mediterranean, and the wonderful hold she obtained in the Black Sea. In connection with her former trade she secured immunities fOr her commerce in Spain, andheid a most extensive inter- cOurse with France. And further, as Mr. Bent remarks:— Along the coast of Western France, past Bordeaux, La ochelle, and the Isle of Oleron, the Genoese found their way to the Low Countries. Here they exchanged the goods of the South for the carpets, tapestries, and woollen goods of Flan- ders, and at the Dutch fairs they shook hands with their suc- cessors in the commercial world, the men of Holland and the Tien of England. Bruges wasthe grand emporium of all this wealth, Owing about as nanch allegiance to their Brabant liege lord as the Genoese did to the distant Emperor of Germany. Here Genoa had warehouses and foundries; also at Antwerp, where in 1468, on the event of the marriage of Margaret of England to Charles the Bold, we read of ' the emulation of the , foreign merchants in doing honour to the occasion. In the ' procession which went forth to meet the bride; appeared • Gienoe,se and Venetian banners side by side with the Hanseatic and German companies. The Genoese company was called "La Spinola," from the name of that noble Genoese family who figured largely in those northern 'countries as extensive Merchants and money-lenders, holding much the same posi- tion as hereafter the Fuggars of Augsburg and the Rothschilds held. Larger ships were built purposely an Genoa for meeting the terrors of the Bay of Biscay and the German Ocean, which carried their intrepid warriors to all the Hanseatic towns Of the far North. to. Wisby in the Island of Goltand, and to the coasts of Russia, to participate in the fair of Noveirod. During the middle ages the products of the East found their way into Europe by three channels. One of these Was the Black Sea Channel, of which Genoa had almost un- disputed monopoly for two centuries. She ruled in,the Black Sea, in Constantinople, and in the Greek Archipelago with almost as firm a hand as we to-day rule in India. The foundation of this supremacy was laid in dealing with the decayed Byzantine Empire. Her footing in the East she lOst with the fall of Chios, Petrarch, in 1331, when seek. leg to heal the hostilities and factions In the rival republics of Genoa and Venice, retYlinded the former that "no sea exists with which the echoesot your triumphs do not resound. The ocean itself dreadayou. The Indian sea is rejoiced for once to be released from your trir.mes." " But," eloquently observes our historian, "the laureate's enthusiasm was of small avail. The evil which he strove to check was the one bane of their prosperity and success. In vain was it that they filled their coffers with gold, if it was lobe squan- dered on internal quarrels and contests with a rival.' We have seen bow England became connected with Genoa through the Crusades. Let us follow up the intercourse in Mr. Bent's language : In this commercial intercourse med bevel Genoa and mediaeval England offer much of interest. In England it was that leather and steel were produced cheaper than elsewhere; her woollen goods rivalled those of Flanders, and thither did Genoa bring the silks and velvets of the south, the drugs and aromatics of the Indies to exchange for those commodities ; and as incipient ideas of luxury began to develop this intercourse became more marked, and Genoese families / ound it by no means unprofit- able to establish commercial houses in London, and to have warehouses along the Thames, as they did in. Constantinople, Cyprus, and other centres of commerce. The commercial loving Edward the Third aimed at establishing on our isle a commerce which should' rival and eventually surpass that of Flanders. Thus during the most flourishing period of Genoese history, and during,the period of youthful development in England, we find many points of interest which bound together these com- mercial powers, of which the small Italian Republic was to pave the way for much of the greatness 'of the other. . In addition to our lessons in commercial enterprise it was in Liguria that our earliest poet, the morning star of our litera- ture, learnt one of his sublimed stories, wader the tutelage of Petrarch, and in the land where Dante loved to roam. In 1347 Edward 111. hired Genoese galleys for his wars, and in 1372 the King appointed Pietro di Campofregoso, brother of the Doge, as commander of the Genoese vessels in his serviee, with Sir James Pronan, an Englishman, as his lieutenant. A mis- sion was sent three years later to settle, as some say, about a port for their factory in England, or, as others say, to nego- tiate for a further supply of galleys. Be this as it may, Sir James Pronan, accompanied by Giovanni de Mari, a Genoese, and Godfrey Chaucer, were despatched to Genoa in 1375. Thus far we can satisfactorily trace our poet to Liguria; whether Petrarch was there at the time or not we cannot say. Certain it is that he stayed more at Genoa in his later years than any- where else in Italy, and certain it is that his old friend Guido Scettem WRS at this time reposipg in the monastery of Cervara. This was the spot Where Petrarch passed his days when on a visit to Genoa, and what more likely than that here Chaucer, on his mission to Genoa, learnt from Petrarch's lips the story of the patient Grisaldis.' Over the futnre of the English language this journey to Genoa had an unlimited influence. Petrarch and Boccacio much esteemed the story. They considered it as one of their gems in literature, and the fact of Petrarch's having imparted it to Chaucer when on this visit shows how friendly must have been the reception given by him to the English poet. On returning to his native land Chaucer delayed- not to put pen to paper, and gave to the world the most pathetic and ' best known of his Canterbury tales. . . During the four- teenth and fifteenth centifries large loans were from time to time negotiated by the Rings of England for Genoese capitalists, and in turn Ligurian merchants obtained the right of import- ing wool free of charge, and not unfrequently the Genoese were employed to furnish letters of change, payable in Rome, to acquit the annates of the English bishops with greater ease; and in London a Genoese consul WA9 in perpetual residence to superintend the Interests of their British society of merchants, and in those days most of the English export was done on Genoese bottoms._ _ _ _

---__ _ A history of Genoa would be woefully imperfect which did not recite in detail Genoese voyages and discoveries. At the close of the 13th century a Venetian, Marco Polo, the patriarch of mediaeval travellers, whilst in prison in Genoa, compiled a volume of travels which aroused in the breasts of his jailors that craving for discovery and adventure which wts consummated by the greatest of Genoese sons—Chris- topher Columbus—when he found the New World. In like manner the Genoese story would he incomplete that did not treat of the famous Bank of St. George, where was first mooted the development of capital, the funding of money and interest which the advance of mercantile ingenuity has so perfected and unravelled. Concerning this celebrated institution, we take the following striking passages:— Elsewhere than in Genoa we search in vain for a parallel for the existence of a body of citizens distinct from the Govern- ment—with their °yin, laws, magistrates, and independent authority--a State within a State, a Republic within a Repub- lic. ---All dealings with the Government were voluntary on the part of the Bank. Over their deliberations the Genoese Go. vernment and enators could exercise no influence, nor could they interfere with.their general assemblies, without violating the Most stringent oaths, and without destroying the very basis of the constitution. But far from working without har- mony, we always find the greatest unanimity of feeling between these two forms of Republic within the same city walls. The government of Genoa always respected the liberties of the bank, and the bank lways did 'fittest to assist the government when in pecuniary distress. And whilst the State was convulsed by continued revolutions from within and tyrannies from without the Rank of St: George or' the eonsti tdnetvii oantedof ftrhoem" its path of always kept an equal course, never justice, grew in riches and in credit—in short, was the boast of the Ligurian Republic. . . . It is melancholy to have to draw a veil over the career of this illustrious bank with the Revolution of 1,708. The new order of things which Genoa had learnt from France deemed it inconsistent with liberty that the taxes, the property of the Republic, should remain in the hands of the directors of St.. George; it was voted a tyranny on a small scale, and the directors were compelled to surrender them; and inasmuch as the taxes represented the sole source from which their income was derived, they soon discovered that their bank notes were useless, and the building was closed shortly afterwards. In 1804 and 814 attempts were made to resuscitate the fallen fortunes of St. George, but without avail; an so this bank, the origin of which was shrouded in the mys- teries of bygone centuries, fell under the sweeping scythe of of the French Revolution. The history of the bank is the pre- - face to all the leading commercial undertakings of Europe; banker,it is the d a end sanctuarycompared o f tht h emerchant and the shrine of the , i tda l itthye, whichß o t hs ell: di resuscitations after overpoweringtheconguls—the, protectors and di- rectors of the bank—the managers of our own Bank of England ldfslieareEnibut parvenus. . . . Her (Genoa) disasters • her extraordinary one could crush -Genoa,if Genoa did not crush herself" all We have no roomanldefittato these had their cent Emperor Charles sth to say that "no won- derful constitution re in the Bank of St. George, its lworld-wideie ee en thfame.these estate, and eturaceeueeheefr amongst the dominions of th Bent's delightfully-told g tale, which relate the fall of Genoa from her proud e sftanvaov . chapters 1 vo of willM r . l enrolment merely say that the rule of Andrea D'Oria—who introduced, into Genoa a system oaristocratic he r tyranny which prosperity i cahn db tyhz' process of alow decay undermined romantic Fieschi con: pp hi riaccaTir eyaa, dgaawni ndi with thwetuhnoenu only yucanwl need pleasure no f as duDdr ' eot ahr ni that ;. are described most gr the volume, which may be profit, is handsomely embellished lent illustrations. . with a number of excel-! * Genoa: How the Republic Rose d anFell. / Bent, 8.A., Oxon. • THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY AP IL 164 1881 • . DEATH Or THE PEV. 1110,1,EY .13 NSHON. The deceased, •wfm had gone iti`a centincintal tour last month for the benefit of his health, Was taken seriously ill .at Genoa, and his medical adviser (Dr. Hill) was at once thlegraphed for from London. Dr. Pnnshon, under Dr. Hill's care, warr-removed to England, and arrived at his house in Brixton last Wednesday week. After his return he became alarmingly ill; his symptorns much resembling those of Lord Beaconsfield. On Tuesday night he slept comfortably, and on Wednesday seemed slightly better; but at six o'clock in the evening he was seized with an attack of spasmodic breathing, which continued at intervals till about 1 o'clock on Thursday morning, when he expired. The illneas was complicated by heart disease and inflammation of the langs. One of the deceased's sons was present at the a the time of the death. A public funeral is in contempla- lion. The Rev. William Morley Punshon, Wesleyan Minister, born in 1824, at Doncaster, where his father was a draper, entered in 1838 the office of his grandfather' a tim- ber merchant of .Hull, where he obtained a position beyond his years, and soon became possessed with a strong desire to study for the ministry. He accordingly zealously strove to qualify himself to fulfil this self-imposed task, and cpmmenced his career at Sunderland in 1840 by undertaking the duties of a "local preather," a preparatory ministerial office peculiar to the Wesleyan. Methodists. Four years later, after passing a short terra as a probationer at'the Wes- leyan College, Richmond, he accepted his first pastoral charge in the ministry at Marsden, in Kent. The report of hie success here was not long in reaching the leaders of the Wesleyan connection. At the Conference of 1845 he was appointed to the ministry of Whitebaven, Cumberland, and, although only twenty-one years of age, his reputation was such that people flocked to hear him from all parts. He ministered in various parts of the country, beside visiting the metropolis; where his addresses both from the pulpit Mid the platform attracted considerable attention. In 1888 he left this country for Canada, and married bis deceased wife's er' a proceeding which led to his being struck off the "Legal Hundred" by the Wesleyan Conference. The lady with whom Mr. Punshon formed this connection died in October, 1871. During hi ti regilence in the Dominion he was five times president of the Canadian Conference. He returned to England in 1873, and in July, 1874, he was elected president of the Wesleyan Conference for the en- suing year. Many of his sermons and lectures, published since his removal to London in 1858, are very popular, es- pecially the lectures on " John Bunyan " and the "Huguenots." Mr. Punshon has also published a small volume of poems.

---ulj scholaferfirthe afternoon is very little more than half the Otal number on the hooks, and the number of teachers is ar too few even for that number; the number of teachers to the scholars In attendance is as low as any school in the • union. The buildings are very good, and with a little; , cleaning out and re-arrangement would hold a school at least twice the size. The day I was there there was a great .deal of noise, this being in consequence of almost every class having twice as many scholars as it ought to have bad, and oonsequently the teachers were unable to manage themproperly. From the position in which the school is at present they hive not rnany of' the helps to Sunday. school life such as other schools .have, viz., Missionary Society,or Band Of llcpe. Ido , not think the present stale of the school, however, is any refiection on the teachers, as the average attendance of the teachers is very fair indeed, being 20 out of 25 on the books, almost as high as the highest average shown by any of the schools, and better than some. The only thing that they require is more strength in the teaching power; there is no doubt but that what they have is good, but the work must be very hard. METHODIST FREE CHURCH, ORMSKIRK-STREET.—This school is also struggling with difficulties; their average attendance, compared with the number on the books is very poor. Then, again, the average attendance of teachers is only 11 in the afternoon out of 29 on the books. There may be here some great mistake in book-keeping. Of course, I can't tell; but unless there is a mistake in the book-keeping, these figures are decidedly on the poor side. I 'visited the school twice, once in the morning and again in the afternoon. In the morning I found them very short of teachers, there being only the superintendent and two teachers present, and these three were struggling under adverse circumstances, and no doubt doing their very best. In the afternoon I found them ninth better, there was Po -fault whatever with those who were there, they seemed to be 'teaching very earnestly and doing their best, but the estab- lishment of teachers is evidently not sufficient for the work, and I would recommend them to look through their book and see who the 29 teachers are, and whether the 11 out of the 29 who attend, are the same people every Stinday, or whether the irregular attendance of teachers runs right through. If there are 29 fair teachers on the books, and if' they can get them to attend regularly, they will soon put the school in first rate order. The schoolrooms and arrange-- menu! are riqlte sufficient for the average attendance that ought to turn up out of 181 en the books. As a qualifica- tion for this report, which may be looked upon as not very 'good, I may say that, being a small church and a small chapel, they are not able to show as good an organization and disctpline as stronger and richer churches. Still they are in the race with the rest of the schools and no doubt when they see that they are a little behind, they will strain pn u.every nerve to put themselves in their proper laee o infant • Vicyoura Ha.—l found the teachers here labouring under many adverse circumstances. The children seemed to me to be rather on the small aide, and they had room, but had the infants in the general school. This of course, is always a disadvantage. Nor had they any class- room, they seemed, however, working very hard and are no doubt doing a good work. Their average attendance of teachers is 12 out of the number on the books, 13. This is exceedingly good, and the average number of scholars in attendance out of those on the books is good for a school situated as they are. Having the uphill work that they have I think a great deal of praise is due to the managers and i teachers of the school. WHISTON.—I found this school much as I found it last lime; they seem to be doing a good work, they appear to be one of the schools that has a good morning as well as afternoon attendance of both teachers and scholars. Whatl saw at Whiston was in every way satisfactory. Ido not know whether one secret of their success is that I was told that tneir superintendent was nearly eighty years old, having worked hard at the same sort of work for many years, and being quite hale and hearty, and one of the best singers in the school. . Tug Two HAYDOCE SCHOOLS are in very good order, they are under one superintendent, Mr. Barton (7) The premises of both schools are first-rate, especially the one at Blackbrook. There is very tittle noise in either school; and although Mr. Barton said they were short of teaching power—and very likely he is right—still they have quite as much teaching power, in proportion to their scholars, as almost any of the schools; and they seem to manage their classes very well. The attendance of the teachers at the Haydock school is 12, with the number on the books 12; and the attendance at Blackhrook is 10 out of 11. This of course, is excellent, and in the case of the Haydock school could not be beaten, as you cannot very well get 13 of an attendance out of 12 on the books. Another featnre in this school is that their morning attendance of both teachers and scholars is very much above the, average, and is practically almost as good as the afternoon, if not suite. I asked the superintendent how he accounted for it. He said, "Weil, we have nothing else to do. We have no place of worship in the neighbour- where we go, so that we concentrate all our energies on the morning school." GERARD'S BRIDGE—This school is similar in one respect to the two Haydock schools; i.e., that the morning school is good, though not as good as the Haydock schools in pro- portion to the afternoon school; but far better than any other school in town. Mr. Glover attributes this in his case to there being no morning service and to the teachers being content to forego attendance on morning service and devote their energies to teaching instead of being taught. They seem to me to be in. the .same healthy state that they wera when I visited them last.year. The discipline and order of the school is exceedingly good. Barns; PARK-nosn.—There seemed to me a great mm. provement over last year in the appearance of the school at this place ; the rooms themselves looked cleaner and brighter, and the teaching and discipline seemed good. The singing was also good; better than last time. The library was in a very good order, and in my judgment everything looked much more encouraging. I am glad to be able to give a good report about this school, as last year I could only give a moderate one. CONOREGATIONAL SCHOOL, PEASLEY CROSS.—The school here seemed to be in about the same state as it was last year. The discipline and arrangements of the school are excellent in every respect, and if they suffer from anything' it seems to be that they are a little short in teaching power ; , this, however,,did not seem to produce any disorder, as the classes were quiet, and there was no more than the noise that is absolutely necessary to conduct the teaching of the school. BROOK-STREET Sciroor..—There is no change to note with respect to this school—the largest, undoubtedly, and one of the best organised in the Union The general impression t vl- bodabodonyue,tutßhuradoteortksh-teastncrdelaessthsteioss work, are n visitor ieaspintt,oi ntis h goodetrhea t sceonvnoetrrdyootl everything doubt gat that every- body y i a the es well organization is not only good on Sunday, but that during the week they have classes and meetings and gatherings that in my opinion very much add to the attractions and a or k, efficiency of Sunday schools ; and my impression, up to a very short time ago, was that they had more teachers in comparison with their numbers than any other school in the union, but on looking at the statistics I was surprised to find that this was not so,and that in comparison to the number of scholars on the books or the number of scholars in afternoon attendance, they have fewer teachers perhaps than any school in the union. This, of course, speaks very highly for the individual efficiency of each teacher, and ought to show to the other schools in the union that even if they are suffering from a scarcity of teachers they are quite as well off as the Brook-street school in point of numbers. The morning attendance at Brook-street school, like all schools in the to-vn of St. Helens, is poor compared with the afternoon, and it only seems that in places like Whiston, Haydock, and Gerrard's Bridge where there is no morning service, that anything like a good morning school can be got. PRESBYTERIAN SCHOOL.—TbiS school was excellent in every respect last year, and has not in any way gone back. The ituagements and discipline, and thewhole tone of the school are as good as any in the union, and they seem to me to have the most numerous staff of teachers and officers, compared with the number of scholars, of any of the other scheols. Of course the result of that is that no teacher is overburdened with scholars. This state of things Sunday after Sunday must tell greatly in favour of the school, because it enables the teacher to do his work very much better; it is not so wearying and tiring to him, and the scholars receive more benefit every Sunday afternoon, than they do when the teacher has to be continually bringing to , order the disorderly tail end of a large class. Mr. B. L. GREEN, of Manchester, addressed the meeting at some length, and spoke in eulogistic terms of Mr. Mac- fayden, now stationed as minister at Manchester, but formerly minister of the Independent Church at St. Helens. Referring to the training of the young, he said some ola. fogies would say that it was not good to train children up to Christ when very young, as children would be children still. But they wanted children to devote themselves to Christ in the freshness of their youth, before the world had got its hold upon them, whatever old fogies might say. Old fogies would be old fogies still. (Laughter.) In giving advice to the teachers, he said they must thoroughly under- stand the nature of their work. They had not to deal with children as manufacturers dealt with so many hands, nor as mothers did with so many months—(laughter)—but as so many souls who, by the teachers' instrumentality, might be led to the feet of Jesus. He could give a prescription for a full school which could not fail to ensure success if carried out. Let the superintendent be always at school a quarter of an hour before the time; every teacher ten minutes before the time, and every scholar five minutes; and this dose to be taken twice on a Sunday. Speaking further upon the qualifications of a good teacher he said that although be could not send teachers away who had not given their minds to Christ, he could not allow them to take a class unless he knew their hearts were right on that point. It was an anomalous thing that an unconverted teacher should be the acknowledged guide of the road to Heaven. (Applause.) Speaking of the good accomplished through the Sunday school agency he instanced the case of a church which had received in its ranks 8 per cent, of members from the world and 61 per cent. from the Sunday School. Mr. Wenham was appointed president of the Union for the next year, Messrs. Boydell and MeKeeknie were re-appointed secretaries, Mr. J. Marsh was re-appointed treasurer, and the old committee was again elected. On the motion of the Rev. J. P. RITCHIE, a vote of thanks was accorded to the chairman, the speakers, and the ladies who presided at the tea tables.
