div.head: IRON AND COAL TRADES.
div.p: IRON AND COAL TRADES.

Bannow-Irr-Fnastass, Monday.—There is a good inquiry for all descriptions of hematite pig iron, and the business done by makers has increased on the week, but there are I still several large producers of iron who are declining to sell at present prices. Business has been done at from 58s. per ton at works for all round qualities of Bessemer iron, and forge iron finds a market at about the same figure. The output of pig iron is very considerable, and deliveries are very fully maintained. There are evidences of a great re- vival in the shipping trade, as large cargoes of iron and steel have to be shipped to the Continent, America, and elsewhere. In steel the trade doing is very large, but as,most of the makers in tlils district are exceedingly well employed, they are unwilling to take contracts at low prices. MANCHESTER; WEDNESDAT.—With the exception that the warmer weather is beginning to wake itself felt as far as the demand for house-fire clasnes of fuel is concerned, the posi- tion of the coal trade of thfs„district has remained without material alteration during the week. In the immediate neighbourhood of Manchester the principal colliery firms have continued well supplied with orders, which have kept their pits going full time, and prices in the Manchester dis- trict'are steady; at late rates. From other Lancashire dis- tricts, however, a less favourable state of things is reported, and so far as round coals are concerned a general weakening tendency in prices is apparent. Up to the present the better qualities of round coal have fairly maintained their price, the recent cold weather having kept up a tolerably good demand for house-fire purposes. Best Wigan, Arley, and similar qualities of hem coal arq still fetching from 9s. to 9s. 6d. per ten at the pit,' but 4econd and inferior qualities of round coal, which are only in poor demand, are decidedly easier in price; Pemberton four-feet and common Arley averaging about 7s. 6d. per ton at the pit, whilst common round coals for steam purposes, which are a drug in the market, are to be bought at almost any price, from ss. 3d. to ss. 6d. per ton upwards. Burgy is also abundant in the market, and both in this class of fuel and common round coal stocks are going down, with very few of the col- lieries working, only inferior mines running more than four days a week. Slack is moderately plentiful, but there is no pressure to sell, and prices continue firm. Burgy at the pit mouth ranges from about 4s. 61. for inferior qualities up to ss. for the better sorts, and slack from 3s. 3d. to Ss. 13d. for common up to 48.6 d. for good qualities. An absence of demand is reported in the shipping trade, and for the few cargoes in the market there is a keen competition at extremely low figures. The iron trade of this district has during the past week been dull in the extreme, and no inquiries of any importance have been reported in the market. No doubt to some extent the quarterly meetings and the Easter holidays have operated against orders being given out at present, and there have been no transactions on which to base any re- liable quotations as to actual selling prices. A weaker tone, however, unquestionably characterises the market all through,but the low prices which sellers are now willing to accept for deliveries deferred over long periods, to which makers at present do not care to commit themselves. For Lancashire pig iron delivered into the Manchester district local niakers are still quoting 455. for forge, and 465. per ton for foundry qualities, less 2i per cent, but as these quota- tions are open to offers they are simply nominal, and a re- duction of the list rates before long is not impossible. For manufactured iron prices are easier; and although makers of common iron have already fully discounted the reduc- tions announced during the last few days in marked brands, buyers are taking advantvge of these to press for further concessiona. Very few new orders areNaffering, and the comb mon bars delivered into the Manchester district are to be bought in quantities at from £5 121. fid. to £5 15e. per ton, with hoops averaging about £6 ss. to £6 10s. per ton. Some fair foreign inquiries for. machinery are reported in the dis- trict, but still there is very little new ishrk on home account coming to hand; and both engineers and machinists) as a , rule are but moderately employed.

ST. HELENS SUNDAY -SCHOOL UNION. On Sunday the annual prayer meetings in connection with this Union were held in the Brook-street and Blackbrook New Schools, the former at half-past eight, and the latter at a quarter-past eight in the morning. There was a fair at- tendance. lie the afternoon a united scholars' service was held in the Congregational Chapel, Ormskirk -street. The place was full, and Mr. B. L. Green (deputation from the Parent Union) gave an address suitable fer the occasion. On Monday evening a tea meeting was held in the United Methodist Frea Church, Ormskirk-street.. After tea Mr. C. Sharpies, president of the Union, took the chair, and was supported on the platform by the Rev. W. C. Tayler (Bap- tist); Messtk. J. Marsh, B. L. Green, and Wenham. 'I he attendance was good. After a brief address from the Chair- man, Mr. JOSHUA BOYDEtL, one of the secretaries, read the following report :—Your committee have pleasure in pre- senting their report at the close of another year, the cen- tenary year of Sunda?schools, which has not been an un- eventful one in the history of the St. Helens Sunday School Union, but has been characterised by much activ, effort, and has, we trust, been also marked by great usefulness. As an organisation we can but speak of this as our 16th anniver- sary, but we gladly recognise as an important fact that the instruction of the young on the Lord's Day has been con- tinuously cared formn this town since the beginning of the present century. The year 1880 found us with eight schools in the association. During the year three others have joined, namely, Victoria Hall, Haydock Colliery, and Blackbrook, making our present strength eleven schools, with a total of 2,859 scholars, and 233 teachers, thus showing an increase of 40 teachers and 540 scholars in the union. The average attendance of teachers in the morning has been 83; in the afternoon 185, givingan increase of 6 per cent, in the morning and 4 per cent.,in the afternoon over that of last year. The scholars' morning attendance has been 763; afternoon 2,015, an in- crease of 5 per cent. in the morning and 3 per cent. in the afternoon over that reported last year. Of the 233 teachers returned 183 are members of chdrches, of scholars 99 are members. During the year 4 teachers and 10 scholars had been added to the church. This shows a proportion of only about 4 scholars out of every thousand who have been led to make a public profession of their love to Jesus. The scholars local scripture examination was held on February 27th, the subject being "The 'history of Samuel." There were 173 entered, and 93 presented thernselvee for examination from the following schools: Baptist, Brook-street, Peasley Cross, and Presbyterians. In the senior division 11 passed,4 with honours; middle division, 27 passed, 6 with honours; junior division, 25 passed, and 2 with honours. Out of the ' 90 who presented themselves 63 passed, 12 with honours, to whom prizes and certificates were presented at the service, yesterday. The committee hope that the teachers and officers of the schools in the Union will interest themselves in promoting these examinations as they are a valuable means of fixing the truths of scripture on the minds of scholars. Your committee are also pleased that teachers' examinations had been held, the results of which are not yet 'known. From the reports sent in, it appears that only four preparation classes are held in connection with the Union, as the means and opportunities of study in the case of many teachers are very limited. The committee would urge the necessity of forming weeky preparation classes in connection with every school in the Union. While we are able to look back NOtth some degree of pleasure we can look forward with hope and increasing expectations, though all of us need to be more alive to our responsibilities and to consec,ate ourselves snore fully tq our work, each cheerfully devoting his time and talents to the service of Him whose we are and whom we profess to serve. Mr. R. PIULINGTON, who was appointed to visit the scheols, read his report as follows:- -Mritalts Smiciot..—l am sorry that I am not ;We to give a very .good report of this school; there are many weak points us it. Moarpar.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Pickniere) and ex-Mayor (Councillor Fairclough). . fittreACH OF 'rue i'IIACK.—A young man named John Duane was charged, On warrant, with committing a breach of the peace by assaulting John O'Donnell, on the MN December last, near the Central Station: P.C. Crickett proved the case, and the prieoner wits ordered to be bound over in pne surety of £lO to keep the peace 6 thotaths. be prisoner ,eria also charged with the non-payment of the arrears of a bastardy order, and, the Bench committed Idifi for two months' imprisonment. KING A bon WITHOUT" A LtCENsE.—For this offence James Waywell, Latchford, was fined ss. and costs. AN ExpEwsrvE "DRUNKEN Faux.”--James Cardwell, a young man-employed by Messrs. James Quinn and Co., Limited, indiarubber works, Leyland, was summoned for having on the 13th March been•in a carriage belonging to. the London and North-Western Railway Company in a state of intoxication, contrary to the by4aws ; and also with having on the same. day trayelled between Preston and Warrington 'without having paid his fare, and with intent to avoid payment. The defendant pleaded guilty to the first, and- not gtilitylto the second charge. Mr. Preston, solicitor to the Linden and North-Western Railway CompanY,i4ase- cuted. He stated these, proceedings were taken at the instance 'of the post dee. It -appeared that on the-13th March the defendant was on the platform at Preston station, when-J.lle mail train arrived, The letter sorters got out of the post office =Flap by the trap-door through which the' mail bags are thrown out; and on .the mail starting from Preston, the defendant bolted through the hole into the sort- ing office, The train was in motion and they could not turn defendant out, or the chances were he would have bee* killed. The defendant behaved himself in a mest indecent manner in the sorting office, and when he arrived at War- ringtonbe was removed. Of course that was considered by the post office authorities to be an outrage, and the. Bench must Judge whether the circumstances of the case warranted them in dealing with it in a severe manner.---Alfred Edward Smith, tiorter at Preston station, deposed to seeing the defen- dant on the station and missing him when the mail started, and William Birkett, overseer of the post office carriage, stated that defendant got in the van in a state ;of intoxica- tion. He thought defendant got in the van as a drunken freak.— The Magistrates' Clerk (to Mr. Preston): I don't Oink you can sustain the second charge.—Mr. Preston : Why ? The Clerk: He did not want to travel at all.—The elver: It appears to me he was a very unwilling traveller. -rThe defendant said he came from Leyland to Preston station with a spring cart to take luggage to the mail van. He had had a drop of drink and did not know he was doing wrong. He merely got into the train to see what they were doing.- He had never seen the van before, and thought he would get in to see it.—Deferdant called a witness who stated he and defendant were taking some goods ordered by Government to go to London by the mail for Portsmouth.— The Mayor said it was a drunken freak. He did not think defendant had any intention of riding in the carriage. De- fendant was fined 10s. and costs, (total XI 17s. 6d.) on the first charge, and the second was dismissed. ALLEGED RODBERY.—AN ALL-NIGHT DRINKING BOUT. —Michael King, a discharged soldier, and Annie M'Carty, a dissolute character, were brought up, on remand from Satur- day, charged with being drunk and disorderly on Friars' Green on-Friday afternoon, and also with stealing from the person of Peter McGourley, at the house of William Noon, a purse and £1 35.; and Margaret Burns, a young woman was charged with'beihg' in -company with them, and taking part in the robbery. From the statement of the Chief Constable, it appeared that the prosecutor was all engine tenter from Preston, and had recently come to War- rington and taken up his abode in Stanley-street, Friars' Green. About four o'clock, on Thursday afternoon, the Prosecutor was walking down Bridge-street and was accosted by Annie M'Carty, and they went to the Shakespeare pub- lic-house, where they remained drinking until 9 or 10 o'clock. The prosecutor obtained 2s. worth of whiskey and 2s. worth of rum, and vent with M'Carty to the house of William Noon, Jolley's-yard, Friars' Green. After having been there some time Noon asked prosecutor if he had any money, and he said he had and produced Ll 12s. A quantity of beer was fetched into the house, and they stayed up drinking all night. About six o'clock, on , Friday morning, prosecutor went to sleep in a chair and when he awoke about seven his purse and money were all right. He was then asked for some money with which to purchase. something for breakfast, and he gave Barns Is. 6d. Prosecutor went to sleep again, but awoke about 9 o'clock, and found his purse money, and a knife had gone. On Friday afternoon the prosecutor gave in. formation to the police, and P.C. Hennessey went to Noon's house, where he found Mrs. Noon and the two first-named prisoners drunk. P.S. Spinks searched for the purse and money but had been unable to find anything.—The charge of robbery was abandoned, and Burns was discharged, but on the charge of drunkenness, which, the Bench remarked, seemed to be a very aggravated case, King and M'Carty were each fined 20s. and costs. ASsAuLT ON A WOMAN WITH A CLOTHES' PROP.—John • Higgins, farm labourer, was charged on remand with having assaulted Mary Naughton, by striking her on the bead in Pump-yard, School-street, Latchford, on the Bth inst.—The prisoner pleaded guilty to hitting the prottecatrix with a clothes prop.—Mr. Hunt stated that prisoner went home with a strange man, on Friday, and told the prosecutrix to leave. She refused to do so, and prisoner got hold of her and threw her in the yard. She resisted the prisoner, aid from her statement she was struck on the head with a bill-. hook produced, but that was simply her statement. She was then struck on the heart with a clothes prop. There was a long deep wound on the forehead, and at the back of the head there was a bruise as though prosecutrix had been struck with a prop. When taken to the Infirmary she was in a beastly state of drunkenness, and was sent to the workhouse. —The prosecutrix, whose head was enveloped in bandages and whose apron was covered with blood, thengave evidence to the effect that prisoner put her out of the house, struck her on the eye, which was much discoloured, and then struck her with the clothes prop produced.—The prisoner acknow- ledged that he "just dropped the prop on her head," and the Bench, taking into consideration the time the prisoner had been locked up, fined him .ss. and costs. Scrtoot. Arnorumacia CasEs.—Patrick Corfield was sum. rnoned for neglecting to send his son Michael, to school. Mr. Riley proved the case, and stated the defendant had had tree schooling allowed for two children for about three ' years, but the last order expired in December last and had not been renewed. Defendant was fined ss.—James Barker was fined a similar amount for not sending his child, Marv, to school. The girl, although 10 years of age, could not tell her letters.—Peter Hines, forge labourer, was summoned for neglecting to send his daughters, Anne (12) and Mary (10) to school. Mr. Riley, in stating the case, said be did not think either of the girls knew their letters. They had missed the examinations for years, and had cost the school about £2 2s. each year. Defendant was fined ss. in each case, Alderman Holmes expressing his sorrow that the eldest girl could not read the simple words he had asked her to- real—Thomas Kay was fined ss. for not sending his child. Mary, regularly to school.

ATTEMPT TO DEFRAUD THE MILITARY. - Thome; Knockton was charged with being on the premises at Orford Barracks, on Monday, for an unlawful purpose, viz, to ob- tain from Sergeant-Major Bourne money or provisions by false pretences. He was deo charged with being in posses- sion of a pair of military boots, and not giving a satisfac- tory account of them.—The prisoner, it appeared, went to the Barracks, on Monday afternoon, about four o'clock, and said he wanted to enter the ser eice. All the necessary pre- I

liminaries were gone through, and, as the prisoner stated he had no money and was ia want of something to eat, the sergeant-major gave him sixpence. It was then discovered that the prisoner had previously served in the 40th Regi- ment, whilst stationed at Limerick, and had then enlisted in the Royal Marines. For bad conduct, whilst in the latter service, he was tried by court-martial, sentenced to 84 days' imprisonment, and discharged as a bid and worthless character.—Sergeant-Major Bourne said these cases were very numerous. They came in dozens and offered them- selves for enlistment, and, after staying a night and getting all they could, they jumped over the wall, going to either Manchester or Liverpool. He had had a dozen cases of that kind himself during the last montb.—Prisoner said he never wanted to enlist, but he took another man,Arho was too short.—The Chairman was satisded that it was a deliberate attempt at fraud, and prisoner was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour.

ESCAPE FROM AN INDUSTRIAL SCHOOL. John Dooney was charged with having run away from the Boys' Refuge, St. Ann's-street, Liverpool, on the 22nd January last.— Prisoner stated be ran away because he did not get enough to eat.—The Chairman remarked that he looked as if be got sufficient food.—Mr. Hunt said this was the second or third time prisoner bad escaped.—The Chairman asked if the schools were subject to Government inspection, and Mr. White answered in the affirmative.—Prisoner (crying) : Let me go home and I will go to school awain.—lnspector Singleton said he aprrehended the prisoner in Silver-street. The father said he could do no good with the boy and did not want him at itome.—Prisoner lie is very sorry now for sending me.—Prisoner was remanded to the industrial school.

TflustanAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman rickmere), the ex• Mayor (CounCillor Fairclough), Captain Litton, and Zlba Armitage, Esq. Mr. lisamsrON's Crucus.—Mr. Moore applied on behalf of Mr. Harmston for a license to perform the play of "Dick Tarpln "this circus in Sankey-street; and Mr. Buckton, for Mr. Sheridan, of the Prince of Wales Theatre, opposed the application. As there was a diversity of opinion among the magistrates on the Bench the application was refused.—Mr. Moore asked that the application be adjourned to another session; but the Mayor said he must have a fresh summons and a fresh Bench to hear the application, or find out which magistrates disagreed. . • • . _ _

ALLEGED ASSAITLT.—Joseph Swift, a young man, was charged with assaulting Catherine Wheeler, an old woman, with whom he lodged.—On Sunday at noon defendant went home in a temper and ordered complainant to pack up his things, using bad language all the time. She did so, and was carrying them to the door when he struck her on the face with his fists knocking her a- distance away. Her husband eventually put defendant out, and he then picked up a large stone which he sent at the door.—A witness was called, who stated defendant was drunk.—Defendant denied striking the complainant, and said her husband took up the poker and struck him on the head.—Edward Boyton said

about three o'clock on Sunday afternoon he found tho de- fendant sitting on his kitcLen doorstep moaning, and he took him in. He was bleeding very much from two wounds on his head, which complainant dressed.-7rhe case p dismissed.

His father interfering be struck him' on the jaw, aiid ear and otherwise abtre'ed liini Complainant stated he was a very bad son, hut he could net get hint out of the way. -1-The Mayor observed that defendant had a very bad character at the Court, and he was sentetiCed to a month's itnpriaontnent. i Gasvancvmea THE THOROIIGHFARE.—WiIIiiIM Rounds, aid Joseph Taylor, ware charged with obstructing Butter- market-street, on the 7th inst. by allowingtwodrays to stand , an unreasonable length of.time. Mr. -Graham appeared for ete defendants,--P.C. Lawrence said he noticed defendants, who ire carters in the employ of the Wilderspeel Brewery Co., delivering beer in Buttermarket-street from two drays, and they stood there from 10-15 a.m., to 11-55. They were in the publichouse for 40 minutes without appearing near the drays.—P.C. Chantler corroborated.— Mr. Graham con- tended that consi jering the work the men bad to perform the drays were not standing an unreasonable length of time. He called Mr. Allen, landlord of the public house, who stated the drays were only at his house from 10-50 to 11-50. The Bench did not consider the officers' evidence shaken in the least, and fined each defendant 2s. 6d. BREACH OF THE PEACE. Patrick Foley, and George Cunningham, were charged with committing a breach of the peace in Dolman's lane, on the 9th inst. Foley pleaded guilty, and he was bound over in hia own recognizances to keep the peace for six months. Cunningham did not appear, and a warrant was issued for his apprehension. DAMAGING A. STALL IN THE MARKET.— William Hewitt, 00, was charged with damaging certain stalls in the market place, on Sunday the 10th instant. Defendant and some other lads were seen jnmping on a stall by a police Officer, who on examining it found it had been damaged to the extent of Is.—The Mayor cautioned defendant, and ordered him to pay costs. Twmvx MONTHS OF MARRIED LIFE. William Henry Miter was summoned to show cause why an order should not be made upon him to contribute towards the mainten- ance of his wife Mary Ann.—Mr. Harbourne, the relieving officer, ,said defendant's wife had been chargeable to the Union three weeks, and there was 14s. 6d. owing. When she applied for relief she was in a very destitute condition, defendant having got her discharged from her place.—The wife (20) ?aid defendant had treated her with "contempt and disdain." They had been married twelve months next June, and he left her because she had given a small piece of meat to her brother. He told her three weeks after they were married, that two shillings a week was enough to keep her. She had been a machinist with the Singer Company, and when she was working at Chester he wrote a letter to the manager asking him to stop her wages. Through his conduct she was obliged to leave the place, and became very ill—Defendant: Referring to that piece of meat, did 1 buy five or six pounds for you and me, and your mother bought a steak for the whole family ? Witness: No.—ln answer to further questions, defendant's wife stated -he had ill-treated her, on one occasion by striking her on the shoulder, and he was unable to use her arm for a fortnight afterwards.—Defendant, in reply to the Mayor, said he was a Warrington man, and was married at the Parish Church.—The Mayor: Did she pronounce all the words? Yes.—Did she promise to obey? Yes.—Honour? Yes.—And that she would do all she could for you? Yes, sir, but she hasn't done.—Defendant said he could tell that which would make their worships' blood run cold. (Laughter.)—The Mayor gave the defendant some advice, and said he had no doubt she would make a good wife if ho treated her properly. He was the stronger person and ought to lead and not drive her.—Defendant was ordered to contribute 4s. 10-I. per week towards his wife's maintenance.—Defendant said he was willing to keep his wife, and asked that the order should stand over until he had indicted three witnesses for perjury who had given evidence against him in a case brought by his wife at the County Court.—The Mayor said the order was made.

MISSIONARY MEETING AT ST. HELENS.

The annual missionary meeting, under the auspices of the St. Helms branch of the Wesleyan Foreign Missions, was held on Monday evening, in the Wesley Chapel, Corpora- tion-street. Mr. Henry Mathwin, BA., of Southport, occu- pied the chair, and there were also on the platform the Revs. J. R. Sawtell, of Stourbridge; J. Kilner, one of the General 1 Mission secretaries; J. A. B. Harry, W. G. Pascoe; Messrs. T. Cook and T. Brown. After devotional exercises by the Rev. W. G. Pascoe, 1 Mr. T. BROWN read the report, which said that, with the return of another anniversary, the committee wished to place before them a short statement of the operations of the society. The scope of its operations was now narrowed. The Canadian Conference had taken over all the missions in that • quarter of the globe, and the Australian Conference those in the islands of the Southern Seas-the scenes of so many mighty triumphs of tbe Soldiers of the Cross. Still there were central or principal stations, 483; chapels and other preaching places, 2,620; missionaries, assistant mis- sionaries, and supernumeraries, 519; other paid agents, 1,965; nnpsid agents, 8,678; full accredited church mem- bers, 92,527; on trial for church membership, 10,885; scholars, 94,439; printing establishments, 3. The report of the parent society last issued showed a numerical increase of membership in connection with the missions in Europe, Ceylon the Mysore, China, South Africa, Jamaica, Antigua, and the Bahamas; whilst in Wes- tern Africa and some of the West Indian Islands, there was a decrease, owing principally to the needed exercise of dis- cipline and attention to rule. There was, however, a net increase of 1,169 .nembers, with over 10,000 on trial. Look- ing at the missions as a whole, their working might be said to be not only satisfactory but encouraging. The • chief difficulty encountered by this society was the diminution of its ordinary receipts during the last two or three years. These had been much lower than the ordinary expenditure, and the committee had been compelled to enforce retrench- ments in various parts of the mission field. The committee fondly hoped that soon they might have a return of com- mercial prosperity, so that this and other societies might be enabled more vigorously and thoroughly to prosecute this important work. The report of the parent society for 1880 had not been issued, but they might possibly hear from the Rev. J. Kilner, one of the general secretaries, what the in- come had been, compared with the former year. The total ordinary income of the society for 1879 was £127,876 is 9d, whilst the expenditure amounted to £148,107 fig 10d. The Income of this auxiliary for the year 1880 had been: From collections, subscriptions, and boxes, £143 188 6d; juvenile association, £7B 17s 4d; juvenile offering, £6 3s 3d; total, £228 19s. id.; being an increase of £8 68. Id. on the pre- vious year. It was only right to notice that in this Cir- cuit they had been saved from a decrease by the zeal of their Sunday school scholars connected with their juvenile associations. The total amonbt collected by these for Home and Foreign Missions, was £l7B 14s. lid. If they added to that the amounts raised by Christmas cards and boxes held by scholars. they had thus raised for missionary purposes the noble sum of £193 4s. 4d. The contributions in this circuit during the past year had been as follows :-St. Helens, £77 18s. lid., an increase of £l5 10s. 3d.; Park-road, £l4 10s. 4d., decrease, £2 16s. 4-d.; Prescot, £26 9s. 11d., decrease, £2 28. 9d. ; Nutgrove, £l7 3s. 9d.' decrease, £2 18. 10d.• Whiston, £6 4s. Od., decrease, £2 10s. Bd.; Haydock, £l:6 16s Bd., increase, £3 6s. 7d; Sutton, £7 17s. 3d., Increase, £1 6s. 5d.; Burtonwood, £3 ss. 4d., decrease, £1 lee. Dd.; Earlestown, £42 19s. 101, increase, £2 18s. Od. ; Rainhill, £6 15s 7d., decrease £3 19s. 2d. ; Golborne, £5 12s. 5d., decrease, 12s. 6d. ; Vulcan, £.3 ss. Id., increase, 48. Bd. _ _ _

The Rev. J. Sawymt. addressed the meeting and gave a graphic account of twelve years missionary toil in South Africa. The Rev. J. KILNER one of the generAl mission secretaries gate a rigorous and lucid account of his visit to the various mission stations of South Africa, bristling with facts, and full of humour. He confessed that when he went out he had strong prejudices against the colonists, but hav- ing travelled through the whole of the Cape, the Orange River Free State, the Transvaal, Natal, having been the last to cross the river with his wife before the outbreak of hos- tilities in the Transvaal, and after a careful and minute enquiry he.rame back with totally changed views. He found that missions were being carefully worked without any extravagance whatever, and that out of £55,000 spent in those various localities, only £15,000 was supplied from the General Mission Fund, the rest they raised in the localities. A collection was taken and the meeting closed after the usual vote of thanks had been given.

BREAM OF Puomm CASE—In the Middlesex Sheriff's Court, in the case of Jeffreys v. Harrison, the plaintiff, Miss Alice Jeffreys, employed as an assistant in a confectioner's shop in Liverpool-road, London, sued the defendant, Mr. Harry Christopher Marshall Harrison, clerk, for recovery of damages for alleged breach of promise of marriage. The case was originally entered in one of the divisions of the High Court of Justice, but judgment having been allowed-to go by default, it wai remitted to the Sheriff'. Court for the purpose of assessing the compensation to which the plain- tiff was entitled. Mr. Henry Kisch, barrister, who appeared for the plaintiff, said his client was a young lady, highly educated, and of very prepossessing manners, and in the eatly part of 1878, when she was about seventeen years of age, she made the acquaintance of the defendant, who was now in his twenty-fourth year, at a party given by a mutual friend, and with the consent of their parents they were al- lowed to visit and walk out together, the defendant taking her to various places of entertainment. In February, 1878, he promised her marriage, assuring her that in addition to a liberal salary, at the office where he was employed, he ex- pected £5,000 on the death of an aunt, and a considerable share in legacies left by. other rich relatives. He wrote several letters to the plaintiff, in which he breathed the most tender sentiments of love and affection for the young lady, whom he styled "his duck," "his pet," "his darling,' and "his own beloved Ally." • The courtship lasted two years, and at the commencement of 1880 the defendant abruptly broke off the engagement without assigning any cause for it, and returned the young lady all her letters. In reply to Mr. Allingham, who appeared for the defendant, the plaintiff said he had made her several presents and nom- plained occasionally, that she bestowed undue attentioi, on other young men. She denied that there was any cause for his jealousy or complaint. - He visited her at her mother's I house in Jackson-road, Holloway, and she visited at his parents' residence in the Grove-road, whielf-VtatEclose by.— The jury found a verdict for the plaintiff, for £2O.

A claim of £lO was submitted by Mr. Ridgway, cab pro. proprietor, against the Corporation for injuries sustained to his horse, on Monday, March 21st, in Park-road, by rushiog in a heap of nightsoil, in conseqnence of there not being a lamp.near. Mr. Fleur said he had made inquiries, an I it appeared that one of the lamp glasoes got broken, and was placed on a window sill. The men stated that with the combined light of the lamp and the street lamps there was suite sum. dent light to enable the driver to keep clear of the nightsoil heap. The matter was referred to the Town Clerk to _take what action he thought proper.

THE MONTH'S MORTALITY. '

The MEDICAL- OFFICER reportedthat during the five weeks ending April 9th there had been five deaths from fever ; diarrheea, 1; scarlet fever, 0; diptheria, 0; small pox, 0; whooping cough, 0; other zymotics, 3; total zymotics, 10; all other causes, 105 ; total from all causes, 114. Rate of mortality. 2010. per thousand as compared with 16•80 in the corresponding month of last year. THE STATE OF THE BROOK. Dr. Menem, said that in samples taken by Inspector Williams from the usual places viz., Spray's Bridge, Bridge- water street, behind the timber yard, and Messrs. Lyon's bottle works he found all free of acid, but a sample from the drain of the Bridgewater works showed a weak acid of the strength of 25 grains to the gallon. In the samples of Hard. shaw brook taken by Inspector Houghton from the usual places there was a weak acid in those from the gas works yard. Last Thursday he took occasion to visit the Warrington New-road district with the inspec- tors, with a view to discover the source of the offensive smell that was ever found in that neighbourhood, particu- larly at the ventilator just beyond the railway bridge. As the atmosphere was tolerably clear, the condition of things was net so bad astil It was evident that evil arose from the drainage of old waste in Warrington Ohl and New- rose!. A ventilating shaft would'reduce this evil, greatly, placed near the railway bridge. There was acid of the strength of 470 grains to the gallon in sample from Atlas Court sewer, and acid 25 grains to the gallon in that taken at the new ventilator at Hardshaw Brook Bridge. There was a weak acid in the sample taken from the drain of the Globe Alkali Works, and also in those taken from the over- flow of the canal at Merton Bank Bridge. He had seen Mr. Superintendent Johnston,who had informed him that be gave due attention atperiods to the Sale of Food and Drugs Act. The Medical Officer added, respecting the drainage of old waste in Warrington Old and New-road, that the people who lived opposite were greatly annoyed, the clock's face was blistered, and the paint on the walls was discoloured. In his opinion a ventilating shaft would greatly relieve the evil, but would not cure it. Mr. HART said that when the brook was altered, and the Warrington New-road bridge reconstructed, as he thought they would be, the evil would be nearly done away with.

The Government andlire Liberal party do not oxpeot fully to meet the wishes of Mr. • Parnelland some of his assodates, but it is useful to underatandnxactly what the chief of the Leaguers does demand or desire. Parnell rejoices bectese the Bill does admitie,ets which he says are "practically the programme of the League; " it adMits "the existence of raek-reuting, eviction, and Isaidlord oppreasion,". and " the necessity for a: .i•ts,dioal change in the , law 'which will put it inlthe power 'of farmers to become owners of the land they till." But he •esaseiders "that the Bill provides in- adequate means rsr gaining the objects 'it aims at. Mr. Parnell stees some circumstances about the position of the small tenants in- Ireland which he fears, not, we 'dare say, without good reasons, may frustrate themretection the Bill is intended 'to afford them againet arbitrary eviction. There aro 320,000 holdings hi Ireland *valued under SS a year. Mr. Parnell .saya thatmany of these tenants would be important to learn 'how many), are 'la a bankrupt condition;" that "a very large proportion of them owe severel leer' '&rrears; of rent; 'and he feared the absence of any provision for taking into consideration the stet° of insolvency and poverty to which these people'have been reduced by the recent succession of bad 'seasons and continued exaction of . rack rents, would render the clause as to fixing of judicial rent entirely illusory:" The force of this illustration de- pende very- nitieh upon the propcittion of tenants who arein long arrears of rent. Five or ten per cent, of theyhole being in arrears might not create an insu- perable dillieutty, as fifty or seventy per cent. would. Then'Parliareent will want toqcnow if these arrears ' have for the most part been run up because the ten- ants could 'net pay, or because they have been insti- gated not to pay and fancied they could escape paying although they could pay. The Irish members Should ba prepared with paitioulars as to the general state of the farmers as to arrears,.and likewise with some practicable proposition for meeting eases of bona 'Me inability to pay up. The Government can- ' not possibly invite Parliament to blot out all out- standing arrears of rent at the date of the new Act coming -into force. What, then, would the Irish part3esizggest should be'done ? By all means let them ' try their hands at formulating some feasible new clamie-to protect tenants in arrears from being victim- ised brwholesale, andldeprived of all benefit from the Act when it is passed. Mr. Parnell's other principa complaint is that tenants under the Bill would in many eases derive little profit by the right of sale of their interest in the holding, because these sales wonid be often "nothing more than forced sales," and be greatly feared the sales of their tenant-right by the small tenante.would " amount to nothing more than the payment of their arrears of rent." Again, owe should like Mr. Parnell and his friends to show any righteous means by which Parliament may shield the humbler class .of tenants against sacrifices and ' hardships resulting solely from his 'own impoverished oondition. We fear that when all has been done that legislation can do-to make Irish tenant farmers secure arid prosperous, -there must be instances of tenanM going to the bad and having to leave their holdings 'penniless, simply because they have lost and mort- gaged all their interest. An Act for the abolition of bankruptcy, insolvency, and indigence throughout the United Kingdom would be a pleasant law for tens of thousands of the poorest of the Queen's subjects,' but we are not sanguine that we shall see such an Act 'passed in our, time. What may be done in the political visionary Utopia of the future we cannot attempt to rfreVISO.

There is something overwhelming ix the informa- tion reeeived to the effect that there him' been an earthquake in the island of Chio, ía the Levant, ',which has resukecl in the loss oi several thousand It was at first thought that the effect of the earthquake shocks had been exaggerated, but each day's news add to the ghastliness of the catastrophe. ultfirst it. was estimated that the number of persons •Itillettwas MOO, but the latest computation•puts the

number at 4,000. The awfulness of this colossal digester almost surpasses the power of the imagination to conceive. In -addition to the number actually killed there are hundreds of persons terribly maimed, end it itgaite probable that the full tale of Us:clogs of human life has not yet been told. No less than thirty towns and villages, which a little more than a week ago .were full of life a.nd activity, have been suddenly traugformed into a confused and ghastly heap of ruins. The terror-stricken people who have escaped •the•herrible doom.ef being buried alive are camped out in the open ,fields, mourning the loss of home, 'relatives, and friends, with their agony intensified to a fearful degree by an uncertain dread. ft is estimated .thaft,Bif4o of those who have escaped with their lives have .been injured, and that about 2,1}00 of them are not likely .to recover. Thus the pros- perous ..island of Chios, has been changed into a 'horrible • Golgotha. The record of the appalling calamity is unmitigated gloom, but some colours in the,dark canvass are darker than the rest. We are told that those encamped in the vicinity of the ruined towns-could hear for days after the havoc had been wrought the moans and cries of victims entombed in the ruins, whilst the onlookers were too mach paralysed by fear to attempt at a rescue. What can mesa in its piteous pathos the story of a -young mother whcabacame a raving maniac through listen- ing ttothe,raoans of her datling child buried heneath a heapeof .raina . from which no hand would dare to- rescue it .or.another poor creature who gave birth to a child when half buried &under the rains of her house from which she, but net the child, was saved? And whet can compare in horror with the sudden and complete .overthrew of the convent of Neamonti which, hailt ,ea the slope of a cliff, was swept bodily over a precipiceo taking all its in- mates, with one exeption, intc a fearful doom? , The homelesta,nd,heuseless peopls,no w encamped in j the open field( are in a sad 'plight, for they can do , nothing but wring their hands in the agony of despair.: The disturbances aro,not yet over, :as eight shocks ; -were felt on Tuesday. Whilst in the state of pare- lyais which the fear of ,the earthquake has plunged them into the inhafaitanta can make no .offort to re- store their shattered dwellings or re-build their ruined towns, and the misery from whish they are suffering will increase rather than dimini.sh. Their misery is also made greater .by the daily fear of the outbreak of a pestilence, which may seize e 43 many victims as the earthquake. The effluvium of corpses festering among the ruins of the towns and Tillages has become unbearable, and A may break out in a plague. It need scarcely be said that the unutter- able wretchedness of the poor Oblates cannot be re • lieved by their own hands, and it is the only bright Spot in this gloomy picture that relief to the suf- ferers is belng given with a generous hand, for years must elapse before the smiling face of the island is restored and the prosperity of its towns recovered. We know the horror it'd distress occasioned in Eng- land when a colliery accident destroys 200 or 800 lives, or when a railway accident claims 30 or 40 victims, hut these are about the limits of our disas- ters an the sudden destruction of an entire com- munity in the way we have described, is almost more than thc mind can comprehend. Nature has no more terrible ~gf_pcy of destruction than the earthquake, and hi- tory , rosords appalling instances of loss of

life effeeted by this means. The. Levant and the tiouth-East •of Europe have often been viaited by. such calamities. Eightettu years ago an earthquake at Rhodes destroyed many villages. Mitylene war. ' much injured four Vara later, and since then Smyrna I and ether towns have been partly destroyed by earthquakes. Otilr a few weeks ago the town of Agram, in Iltragary, experienced three or four earth- quake shocks, but this earthquake at Chio is one of the most destructive that has occurred for many years. The climate of the Eastern Mediterranean is often •envied by Englishmen, and when, as lately we; have been suffering from the prevalence of keen winds, it is probable that many have wished that this country possessed the soft :and mild: climate of southern countries, but the reports from Chios remind us that we have our compensation in the absence from:alexia of fearful catastrophes which .the victims are pow er- less to prevent. Timm is every probability that the important con- test in which the electors of West .Cheshire are now engaged will be fought out on strictly party lines. It appears that the two candidates now before the con- stituency are cousins, but holding widely different political opinions. Mr. Tellemache comes before the electors as an avowed Conservative, whe, limiting his observations principally to foreign affairs in the ad- dresses which he has op to the present delivered, argues that because the British Reapire extends "over millions of miles" and that "the sun never sets on it" we ought, for the present at any rate, to retain Candahar. He condemns the policy of the Govern- ment in making peace with the Boers, and does not agree with the way in which the Government have ruled Ireland. He objects to the extension of the county franchise to the agricultural labourers because he would not like to see the whole representation of the county "handed over to a body of men who, how- ever worthy and excellent they were, were not from, their bringing up and from their position as likely to' exercise a proper respeet for the responsibilities of voting as those who were at present on the register." Although the constituency he seeks to represent is; essentially an agricultural one, Mi. Tollemache has not yet told them4bether he will support Mr. Glad- stone's Land Bill or not—and this is suet an impor- tant question to the' Cheshire people that it ought not' to escape their attention. Mr. Tomkinson, on the other hand, has come forward as a Liberal ready to give his hearty support to the present Liberal Government, approves of their peaceful foreign policy, and is in favour of the abolition of the law of entail, and any measure calculated to cheapen and simplify the transfer of land. Mr. Tomkinsou is in fact a thorough !Liberal, who does not hesitate to empress himself in favour of "Peace, Retrenchment, and iRe - form," .and-reongnises " an immutable law of change and progress," and is such we heartily wish him success. The sympathetic) letter of approval from Mr. Gladstone read by littr. Tomkinson at Frodshain, on Thuisday, comet fail to be most encouraging to the Liberals of West Cheshire, and to stimulate them, if anything was needed to,do so, to work hard and well to secure the returtrof ;theircanclidate. We are pleased to notice that the Trader, when writing to Mr. Tomkinson, stated that when the discussion of the polity of the Governmentin the Transvaal takes place in the House he will adopt no apologetic tone. We heartily agree with him that it really was " &question of saving the country from sheer blood-guiltiness," and we hope the electors of West Cheshire will endorse that opinion by returning Ur. Toulkinson as their representative to the House of Commons.

I.O.G.T.—The District Executive of South-West Lancashire have selected Mr. William Roberts for recom- mendation to the Grand Lodge as Visiting Deputy for Warrington for the ensuing year. ELEMION OF WIDNES GDAUDIANB,—MIO returns 84 to this election were ,published on Tuesday mousing, and were as follows:—Messrs. W. Gerrard, 1,760; John Matthews, 1,628; T. Sadler, 1,342; Rev. Father Finegan, 1,312; David Wright, 980. The first-named three are elected. • IsTaLs3N-Brannr BAND OF HOPE, RUNCORN. —Mr. S. C. Beckett presided at the monthly meeting of this society, held on Monday night. The room was crowded. The pro- ceedings were of a very enjoyable character. Two songs given by Miss Worrell and Mr. J. Withington were much appreciated. Mr. J. McQuinn, who is leaving town for Australia, gave a farewell address during the evening.

ST. LUKE'S- CHAPEL, PERNINGTON'S-ROW.--On Wednes- day, a public tea meeting was held in the above Calvanistic Methodist Chapel. About 50 people sat down to tea, which was followed by a miscellaneous entertainment. Mr. James Wilson occupied the chair, .and in the course of the evening the Rev. J. D. Thomas, of Bethesda, addressed the meeting. A choir of children (under the leadership of Mr. G. Lacey) sang selections from "Songs of love and mercy," and several dialogues and recitations were given by various members of the choir.

AT THE RUNCORN POLICE COURT on Wednesday, Before C. Reynolds, Esq, Martin Towey was charged with having unlawfully wounded, in August last, three men, named Michael Bones, John Bones, and Michael Fee- ney.—Prisoner was one of four other men who set upon complainants, and seriously assaulted them. Prisoner left the country, and was arrested at Ballaghaderren, in Ireland. —Remanded.

BAND OF HOPE ENTESTAINMENT AT WIDNES.—.& public meeting in connection with the Milton Congrega- tional Sunday School Band Of Hope was held on Tuesday evening. The Rev. T. Peters (pastor) presided, and ad- dressed the parents and friends present. He said that the children would wield a moral influence in the circle in which they moved, and therefore he believed in training up children in the paths of sobriety. A lengthy programme of recitations, dialogues, and songs, &c., was then rendered by about 25 children, who acquitted themselves creditably. Mr. F. Travis ably acted as accompanist. •

- - - TEA PANTY AT RIINOORN..--A tea party in connec- tion with St. Luke's Congregational Mission Chapel, Pen- nington's row, Runcorn, was held -on Wednesday evening. About fifty persons sat down, and the tea was followed by a miscellaneous entertainment under the presidency of Mr. James Wilson. A number of selections from " Songs of Love and INlercy " were given by the scholars' choir. Reci- tations and dialogues were also included in the programme. During the evening the Rey. J. D. Thomas, pastor of Bethesda Church, briefly addressed the meeting. SEBAHOB OF SONG AT WIDNEELL-A SUCCOR/611 series of winter evening entertainments, which have been given under the auspices of the Mutual Improvement Class con- nected with the Zion Primitive Methodist Free Church, Oakland-street, Widnes, was terminated on Tuesday even- ing,•by the performance of a service of song, entitled," Her Benny." The story is illustrative of street life in Liver- pool. The musical portion consists of about 15 sacred seleetioes. These were well rendered by a choir -of 70 voices aod several instrumentalists, under the conductor- ship of Mr. Joseph Betney. The only solo in the service was' Love at Home," which was tastefully sang 'by Miss Bold. .The Rev. J. Billington, of Runcorn, acted as reader. There was a large attendance,' and the entertainment vas a thorough success. The profit on the entertainments is to be expended on the library of the Sunday school.

• AstitakiED Hann Pstocannutos.—At the-Chancery Court of Lancashire, on Saturday, before Vice-Chancellor Eris- towe, application was made by Mr. Hopkinson for the appointment of a receiver in the-matter of the estate of the late Thomas Taylor, of the firm cf Taylor, San, and Jack- son, Braz,nnose-streot, Manchester. rhe application was made on behalf of Helen Burrow, Emmeline Burrow, and Leonard Taylor Burrow, all infanta, through sames Edward Burrow, their father; the defendants being Isaac Platte Taylor and William Taylor, sons of the teatator, and Frances MaSilda Burrow, wife of James Edward Burrow.—Mr. Hop- kinson, in making the application, stated squat one of the defendants, Isaac Platts Taylor, had died during the present week. The testator's other son was the other executor under the will, but had not proved the will leave being re- served-to him to do so. The testator died in 1679; it was quite time, therefore, the requisite steps were taken to prove the will.—Mr. Maberly, who appeared for the defendant, William Taylor, opposed the application on the ground that it was totally unnecessary, and that the suit WRB vir natty a wrtking action. He stated that his client had applied for prebate, and was willing to net, and therefore the appoint- mentof a receiver was wholly unnecessary. He also read portions...at affidavits which complained that the proceedings in the matter had been harshly instituted, and set forth that the deceased, Isaac Platts Taylor, had been served with a writ during his confinement to bed by illness, the result being that it had so acted on his naturally nervous disposi- tion as to lead to the calamity s high occurred at Weaste on the previous Tuesday, when he was run OM by a railway train and killed.—The Vice-Chancellor said that under the circumstances he thought it was unnecessary to appoint a receiver; he would, however, direct that William Taylor should prove the will within three weeks and .ha ap- pointed interim receiver, giving such security as might be necessary.

MAILBIAGE OF Mass :NOWELL, OF RUNCORN. —On Thursday morning, Miss Martha Ellen Nowell, only dangh- ter of the Rev. J. Nowell, superintendent of the Runoorn Wesleyan Methodist circuit, was married to Mr. Willitm John Tyne, wholesale stationer, of Bacup. The interesting event took place in St. Paul's chapel, and, though the ',feather was not of a very propitious character, there was a fair attendance of friends. The bridesmaids were Miss Roberts, of Huddersfield ; Miss Brewer, and Miss Kate Brewer, both of London (nieces of the bride). The grooms- men werethe three brothers of Miss Newell, viz., Messrs. 'Joseph' B.Nowell, Charles H. Nowell, and Arthur T. Nowell. The" knot" was tied by the Rev. J. Nowell, the father of the:bride. Amongst those present were the Rev. Henry Valentine, Mr. Joha Simpson, Newton Davis, of Halton; Speakmao, and Mr. Timothy Shnister. Mr. G. S. liaalehurst presided at the organ, and played Schuman's Birthday March on the party entering the chapel, and Mendelssohn's Wedding March on their leaving. Shortly after the ceremony the medded :pair left Runcorn by train for the,Grange, near Windermere. Several leading friends of the congregatiorr, who bad be:n invited to attend the ceremony, were unable to be present owing to their absence from home for the Easterholidays. The bride has received about4o presents, including a cmsiderable number from friends in the town. We may state that the bride's dress was of Esterhazy silk, trimmed with rich brocaded velvet. The head dress consisted of orange blossom wreath and veil. The bridesmaids' dresses srere of ivory white cashmere, -trimmed with lace and ruby,aatin, white chip hats trimmed with ivory white feathers and lace, with ruby satin. Among the brides' presents were the following : Vessert case, cake basket, biscuit box, gold brooch, cake knife, loeicet and chain and bracelet, portrait Mr. and Mrs. Nowell, timepiece, dessert knives and forks, silver- mounted egg stand, silver-mounted salt sellers and spoons, silver-mounted sardine box, 2 butter coolers, custard stand, marmalade pot ad spade, honey pot, toast rack, flower vases, mirror in China clay, China card plate, flower basket, silver bracelet, picture, 2 illuminated texts framed and gold, 3 China ornaments, work box, seal skin bag, pin cushion, card case, slippere, black satin soft pillow, antimacassar to match.,and half-a-doxen antimacassars.:

WINWORD Locam BOARD ELECTION. The election of four meudeers for the four wards in Wineford has just taken place. In three of the wards there was no contest, and the gentlemen %iiho had been in were re-electrd. These were Mr. G. G.utt, land agent; Mr. Robert Stubbs, salt proprie- tor; Mr. John Stubbs, salt proprietor; for the respective wards:—Vale Royal, Wharton, and Gravel. The only con- test was for Swallow Ward, where Messrs. George Hamlet and Ralph Atherton contested, the former polling 223 and the latter 409 votes, and so gaining another seat in favour of non-compensation. KICKING AT GOLEORNE.-OR Th ursday, at ths Occasional Court-house, Warrington, James Sylver was brought up in custody, before Peter Stubs, Esq., charged with having violently assaulted Patrick Cowley, at Golborne, on the previous day. A dector's certificate was produced stating that complainant was not able to attend. Evidence was given showing that the parties were labourers, and that on the morning in question some altercation took place between them, whereupon the prisoner set upon the complainant and kicked him unmercifully, inflicting two large wounds on his forehead, and fracturing two of his ribs. Prisoner was remanded to the next Petty Sessions at, Newton, and admitted to bail.
Mr. F. H. Venn, of Warrington, on of Mr. Vent), Bridge-street, has been admitted and 'morn a nolieitor ef 010 supreme Court of Judicature.

Tim Urosnts BLTUG.—The interior of the building knout by this name has been neatly painted, and presents a very pleasant appearance.. The baths were opened for the first time this season on Saturday last, and there has been a good attendance during the week. ATTER:KED BURGLLRY AT RUNOORN.—Between Sat- urday night and Monday morning an attempt was made to enter the pledge office of Mr. James Lomax, pawnbroker, next door to the Examine). Office, Church-street, Runeor n A hole about nine inches long Was cut in the door near the lock, but it is probable that either the presence of a massive iron bar at the back of the door, or being disturbed by the Pollee, prevented the burglars from effecting their purpose. A MAN DROWNED AT VERTGEL—On Wednesday, two men, named William Manning and William Lambert, car- penters at the Weston, Chemical Works, were eagaged patting some rollers in a sewer which runs from the works to the Hier, when one of them was drowned. They entered the sewer I,:y a manhole with aladder and Lambert was the first to leave the sewer. When Manning reached the top of the ladder he fell back into the sewer, and there being about seven feet of water in it, he was drowned before he could be assisted. It is supposed that deceased fell backwards, owing to being affected with the bad air. • He was married, and about 38 years of age. On Tnuniday, an inqsest was held on the body and a verdiet of "Accidental death" Was re- turned.

GOOD FRIDO AT Rtrrmourr AND WraNns.—Thia day was a gloomy and depressing one owing to the weather being of a very unpropitious character. Despite of a drizzling rain, at the early part of the day, a considerable number of pleasure seekers left the district from the Widnes stations. Not a solitary train started from the Runcorn station on this day—an arrangement Which excited the supreme dis- gust of all travellers, The question twises of how long this antiquated method of compelling all the Runcorn people who wish to leave town on Sunday, or such holidays as Good Friday, tO walk to Widnes, before they can be accommo- dated is to continue? For a town of the position and pop; ulation of Runcorn to be placed in such a singular position, is most anomalous, and the arrangement strikes all strangers is a most singular and unreasonable one on the part of a great company who have a monopoly of the railway traffic. We feel sure that pertinacity in bringing this state of things before the notice of the company and their general manager as often as possible, must bear fruit in due season. DEATH Or MR. ROBERT BARROW, OF FARNWORTH.—AII our readers in this district will regret to hear that Mr. Robert Barrow, of Farnworth, expired on Saturday morning, at the age of 66 years, from paralysis. Deceased was born a,t Pres- cot, and Went to live at Widnes, when quite a young man. He was originally a watchmaker, and proved very fortunate in business. He was a popular gentleman with most people. Being gifted with considerable geniality of nature, and an ' open disposition, even when he made an enemy which was not very. often —he . very soon became reconciled. Mr. Barrow was well known as an overseer of the poor, and he had filled most of the public positions in the district. He had a keen eye for any extravagance on the part of the Local Board, whilst a member of that body, which be was on its first formation, and for many years afterwards. The death of deceased was referred to in sympathetic terms at the meeting of the Board on Tuesday, and a hearty vote of condolence passed to his widow. The funeral took place at the Farnworth Parish Church on Thursday, and was well attended.

THE REV. E. LLOYD JONES, OF LLANDUDNO, ON THOMAS CartrALE.—On Sunday, the Rev. E. Lloyd Jones preached the anniversary sermons in connectiorr with Camden Sunday School, at St. Paul's Wesleyan Methodist Chapel, Runcorn. The chapel was densely_ crowded at the evening service. In the. morning Mr. Jones took his text from the passage in Corinthians which speaks of St. Paul's thorn in the flesh, and the discourse might be called one upon the ministry of pain. In dwelling upon the messenger of Satan sent to buffet the Apostle, lest lie should be lifted up above measure, owing to the abundance of the revelations given unto him, the preacher said that a very high state of Chris- tian living was liable to develope vanity. It was even coin regard to worldly matters. Let them, for instance, take the case of two such prominent men as Thomas Carlyle and Ralph Waldo Emerson, the American Transcendentalist. Carlyle was probably the best old heathen who had ever lived since the time of Christ. Though, however, no doubt the Chelsea sage had a high sense of justice, he had not the 1 slightest particle of charity. LA them read the "Reminis- cences" of Carlyle, which ha l just been published, and Ile thought they would be led to the conclusion that though he had been in the school of Socrates and Plata, he had never been in the school of Christ. Carlyle had learnt heathen morality, but he had not learnt Christian morality. Carlyle had not patience; his wife had not to speak to him for a week, some times. Carlyle was like a mere hedgebog—full of prickles all over. In hiscase they bad a man whose un- doubted genius set him on a pinnacle. What did Carlyle say? That there were some 30,000,000 of people in Great Britain—mostly fools. Then there was Emerson, who re- marked that, on the whOle, men were splendid things to be ground up to be made guano of! Men like the two whose names he had mentioned, had been "exalted above measure" through "the abundance of revelations" given unto them. They were men to whom God bad given piercing insight; men of splendid attainments, whilst ordi- nary mortals were only men of one talent, and they looked down upon the puny, little creatures who had only one talent, and said they "Mostly fools !" /I service was also held in Camden schoolroom, in the afternoon, when a est- mon as preached by the Rev. Henry Valentine. Mr. G. S. Hazleburst presided at the piano. The total collections realised £45.

I was at Widnes the other day. Nice picturesque place;. beautiful scenery; no smoke or dirt, and as a `health resort -ought tdbe far better known than it is. St. Udine is 'very ;pretty, hntsot half such a nice place as .Widnee. To pass away a half hour which I had between then and train time, soless than-to shelter myself from a pretty incessant down- pour of rainier., I failed to Ind a good coffee howse I trotted into the bar cf a public-house, and saw thetwa placard which laeallicensethwictuallers might do worse than •cupy—" All spirits sold- bete," it said, "are mixed with .water." No doubt agood many tickets with these words thereon could be found in other public-houses, but this one contained a ' "last line," that, like the postcript, in a lady's, letter, was worth more than all the rest put together, for it read, "and prices charged atcordingly." . Travelling in a late train from Widnes to St. Helens the other evening, my companions were an odd mixture of speci- mens of the human family, and from these odd-characters some quaint jokes came that provoked much -amusement. Arriving at Clock Face Station, one of tho party-said as the train was being brought to a stand-still "litire's Clock Face." •" A nice name to give to a place" observed „another. -"Aye," said a third," and the rnmrniest go about it is that th' clock never goes." ".Oh, but it wur goohi last week," remarked a fourth, "for I seed it." "Ayer.: said the third speaker •"‘Well, I've bin past here mony a hundred times,ate I never; seed it gooin' yet." "Oh, but I seed it," said the fourth man, "for I seed th' fingers drop." "Now, wow "-chimed in a.fifthipassenger, "that'll not lo; draw it mild." "Hut I • did," said No.- 4, ILseed th' fingers drop." "Then some- botly.ud shoved 'em ;" observed No. 5, "thee bet they'd didn't drop thersels." This is the latest concerning Clock •Face-and its railway clock. Thefollowing curious letter was found the other,day in a barrelat American apples:—" Chester, New Hampshire, U.S.AiiFebrnarr 4th, 1881. To the readers.—Just for. Gm I.thoughtl would write this note to tell you these apples were raised in Chester. New Hampsillre, U. b. They .were taken from .our,place two miles to the depot, And-sold for one dollar per barrel. I can only wonder who may read -this: whether it be in America or Europe this may go to. -some palace or perhaps some place far inferior. They may be destroyed by fire or water, or perhaps stolen. -However, -seeingT have wondered-450 much, I would like to have syou write me. lam a young,cchool teacher, age about 40. I live .in the -.country. Wanttoer." 1 tear that the -writer would stand but a poor chance of•eiataining the posit:on he desires if he should coma over bore, for the number of candidates are always in excess of •the. demand. "Owing to the blockade caused by the heavy fall of snow the Nebraska Pioneer ra,:.l out of white paper, and this week Indulges in brown, red, and green colours." I wonder what the ,public would aty ,if you, Mr. Editor, should not Leone your journal for a ,week owing to the cold weather, ,or if you followed the example of your Nebraska contemporary and issued it brown, red, or ,green colours for a week Instead on whiteamper ?

The Easter hallidays arc again upon us and the condition of,the general trade of the country has not }ln uc h improved einem we last celekrated the advent of Good Friday. The spurt which the iron and chemical trades experienced about the time when the ex-Premier, in a glowingoration, pointed to the buoyancy of chemicals as evidence of the return of prosperity, has died away, and all branches of trade are still under;that cloud of depression which has prevailed for about six rears. The late east winds are credited veith an evil effect .npos many branches of industry, especially those con- 1 11 cerned inlarnishing clothing; but unless there is a great upheaving in other departments of business enterprise it is' to be fearedthat when the fierce sorth-easters have ceased to blow in all their virulence, the lack of activity will still he felt, even by those who have clung to the hope that a warm and sunny season will disperse the gloom. At present a great many pamons are to be found in the streets workless; those engaged in the building trades complain that "every- thing is very fiat'; with few exceptions shopkeepers in all grades hive grievances in abundance; and the numerous dwellings to let is the town testify that there is much moving to and fro on the part of the people in quest of places where there is" something doing." It is sometimes com- forting to have a peg os which to hang a grievance. If there is any just cause for condemning the weather for a Perpetuation of business inactivity, then we may lay the flattering unction to our souls that the fierce blasting and blighting north-casters have ceased to whistle through key- holes and crevices and among chimney pots, and that the gentle rani has begun to fall bringing warmth and freshness in its traio to the just and unjust, FLACCUS.

div.head: NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN.
div.p: NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN.
ST.TETERIS CHURCH, NEWTON.—On Sunday evening the last of Lenten sermons, by selected ministers, was preached in this church 'by the Rev. H. Siddall, vicar of St. Thomas's, Ashton-in-Makerfield.

TM; VACCINATION PROSECUTIONS AT NEWTON.—These persons who were brought on at the Petty Sessions on Saturday charged with not complying wiih the Vaccination Act, refused to pay the fines imposed, intocourt. Mr. White, the magistrates clerk, however, issued distraint warrants, and the money was immediately paid in. CONG REOLTIONAL SERMONS AT NEWTON.—The annual sermons in aid of the Sunday school were preached in the Crow-lane Congregational Church, on Sunday last, by the Rev. H. Dainton, of Wigan. Both services were well attended, and collections were made amounting to a little over £l6. During the afternoon a service of song, entitled " Daniel," was exceedingly well rendered by the members of the Band of Hope attached to this well-conducted Sunday school. The connective readings were given by the Rev. Mr. Dainton.

THE NEWTON CONSERTATITE Curd—On Monday even- ing &general meeting of the Workingmenla Conservative Club for the Newton polling district was held in the Town Hall, Newton-le-Willows. The president, Mr. J. H. Birley, occupied the chair. The committee intimated that they had secured eligible premises in Earle-street. Mr. Sander- son, butcher, was the present occupier, but arrangements had been made set that the premises could be quickly handed over to the committee, and the club started at once. The report of the committee was adopted. A number of members were enrolled, and the question of furnishing the premises was discussed and ultimately arranged. GOOD TEMPLARS' QUARTERLY TiA PARTY.—OR Satur- day, the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars held their usual quarterly tea party, when there was only a moderate attendance, owing to disturbing elements connected with the election of Guardians. After tea an entertainment was held, when there was a very good attendance. Mr. Geo. Clarke presided. Songs were given by Bros. T. Mayor, of Newton, H. Warburton, A. Allison, John Taylor, and Sister M. ; appropriate readings were given by Bros. Geo. Warburton, jun., E. Newman, and JO9. Edmonds ; and a Lan- cashire reading by Bro. John Warburton. Recitations were given by Bro. John Warburton and Sister M. E. Barrett and dialogues by Sisters G. Harriman and S. A. Taylor; also by Bros. T. Wakefield and Richard Critchley. A very pleasant evening was much enjoyed. On Monday evening, at the usual weekly session of the lodge, the programme being "Experience meeting," a number of the members gave interesting details of their practical experience as Good Templars and total abstainers.

SUDDEN DEATH OF P.C. MCGIIINESS, OF NEWTON.— On Friday afternoon, P.C. McGuiness (49) after leaving some of the Guardians voting papers in Church-street was seen to fall suddenly. He was at once helped to a cottage opposite the church, and placed on a sofa. A messenger ran off for Dr. Watkins, but when that gentleman arrived a few minutes afterwards life was extinct. An inquest was held on the body on Monday by Mr. Driflield, and it was stated that deceased had not been very well since the Wigan election and the collier's strike and tumult at Leigh, where he re- ceived some rough usage. A . verdict of "Died by the visitation of God " was returned. Deceased was very much respected in the district, and his death is ranch to be re- gretted, as he leaves an aged mother to mourn his loss. His remains were interred at the Roman Catholic Chapel on Tuesday afternoon. About 80 persons were present, includ- ing 30 policemen from the surrounding district, who appeared in full uniform and white gloves. The cortege had an imposing appearance. The Rev. Father Lennox, after reading the usual funeral service, delivered an address, in the course of which he referred to the many good qualities possessed by their departed friend. He had been strictly faithful to his duties, kind, thoughtful, and attentive to his aged mother, and by upright conduct had gained the good will and esteem of his friends and neighbours, whilst chil- dren regarded him as an especial favourite. LORD DERBY AND THE LANCASHIRE LIBERALS.-It is stated that Lord Derby has accepted the vice presidency of the South-East Lancashire Liberal Association, and has pro- mised an annual subscription of £lOO to its funds. Tint Impßxsolororr or THE REV. S. F. GUIDEN. The rule obt lined last Friday by Mr. Charles, Q.C., for a writ of habeas corpus to bring up the Rev. S. F. Green from Lancaster Castle was argued on Tuesday before the Lords , Justices of Appeal. After hearing the arguments Lotd Justice hews' without calling for a reply, decided that the rule must be discharged on all the points raised. The other Judges Concurred, and the' rule was discharged.

FOOT AND MOITTII DISEASE IN CIIESHME.—The Chief Constable of Cheshire has received reports to the effect that dui ing the past week 49 cattle had been attacked by foot and mouth disease. Of the number originally suffering from the disease there had recovered during the week 54, and 45 at I present remain under treatment. The disease has appeared on two fresh farms during the week in the neighbourhoods of liaslington and Talkington, and five farms are at present infected.

SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.— In reply to the resolntion of the council of this association, passed at its meeting held on the 31st March, at the Reform Club, Liverpool, and forwarded to Mr. Gladstone, the secre- tary has received the following acknowledgment:—" 10, Downing-street, Whitehall, April 11, 1881. Sir,—l am directed by Mr. Gladstone to beg you to accept, and to transmit to the South-West Lancashire Liberal Association, his thanks for the gratifying resolution which you were good enough to forward on the 31st ult.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, J. A. GODLEY.—George H. Powell, Esq. " BETSY " AT THE PRINCE OF WALES THEATRE WAR_ RINCTON.—Mr. H. S. Deere's company has during the week had possession of the boards at this popular place of amuse- ment, with the new comedy " lietsY." The piecewhich has had a run of a large number of night's in London is, despite the pruning and recasting to which it has been subjected at the hands of the English adapter, essentially French in respect to its leading and fundamental incidents. Never- theless the comedy is interesting and vivacious. The dialogue is sparkling and witty, the interest of the audience never for a single moment being permitted to flag. At the hands of the dramatis persona of Mr. DacreN company the various characters of the play receive a satisfactory and spirited impersonation, and where the whole company is thus excellent it is unnecessary to signalise. The piece has drawn a well filled house each evening, notwithstanding the counter attractions in the town. Mr. Sheridan announces several standard companies in his prospective arrangements.

div.head: I ELECTIoN OF GUARDIAN.S.
div.p: I ELECTIoN OF GUARDIAN.S.
WARRINGTON UNION.

WARRINGTox.—The voting papers which had been dc- livered in connection with the election of guardians for the township of Warrington were collected on Saturday last, and the work of counting the votes was commenced on Monday. The contest has again been a political one, and both parties have exerted themselves to secure the return of their candidates, several handbills having been issued giving the reasons why the various candidates should receive sup- port. The result of the contest was made known on Wednes- day by the returning officer (Mr. J. C. Sutton) immediately on the rising of the old Board, and was as follows : Name. Occupation. Totes: J. Harrison (0) 'high bailiff C. H. Cartwright (L) glass bottle manufacturer... 3,008 W. Woods • (0) jeweller A. Mackie (C) ...... newspaper pmprietor 2,669 G. Thackburst (L) jeweller W. 11. Jeans (0) solidtor H. Heaton (0) eoettraetor . 2,364- .7. Greening (L) wire manufacturer 2,337 J Tongs (L). Congregational minister ... 2,281 E. C. E. Carleton (0) ..eleak in holy orders.. J Smethurst (0) ironfounder W. Longshaw (L) chemical manufacturer 2,150 J. Brown (L) gentleman 2,150 Y. Bolton (0) glass manufaoturer 2,132 TI Pilkington (0) gentleman S. W. Marsh (0) cabinet maker 2,097 J. Marsh (L) gentleman 2,093 G. Wallington J. Toft i F. Laughlin (L) jeweller ................. . ......... 1,890 The representatives for Warrington will therefore consist of the ten first-named gentlemen—four Liberals and six Conservatives. We understand that, about 7,300 voting 'papers were sent out, and about 1,400 of these were returned as not having been delivered. The fact that so many papers were undelivered—a large proportion of which longed to the Liberals—accounts in some measure for the result of this election. There is abundance of evidence, too, that the Conservatives have not been at all scrupulous as to the means they have employed in order to secure the return of as many of their candidates as possible on the Board of Guardians, as w; are informed that no tactics have been considered too dishonourable for them to adopt this year in order to obtain the desired end. That this has been so is patent from the manner in which the voting papers in whole streets and portions of streets have been filled up, and it is rather a significant fact that voting papers have been re- turned duly filled up for men who have ly.en out of the town for about twelve months, and who have now no interest in the town, but whose names happened to be on the rate book. When these facts came to the knowledge of the Liberals they were considered to be amply sufficient to jus- tify the demand for a searching inquiry into the whole proceedings, but as the election is only for a period of twelve montbg, and a good deal of ill-feeling has already been engendered, we scarcely thin 4 it Will be worth while to go in for an enquiry. We would, however, remind our Conser- vative friends that there is a limit to this sort of thing, and that it will be well for them to he mere cautious as to their conduct in future elections. Notwithstanding these ques- tionable proceedings on the part of the Con- servatives, it is also pateht that a large number of Li Iseral s split votes with the Conservatives, and this contributed to the success of the Conservative candidates. Some years ago this election was first made a party question by the Conservatives, since which time the Liberals have always had, a majority of the Warrington Guardians, and now the first time that a large number of Liberals have disregarded party politics in this election the result is that the Conservatives have a majority. Such a course is much to be depreciated, and we hope that those Liberals who failed in their allegance to their party in this election, and thus contributed in a large measure to the re- turn of a majority of Consarvatives will by this time have seen the folly of their actions and have resolved to be faith- ful to Liberal principles in the future, instead of playing into the hands of the retrogressionists. NEWSON.—The contest in this township has resulted in the re-election of three of • the retiring members, and there is little doubt that the whole of the guardians from Newton on the old Board would have been re-elected had not Mr. Joseph Pennington decided to withdraw on the ground of ill health. It is to be regretted that Mr. Pennington has bees compelled to take this course, as the practical advice he gave, and the sound judgment he brought to bear upon all subjects which came before the Board, made him a valuable kcquisition. The efforts of the anti-vaccinators to secure the election of their candidates were not very suc- cessful, as only one of their nominees—Mr. Hall—was amongst the fortunate four.
