div.head: LATEST TELEGRAMS, ea.
div.p: LATEST TELEGRAMS, ea.

THE EVACUATION OF CANDAHAR. ' BOMBAY, April 13.—The evacuation of Candahar by the British troops will commence to-day, and be completed by the 22nd inst. The British occupation of Charnel), Kern, Abdulla, Gulisten, Karez, Kushdil, and Kakilla will, how. ever, continue for the present, as a measure of protection for A rumour has reached here that Ayoub Khan has fled to Meshed.

div.head: "STORMY PETREL" IN NEW YORK.
div.p: THE "STORMY PETREL" IN NEW YORK.

Nsw YORK, April I3.—The Irish National Land League held a mass meeting last night at the Cooper Institute in this city, to expresl sympathy with the struggle of the Melt for land reform and self-government, and to protest against the imprisonment of American subjects in Ireland without trial. Among the speakers was Mr. Stephen J. Meany.

div.head: LORD BEACONSFIELD'S ILLNESS.
div.p: LORD BEACONSFIELD'S ILLNESS.

Lord Beaconsfield's condition again gave rise to much uneasiness on Wednesday. Towards evening his lordship took a favourable turn, and at night the doctors were able to report a slight increase in the strength of the patient. At the same timel. this intelligence can only be received as comparatively reassuring, an 4 as indicating that his lord- ship has rallied from the severe attack of Tuesday night.

There was a marked improvement on 'Thursday in the condition of Lord Beaconsfield. The doctors believe that recovery has set in, the change to warm weather having greatly aided the medical treifitient. The Queen has caused it to be made known that she has b?en greatly pleased by the pablic solicitude manifested in the condition of the noble earl.

div.head: GREEK QUESTION.
div.p: THE GREEK QUESTION.

A correspondent at Athens telegraphs that the position which the Government has taken up in its reply to the col- lective Note—namely, tbat of the champion of the Hal- lenes whom the Powers pi opab^ to leave in the power of the Turks—will enaare for Greece the moral, if not material, aid of all the discontented populations in the Ottoman Empire. A Vienna correspondent telegraphs that the Greuk Govern- ment demands that the Porte shall grant autonomy to Epirus.

div.head: EARTHQUAKE AT CHIOS.
div.p: THE EARTHQUAKE AT CHIOS.

PER, Thursday Afternoon.—The latest: telegrams state that the subterranean forces are still active, and that re.. markable changes are taking place in the elevation of the land. Soundings taken between Scios and Tchesme show a rapid decrease in the depth of the channel, whilst on the western shore the land is sinking, as shown by the increas- ing depth of the channel. Great alarm prevails. CHIOS, Tuesday.—The shock of earthquake yesterday has caused considerable destruction. On the mainland opposite this island nearly 100 people have been killed or wounded. Many villages on the island, which, cmnparatively speak- ing, escaped in the first shocks, were destroyed yesterday, and the misery has greatly increased.
THE IRISH LAND BILL. THE LIBERAL FEDERATION AND THE BILL.

At a meeting of the general committee of the National Liberal Federation at Birmingham, on Wednesday, to con- sider the Irish Land Bill, it a-as unanimously resolved, "That this meeting regards the Ell for Irish l'lnd law re- form, introduced into the.llonse of Commons on behalf of her Majesty's Government, as a loyal fulfilment of the pledges of the leaders of the Liberal party at the last election as conceived in the true interests of the Irish people, and earnestly calculated to promote the peace and prosperity of the sister country ; and that this committee trusts that whatever amendments the public discussion of the bill may show to be advisable the federated associations will do their utmost by public resolutions and by petitious to sus- tain the Government in the determination avowed by Mr. Gladstone to use ;every legitimate means to carry the bill through Parliament." It was agreed to recommend that in calculating the value of the tenant's holding regard should be had to any sum paid by the tenant within the past two years beyond what the court shall deem a fair rent, and that any tenant evicted since the Ist August, 1880, should be en- titled to compensation.

div.head: SIR HARCOURT JOHNSTONE, M.P.
div.p: SIR HARCOURT JOHNSTONE, M.P.

Speaking at a Liberal meeting at Scarborough, Sir Har— court Johnstone said, as a large landowner, he did not think the Irish Land Bill went far enough in giving security of tenure. He advocated twenty-one years' leases at fixed rent instead of fifteen, and had written to that effect to Mr Gladstone.

MEETING OF THE LAND LAW REFORM LEAGUE. A crowded meeting, under the auspices of the Land Law Reform League, was held on Wednesday, at the Hall of Science, London, Mr. Bradlaugh presiding. The Chairman said the great objection to the Land Bill was its complexity, but many of its provisions tended towards beneficent and useful legislation.—The following resolution, propr.sed by Mrs. Besant, and seconded by Dr. Aveling, wee carried : " That this meeting declares its general approval of the Irish Lind Bill, and urges the Government to carry it without admitting of any amendments that would weaken its remedial power, and rather to enlarge than narrow the clauses dealing with peasant proprietary."

THE ALLEGED PLOT TO KILL MR. GLADSTONE. NEW YORK, April 12.—The trustee of the Fenian fund at New York declares that the report of a plan to kil Mr. Gladstone is baseless, and that such an act would do no good.

Pork, in consequence of the advancing cable quotations. is held more firmly. but the demand is only moderately active. Bacon has sold better this week, but exports are resuming their operations sparingly ; still the home demand is better. Hams are very dull. Shoulders are less depressed. Lard is again dearer Is 6d per cwt., and the market closes very firm. The cheese market is very firm, and the transactions more extensive than for some time past. Medium and ordinary butter has changed hands freely this week _

THE LAND QUESTION. Sir,—l have not time, nor do I feel disposed to follow Lynx" into subjects wide of this question. The point I laded from WA'S " H. W.'3" assertion that all landowners are robbers, Ac., and I do not moan to enter into controversy other matters into which your correspondents ramble. thank you for inserting my letters, and hereby end the scribbling on my part.—Yeurs,lc., J.

------- Sir,—The late Richard Cobden is his last speech said "It I were five and twenty or thirty, instead of, unhappily, twice that number of years, I would take Adam Smith in hand—l would not go beyond him—l would have no politics in it= and I would have a league for free trade in land, just as we had a league for free trade in corn, and if it were taken up, as it must be taken up to succeed, not as a political, revolu- tionary, Radical notion, but on politico-economic grounds, the agitation would be cumin to succeed, if you can apply free trade to land. The men who do it would have done for England probably more than we have been able to do by making free trade in corn." Now, Sir, whilst stating the land laws of this country, it must be noticed that mines are private property, and belong by common law to the owner of the surface. There is no reason on earth why this should be. No man made the mines or improved them, and they , ought to be, as they are in every other country in Europe, the property of the State. On the continent, any man who discovers or desires to search for mines, makes his .bargain with the authorities and pays his dues to the public purse, making also compensation to the owner of the surface, for any damage he may do. On what principle of justice should all the mines under Cannock Chase (about 25,000 acres) become the property of four or five gentlemen, and why should Parliament sanction it? It is simply because the Government of this country has been and is carried on by and for the benefit of the landosvners, and publii rights and interests have been utterly ignored. "The earth is the Lord's and the fulness thereof." No doubt, and the landlords per- haps understand it to mean.. the lords of the manor, at least they act upon that view of it. We have already seen that the effect- of primogeniture settlement and entail has been to I confine the whole of the land to a comparatively few persons. Let us glance briefly at one or two places on the continent. Whilst our land laws are substantially those of the dark ages, all other European States e Since 1790, more or less emancipated themselves from the evils of the feudal lair, and with the happiest results, although prior to the French Revolution of 1879, most of the land in Europe was governed like ours, by the principles of feudal law. The French demolished it, and passed the. famous code Napoleon, mmich provides for the equal distribution of the property of the deceased among his children without regard to age or sex. Provision is made by law for the wife, and there are of course other enactments which it is not necessary here to refer to. Wherever the French carried their arms they carried their law, and it quickly became rooted in Belgium, Holland, and other neighbouring countries. After Waterloo, the despots of Europe sought tla reverse all this, and desired to return back again to the feudal laws. But the people had tasted the benefit of the change, and protested so strongly that their rulers were forced to give way, awl leave the famous code unaltered. The effect of this law has proved both a boon and a blessing to the country, and it can be shown that the small landowers in France are a very wealthy people. The National Debt of that country is £750,000,000, and is held by 4,380,933 persons, giving an average of £l7l to each holder. In England the National Debt is £725,000,000, and held according to the latest return by about 300,000 persons, or an average of £2,616 to each holder. We may judge from this contrast how the distri- bution of land affects the distribution of money. It also shows that the small landowners in France have a large amount of surplus wealth. If further proof is necessary, let us look back on the Franco-Prussian war. We saw France desolated by hostile armies, and for two years endured the horrors of both foreign and civil war. That war cost her 371 millions peunds sterling. Ihe world thought she was ruined, but she has astonished the world, and paid every farthing, and, what is more, seems no worse for it. Let me ask your name- less correspondent could England perform the feat? In Prussia, land, except certain properties called knights' estates, descends equally to the children. The population of the state is 25-i millions, and nearly five millions possess landed property, of whom 1,092,060 own less than 3± acres each. In Switzerland, on the death of the owner, his land descends equally to his children. The population is 2,665,000, and it is said that nearly two millions are land- owners. In Austria, in 1848, the feudal system was com- pletely abolished without, it seems much regard to the legal rights of the lords. Land now descends to all children I equally. Russia, is 1561, emancipated her serfs and abolished feudal law, and a vast quantity of land was awarded to the serfs. There land now descends equally to the sons, daughters claiming one-fourteenth, and widows one-seventh. In Greece, real property on the death of the owner is equally divided among the children, the owner having power to devise the share of one child. In Sweden, out of a popula- tion of four millions, there are 290,000 landowners, and a large majority of them cultivating their own land. Real property descends to children equally, and cannot now be entailed. In Norway the law is the same, and in 1821 that happy and educated country abolished all titles of nobility. In Spain, land descends equally to children, the owner bay- ing power to devise one-fifth only. In Turit...." land descends to all children equally, without regard to age or sex, or of primogeniture. The evidence that land is far more pro- ductive in the hands of small proprietors than under occupation by large tenant farmers, is of an over- whelming character. Common sense tells us it must be so. We pay annually over one hundred million pounds to I foreign countries for agricultural produce; and a consider- able portion of this could be saved to us if our land could be cultivated as it ought to be, and the advantages to our home trade would be correspondingly great. Now, which state is best? Which is the most promising for the future well- being of society? The state which has spread and is spreading over the continent of Europe? the distribution of land into small estates of working proprietors, or that which exists now in its full integrity and vigour in Great Britain only—the aggregation of land into the hands of a compara- tively small body of great landowners and large farmers ? There is no question more important, for during the last DO yea rs we have not even stood still; we have retrograded; whilst a mighty and beneficent change has taken place in every other European nation. The decree has gone forth to educate the working classes. Let education be accompanied by an im- proved social condition to those who have to walk in a humble sphere of life. Give them a stake in society, and we shall soon reach that happy state that is so greatly to be desired.—Yours, !cc., JOHN SLIUFFLEBOTHAM.

- _ BURGESS. Sir,—The most surprising portion of your correepondent J.'s letter is where he informs your readers that he, a Con- servative, has written a pamphlet on the land question. Really, I must confess to a great desire to see what must be a most unique production, and, if the butterman has not used them all, I hope I may ultimately possess a copy, as I have rather a failing towards literary curiosities. our correspondent differs not one iota from the rest of Conserva- tives. However clear an argument may be stated, however it may be illustrated, still the Conservative intellect has not sufficient perceptive power to receive it, and consequently I am afraid that Councillor Burgess's advice, as quoted above, will fail in its object. Allow me to confess, Mr. Editor, that "J." is at least in one particular right—in saying that I have no land. "'Tis true, pity 'tis 'tis true." "J." lays down the following :—" On land and buildings are thrown and based nearly all rating and taxation." I ac- knowledge this is quite true, but not all the truth, to get at the truth is all that is required, and with this object I suggest that your correspondent answer the fol- lowing questions, no difficult task for one who has written a pamphet on the subject. A landlord lets a farm, the tenant of which, through skilfull and careful attention, and also through the liberal use of capital raises the farm in value, the landlord, taking advantage of this, increases the rent. I wont say hew much. Does the landlord pay an increased land tax? Again, the Bewsey Forge, Whitecross Mills, and Itylands Bros.'s works, all stand upon ground that a very few years since brought to the owner an insignificant rental. What the rental is now I know not, nor care, but the differ- ence between then and now must be enormous. Will "J." be kind enough to say what difference the increased rental has been made in the land tax? I don't wish to be abused ten account of ignorance, I desire to remedy that defect, and if "J." will answer the questions put he will render a great service to all who take an interest in this subject. It will not be sufficient to tell us that the land tax, as originally fixed, has been superseded by a tax laid upon land and houses, or that it is levied on the beneficial proprietor, as distinguished from the mere tenant at rack rent. Thi,ft,it is well known, means noth- ing less than that the tenant or producer pays all taxes, and the landlord gets off scot free. At the time of the Restora- tion, the revenue of the greatest estates in the kingdom was only about £20,000. What are they now? Scarcely one umongst them but what have multiplied from three to ten times in value. J. suggests that some practical idea be . involved. Well, in my first letter, I Made a suggestion, why didn't he deal with it instead of talking about wasting time? I would give the Government full power to buy up all the land, the same to be worked by a competent staff of commirsioners. Then, instead of selfish landlords with no aim but that of seeking their own ease and comfort, we should have the land managed according to the most ap- proved farming methods. Farmers, so long as they did their duty, would have a feeling of security they have not at present. Their children would look with confidence to the future. Instead of importing breadstuffs, we should almost be in a position to export. Of course, lam quite aware that this is Utopian; but somehow it seems to be the life's work of "low Radicals --as Councillor Bur- gess teros them—to bring forward thee notions; and the work of Conservatives to make thorn law, as witness the Corn Laws Repeal and Household Suffrage; and, of course, they may ultimately make this Utopian idea possible. Unless I put forward some argument worth dealing with, or cures to defend the law of primogeniture, of which he seems proud, I must consider him too good a Conservative to understand the land question.—Yours, H.W.

, THE HOUSE OF LORDS. Sir,—Lord Beaconsfield addressing tie Rouge of Lords on the Irish Dieturbance Bill, said " The Bill Is a reconnais- sance in force to see what is the feelin.4. of Parliament and the peopleht England upon the preseht tenure of land in England and upon the constitutional position of the landed

interest in our system of Government." The bill then before, the House had for its object the pacification of Ireland, the meting out of a small portion of justice to those of her Ma § subjects who are unfortunately surrounded by the melancholy ocean.". This measure, put forward by re- sponsible ministers was vetoed by a body of men who chiefly owe their position to the accident of birth ; men who have done little or nothing in return for the privileges they enjoy. Lord LanSdONVIIC, speaking in the House of Lords on the Disturbance Bill, said it "appealed to the sordid instincts of the people. " The Irish people might well have hurled back in their lotclsbiPs teeth, that it was the sordid instincts of a luxurious class of irresponsible legislators who were robbing them of their birthright. They rejected a measure—and rushed from all corners of the earth to do it—which the Cabinet of the United Kingdom believed to be necessary, and they rejected it with most shameless selfishness. Lord Derby said it was not a wise thing for those interested in a suit to act as their oven judges. Now, sir, what does our ex- perience teach us? That no bill, has yet gone through the House of Lords without being so mutilated that it became almost a dead letter, that whenever it ha's been possible they have rejected, aye, almost with scorn, bills of the greatest importance. Parliamentary reform, municipal reform, re- ligious liberty, nay every possible measure that progressive statesmen and the best brains of the country could devise have been obstructed by them, and still we have canting hypocrites who turn up the white of their eyes and " thank Goa we have still a House of Lords." The lords voted for retaining Candahar. What has been the result? Nil. The House of Commons still goes on with its work. Mr. Forster speaks out plainly, and Lord Carnarvon wails out: in a very impotent fashion, and fails, in a most ignominous way, to tell us what good to the nation the " sordid " body to which he belongs are. Now, sir, my object in writing on this question is to urge upon the people of Warrington -to be up and doing, and that at once. There is a line in one of our popular songs that says "I will stand by my friend." Mr. Gladstone is our friend. He has declared that "Just is to be our guide." Let us act out what we sing. Lefus have a great demonstration, so that Mr. MeMinnies when he goes back to his duties may say the pea:,,e of War- rington, to a man, are in favour of justice. Our Csoqerva- tive friends are bound to support the demonstration, or else prove themselves traitors to their country. One of them. speaking in your local parliament, expressed a hope that it would be the last bill that Ireland would require at the hands of Mr. Gladstone on the land question. To attain this wish, and to enable our representative to feel not only the strength that is behind him, but the unity of public opinion, I call upon the leaders of our political parties to demon- strate, and not to cease until Mr. Gladstone's Land Bill becomes law.—Yours, CLIFFORD DIX.

THE VACCINATION PROSECUTIONS AT EARLESTOWN. Sir,—Anent the prosecutions of anti-vaccinators at Earles- town, Newton-le-Willows, I have received the enclosed letter (copy) from Mr. Hume Rothery. Trusting you wiii kindly publish same in this week's issue of your valuable paper, I a sir, yours, &C., A. FORSTER. 19:m Regent -street, Earleston. (coPr.) The Pines, Cheltenham, April 12th, 1811—'fr. A. Forster.— Dear Sir,-1 have read your letter in which you state that five of your townsmen besides yourself have been punished as criminals, having been fined 205. with 9s. costs in each case, b?- cause as dutiful parents you cannot allow your healthy and harmless children to be diseased. Though the treatment you six peaceable men have received is wholly unjust and unchris- tian. it is nevertheless legal; and so long as the wicked vaccina- tion law is permitted to exist, magistrates, largely wanting in human thought and feeling, will not hesitate to harshly administer it. Men can be hired to flay their fellowmel, to hang their fellowmen, to shoot and stab their fellowmen by the score. In such an unchristimised state of society, when it is taught, though falsely taught, from thousands of pulpits every Sunday that a good life has nothing to de with man's ' salvation, how can you wonder that a few country magistrates. I who probably have never given the question an hour's serious thought, should inflict upon you the highest passible fine because you most properly will not allow an ignorant doctor to endanger your children's health and lives? You have the hostour to suffer for a good cause, Thank God for this privilege. Bear your infliction like men. All your really good neighbours will readily help you, for you are fi.4llting not only for yourselves, but for them, and for the country. I hope your magistrates will be made to feel that in fining you, and thus outraging your feelings, they have fined and similarly outraged every good man and woman in your neighbourhood. But you must not stop at this point. Nearly the whole country is to blame for the disgraeeMl legislation which oppresses us. At election times the people are insane. They sell themselves in very many instances. They prefer party to principle. They send to Parliament ignorant ar d tyrannical men who are sure to do mischief. Now, you and all lovers of equal political freedom and justice irk your locality should band yourselves together in the resolution, which you ought to publish, that in future you will vigorously oppose every candidate fm- Parliament who will not openly pledge I himself to labour for the entike repeal of the Vaccination Acts. By so doing, you will make yourselves a power for good in the country, and really assist in the effort that has long been made to destroy the despotism under which you, like many others. are suffering.—With best w'shes f kr your Levue, I am yours very truly, WILLIAM RU:VIE ROTHERY, President of the N.A.C.V. League.

THE DEPRESSION IN "TILE TRADE." Sir,—l am sure all your readers must feel some little sympathy for those people who have had to suffer through depressed trade. We have had during the past few years an exceptionally bad time. All branches of industry have been affected, and many business firms had to be sus- pended, being altogether unable to withstand the pressure put upon them. Thousands of our fellow creatures were literally wanting the necessaries of life (apart from pauper- ism), and soup kitchens, with various other institutions for the distribution of food and clothing, were established in different towns and villages throughout the country in order to relieve the distress which was so severe and wide- spread. But amid all this suffering there was one branch that did not seem to share this distress to any degree; at any rate, whilst other trades were paralysed anl languishing, the "trade of trades" itself does not seem to have experi- enced a much-diminished income up to the year 1879. Perhaps you will pardon me repeating a few of the figures from a late issue of The Examiner, but which, I venture to say, would be overlooked by many of your readers. Ac- 1 cording to the eminent statistician, Mr. William Hoyle, of Bury, our national drink bill for the year 1360 reached £86,897,683, a sum exceeding the total revenue of Great Britain last year. Year by year, with little exception, it con- tinued to rise and grow up to the year 1876. whin the amount reached the enormous sum of £147,288,760; in 1877 it fell to £142,009,231; and in 1878 it rose again to £142,188,900; but during the two following years it has experienced a great reduction. In 1879 the total amount was £128,143,863, and last year the expenditure was £122,279 275, thus showing a fall in 1879 of £14,045,037 on the previous year, and in 1880 a further reduction of £5,864,588. May it continue to fall. lam sure all right- minded and sensible people will experience a decree of satisfaction at this reduction in the expenditure on inCoxicat- ing liquors in our own country. Of course, it would be premature at present to say that this reduction is of a permanent character, ard that we may fairly consider the tide of intemperance in our land is at last stemmed; it may not be so, but let us hope that it is. It may be as the Times suggests, that it has been mainly caused by the slightly improved habits of the people of this country, and brought about by the recent distressed period, and that with better times may come a reaction when our drink bill will again conmence to rise. But the Times goes so far as to say that 1 in all probability by the year 1900 our drink bill will reach , the sum of £250,000,000. But this I entirely disagree I with, for I feel certain that, nothwithstanding the enormous power wielded by the beer interests, the great influence of the numerous temperance societies and Christian churches throughout the country, if rightly used, is powerful enough to take this Bacchanalian monarch and hurl him from his elevated position. The present state of public opinion on this question clearly indicates that if this tide of evil accruing to us from the iniquitous liquor traffic has not already been stemmed, the time is not , far distant , when this most desirable period will have been reached. 1 ' find, sir, that those in this neighbourhood have been ex- periencing something of this diminished income to the trade, for according to our "eminent townsman," Mr. Win- stanley, there is not a public-house in Newton that is pay- ing. So far, so good. I cannot say I feel sorry for them, as I certainly should, and so would your readers, if it was any other branch of business. The fall of the drink traffic 1 means the rise of the people, socially, morally, and spiritually; and lam sure we should rejoice at its continued ] decreasing income. If it is paying so badly, I would recom- mend soma of them to leave the business, and try some other more honourable; say, a cocoa house. I should think the people of Newton, in their so greatly-improved habits, would be able to support one; at any rate, it might be tried. I charge nothing for my advice. Mr. Winstanley very kindly suggests that the magis- trates of Newton ought long ago to have removed some of them to Earlestown, but, Mr. Editor, they seem to have been paying well enough up to a short time since, and so they did not need removing. And again, sir, I know for 2..1 fact that the publicans of Earlestown are no better off in respect to doing business than their unfortunate brethren of ] the good old Conservative town of Newton. In conclusion, , sir, I should like to suggest that before our licensing! authorities in Newton district either remove to or grant licenses for Earlestown that they in some way or other try to find out the feelings of the ratepayers on the question, as to Whether they may require more facilities for drinking or not. I expect if the magistrates are not careful in granting new licenses, the publicans already in the neigbourhoo.l will demand compensation for any loss of trade that may ensue. Who knows ?—Yours respectfully, LOCAL OrtION. Earlestown, April 12, 1881.

FASOIRES AND Trnms.—As the potato-blight helped to bring about the repeal of the Corn Laws, so the spread of agricultural distress seems likely to help the cause of Dis- establishment. The agricultural mind is evidently much excited on the subjEct of tithes, and is looking at it in quite new lights. At a meeting of the East Suffolk Chamber of Agricultare it was first resolved—" That in any Bill for the alteration of the tithe averages, it'shall be provided that the tithe shall be paid by the landowner." Then It was pro- posed—" Tint no legislation upon the tithe questieri will be deemed satisfactory by this Chamber which does not seek to remove a portion of the burden of the tithe from the land.' To that an amendment was moved—" That the tithe reiDt. charge ought, on the expiration of life interests, to be op plied to national purposes, and especially to the relief <, new local burdens, which have been dispror ortionately place( on the occupiers of land.". And this strong amendment ves carried by 25 to 15, although two clergymen and sever': laymen warmly opposed it.—Liberator.

ACTION AGAINST THE WARRINGTON CORPORATION. On Friday, before Mr. Vice. Chancellor Fos-Bristowe, at the Chancery Court of Lancashire, Mr. Hopkinson made an application on behalf of Mr. Jeans, of Winwick•street, War- rington, solicitor, for an injunction to restrain the Corpora- tion from closing two houses belonging to him, and situate at St. Mary's-street, Warrington, as being unfit for human habitation; and also for damages against the Corporation and Dr. Gornall, the medical officer of health. Mr. Hopkinson stated that on the sth inst. plaintiff received a notice from the Town Clerk stating that the Medical Officer of Health for the borough had certified that certain dwelling-houses belonging to plaintiff were abso- lutely injurious to health; and the plaintiff was given notice that he was to attend a meeting of the Nuisance Com- mittee on the 13tait April, to show cause why he should not alter the property so as to make it fit for human habitation. Mr. Hopkinson said, was that the Co:- Tp ohrea ti o plaintiff's h a case, oposver to go on in the manner they were doing in proposing to make an order of this sort. The evidence which he had to adduce on the part of the plaintiff amounted to the man who built the property, and who would state that at the time they were built the houses were approved by the officer of the Corporation appointed to look after such matters, and he had also the evidence of the architect, showing that the defects in the houses were en- tirely due to bad weather. The Vice-Chancellor : But in the meantime the houses may fall and kill someone. Mr. Hopkinson : It islnot a case of pulling down property. There is no im:nediate risk to the Corporation, because the plaintiff is only commanded to attend a meeting. The Vice-Chancellor : But this an application for an in- junction against the Corporation declaring that these two , houses are unfit for habitation. Mr. Hopkinson: Yes, that is so. The Vice-Chancellor: And are not the Corporation the best and absolute judges of that? Mr. Hopkinson: We take it that this is a purely arbitrary proceeding, and tho evidenee goes further than that. The Vice-Chancellor : Well, Mr. Hopkins, I do no care for the evidence. Just now I should like to be satisfied as to the Act of Parliament. You are going to ask me ex parte to restrain the Corporation from doing something as to the necessity of which they are the best judges according to my present impression, I do not say, mind you, that it is a right impression or that it is a wrong one, but which under the impression I have at present as to the law—the Corporation are themselves the absolute judges upon. I think lam right in that, but one ought not to speak of these Acts of Parliament merely from impression. You know the authority must rest somewhere. Mr. Hopkinson : In this case I am not acquainted with all the private Acts the Corporation of Warrington may have; but as far as this case goes the plaintiff's solicitor informs me that there is no special act giving this power. The Vice-Chancellor: Well, I must say, Mr. Hopkinson, that I do not like to hear this application ex parte, especially as there is not any immediate pressure as to time. Mr. Hopkinson: They might go on to something else. The Vice-Chancellor: It is only for a week. Is there any reason why you should not give the Corporation notice to-morrow morning that you are going to make the applica- tion? Mr. Hopkinson : I will be satisfied if your Honour will give me special leave. The Vice-Chancellor: I will give you special leave to serve them with notice to-morrow morning, and then lean thevPi Ultimately, hear whit they have to say on the matter; and in the mean- time I should be glad if you will go through the Acts of Parliament on the matter, whatever they are, because evidence in a case of this sort is not a,f much value. The the case was adjourned until Monday real question is, whether the Corporation have or have not morning.

On Monday the motion came before the Vice Chancellor when Mr. Hopkinson, instructed by Messrs. Jeans and Morgan, of Manchester, appeared for the plaintiff, and Messrs. Botch and Sutton, instructed by the Town Clerk, for the Corporation. Mr. Hopkinson, after explaining the ground of action, said that the plaintiff on the 4th April, 1881, received a notice from the Corporation of Warrington to the effect that the Medical Authority of the Urban Sanitary district of the Borough of Warrington had certified that the buildings at 19 and 21, St. Mary's-street, were unfit for habitation, and the notice went on as follows:—" Wherefore take notice, you are required to attend a meeting of the Sanitary Committee to he held on the 13th April, at 7 o'clock in the evening, at the Town Hall, to show cause why such houses or buildings, or part of such buildings, should not be condemned as unfit for human habitation." So that the question, said Mr. Hopkinson, would narrow itself into a question of law : Had the Corporation power or not to make an order which would virtually deprive the plaintiff of his property ? There was an affidavit bv an architect and a builder. The Vice-Chancellor: Is Mr. Jeans the freeholder ? Mr. Hopkinson: It is a long lease of 999 years. The evi- dence in general goes to this, we have first the evidence of the architect, who says at the time of the erection of the houses he submitted plans to the committee which were I approved in 1873. The Vice-Chancellor: For new houses to be then built ? , Mr. Hopkinson : Yes, sir. ' The Vice-Chancellor: Do you mean to say that new 1 houses built in 1873 are proposed now to be shut up? He said Mr. Jeans was simply called upon to appear and show cause why the buildings should not be condemned as unfit I for human habitation, and they did not intend to shut them up if cause was shown. The Vice-Chancellor: It is a terrible thing for a man's property. Mr. flotch : It will be still worse for the public for this house to stand up and endanger the lives of the people. They have been certified as buildings unfit far human habitation. The tenants swore they are unfit. We are a public body applying the law. 1 :Mr. Hopkinson: I am perfectly willing to go before a legal tribunal to settle the matter. But my clients are not willing to have it judged by persons who are prosecuting parties. I 'The Vice-Chancellor: You must give me the whole of the 1 facts. It is important for a Corporation not to have its powers limited, but on the other hand it is important for the inhabitants that these powers should never be exceeded. therefore I must decide it. Mr. Botch said that before they could go into the facts under sec Con 264 a month's notice must be given. Mr. Jeans was only called upon to show cause. There was no imme- diate danger. The Vice-Chancellor: It is the destruction of a man's property. . Mr. Botch: My friend has mis-stated that all we have done- is to serve a notice to show cause. The Vice-Chancellor : Why his house should not be pulled down? Mr. Botch: No, only why it should not be condemned. He has plenty of time to go before the Local Board, who are a public body. We merely call upon him to show cause why these two houses should not be declared unfit for human habitation. Supposing he appeared and the order was made, the Local Board have no power whatever to pull his house down or interfere with it. The only penalty that-applies to anybody who stays in the house is that he is liable to be taken before the magistrates and fined. The Vice-Chancellor : That is a serious question. Mr,. Botch asked that the prelitninary objection should be over-ruled, as he desired the matter should be fought out on its merits. He said there was a bye-law about the prohibition of the habitation 61 houses unfit tor that purpose, which gave tle, s 0 e,l,time Boardtpoorwdeerr. on its being made unfit for habitation to r Mr. Hopkinson said that if the property was condemned it would be sufficient to rein the selling value of the house. How, he asked, could a man let or sell it after it had been said no one could use it? It was a serious matter that that right should be taken away without the slightest oppartunity of going before a court of justice. It it was, a question of mere &triages it would not matter whether it was done on one day or the next, but. in the matter of on injunction it was different. The Vice-Chancellor ! You say it is the same as pulling down ? Mr. Hopkinson : Practically. It would be condemned finally. The Vice-Chancellor: Supposing I gave you the.injunc- tion, what tribunal would eventually settle it? Mr. Hopkinson: I think the magistrates would have to, decide. It would than go from the mcgistrates possibly to. the Queen's Bench. The Vice-Chancellor : The difficulty is this. As far as I can see, the Corporation has the duty thrown on it of acting under the bye-laws, which are conclusive as far as my jurisdiction is concerned. Mr. Hopkinson: No, sir; we say that the bye-law is ultra vives and to an unreasonabia bye-law; we say that it is not merely unreasonable in itaelf and contrary to the ordinary rule of common law, but also contrary to-the Act. Mr. Hopkinson then proceeded to read the affidavit of Robt. Curran, architect, who said that he himself took the plot 0 land in 1873, and in the same year contemplated building upon it. Ile accordingly submitted plans for two semi-detached houses to the Local Board, which were ap- proved, and the Borough Surveyor directed the surveyor to issue a certificate of approval. The Douses 19 and 21, St. Mary-street, were constructed in accordance with those plans, excepting in some slight modifications which oc- curred to him whilst they were in the course 0 erection, and at the completion they were satisfactory. In 1875 the houses were purchased by the plaintiff for £l,OOO. The last three months bad been very severe, and had exercised A prejudicial influence on all classes of property. Mr. William Owen in his affidavit said he was an architect, and had been instructed to inspect the house of Mr. McCollum, where he found the walls damp and thin considering their .otposed position. though the condition of the weather at chat time was not such as to admit of the work being done. The houses at times of floods were liable to be flooded. Mr. Hopkinson said that if an order to close the houses was

made it must prejudice the future letting of the houses, and would constitute an entire loss. There could be no reason for alleging that they were unfit for habitation except from the damp walls. The plaintiff in his affidavit said he pur- chased the houses, and had since spent a considerable amount of money on them. They were let at £3O and £35 a year. Mr. Hopkinson remarked that there was a slight diminution of the houses, but as the architect had said that was not the proper time to make the repairs he postponed it, and if the Corporation had been reasonable nothing more would have been beard of it. The Vice-Chancellor: hat do the tenants say? Mr. Rotch : The tenants come forward and swear that they are unfit for habitation. Mr. Hopkinson: One of the tenants has a lease, and he wishes to remove. (Laughter.) The plaintiff's affidavit also showed that the two houses were held for a long term of years. In consequence of a letter he had received from Mr. McCollum he had instructed Mr. Owen to inspect the house, and he reported that the walls were damp. He believed the action was caused by ill-feeling on the part of the medical officer. Mr. Rotch : I must ask your Honour to read these para- graphs not as evidence, but to have them struck out of the affidavit. It is monstrous that charges of this kind should be brought into the affidavit, it is a charge of gross miscon- duct against the Local Board, and I must ask your Honour to show your feeling by making the plaintiff pay the costs, whatever be the result of the action. It is monstrous that the costs should be piled up in this manner by making irrevalent charges. Mr. Hopkinson: It will show that between Mr. Jeans and the public officials—this is a town where pablic feeling runs very high—and we say that this is not a tribunal which will give us a fair trial; it shows that this Sanitary Authority is not a body which will give Mr. Jeans a fair trial, because ha is opposed to it. Mr. Rotch : It is a mosrimproper suggestion. The Vice-Chancellor: I think you should never introduce that kind of feeling into affidavits. I can't assume that a corporate body will not do its duty. The only point is whether they, having given yen notice, you have sufficient power to resist that notice, and 'whether something should not be done to give time to investigate the facts. Mr. Rotch : Your Honour has not heard all the evidence. The Vice-Chancellor: No, but I assume the case to be one of an ordinary description. If you go before the Justices and prove the case you get an order that unless certain re- pairs are made the house or houses shall not be inhabited. As soon, however, as the preparations are made, the order falls through. Surely that is the case here. Mr. Rotch : But this is a public body, Sir, and whatever the rule in this instance may be it will govern many other cases. It is therefore a very important matter. The course the Corporation have adopted is in 99 cases out of 100 by far the most convenient course to pursue. They summon before them the owner of certain property which has been reported upon, and draw his attention to the nuisance. He replies that he is aware of it, and undertakes to abate it within a rea3ooable period of time, such as the Corporation, are always ready to allow him. You will thus see there is a great difference between this simple method and having recourse to legal proceedings, which must of course end in an addition to the borough rates. But when we recollect that there are some scores of hundreds of these cases it will be at once seen what an enormous saving there is by this simple method in comparison with the cost of legal pro-

ceedings. The Vice-Chancellor: All this hrises out of the question whether you shall read certain very objectionable passages in certain affidavits. Mr. Hopkinson : It was merely to save the time of the Court that I proposed to take that course. Mr. Hop- kinson then proceeded to read the affidavit of the plaintiff, in which he stated that a gross abuse of power had been exercised by the local sanitary authorities and the medical officer of health in taking the steps they had done, and that the plaintiff could not go before the authority with a reasonable chance of a fair hearing. Mr. Rotch next read the affidavits of Mr. McCollum, draper, 21, St. Mary-street, Latchford: of Mr. Spinks, sur- geon, his medical attendant ; Mr. R. Norman, inspector of nuisances; and the borough surveyor, each of whom had seen and examined the property in question, and declared it without hesitation to be decidedly unfit for human habi- tation. The affidavit of Mr. Gornall, the medical officer of health, entirely denied that he had ever been actuated by any feeling whatever in the report he had made condemn- ing the property. Mr. Hopkinson said that the question which the Court had to decide was not as to the condition of the property in question, but as to whether the Corporation was the proper tribunal to try the matter. He contended that it was not, and that the Act of Parliament never for a moment contem- plated that it should be. But it was not only outside the in- tention of the Legislature that such should be the case, it was directly contrary to the laws ef England that any man should be the judge in his own case. That, however was what would happen if the Corporation were to constitute themselves the tribunal, and decide upon the question in which they were directly interested. A. lengthy argument took place as to the legality of the authority's bye-laws, Mr. Hopkinson contending that while they were ntitled to Make reasonable bye-laws, they were not entitled to make unreasonable bye-laws. The Vice-Chancellor : The Act of Parliament says the authority may make bye-laws to prohibit the use of houses unfit for habitation, and, in fact, do the very thing which you say is unreasonable; and several decisions go to this, that where it is a question of doing a thing for the public good may means must. Mr. Hopkinson said his objection was to bye-law Lumber 30, which certified that the local authority, taking the power on the information of the medical officer, surveyor, or two medical practitioners, required the owners of property alleged to be unfit for habitation to attend a meeting of the Council. The Vice-Chancellor : The bye-law to my mind is not unreasonable. This was a bye-law passed in every instance of this kind. It exists all over England. These things were settled in the most careful way, and these matters are really settled by the Government in pursuance of ti ese Acts. Mr. Rotch : Exactly what to2k place here, Sir. The Vice-Chancellor, in giving judgment, said: I need not trouble you, Mr. Rotel]. I have heard Mr. Hopkinson at full length in this case, and I do not mean to say it is not an important one, but it would be crippling the powers given by Act of Parliament in a terrible way if I were to accede to Mr. Hopkinson's view of it. Before Igo into the wording of the Act of Parliament, or a reference to it, I can- not but express my regret at the way in which the plaintiff Las launched his evidence, and the particular passages in one portion of his affidavit which were read to me. lam very strongly of opinion that that class of evidence should not be brought before the court in the loose and indefi- nite way it is.here, where it is, in fact, an abusive accusation agahast a public body. It is laid down over and over again that the court must, in dealing with public bodies, assume that they are doing that which Parliament gives them power to do in a fair and reasonable and proper manner,and as far as I am able to see from the evidence here, there is nothing in any way justifying these abusive paragraphs in his affidavit, and I very much regret that they are to be found in it. Apart from that, the real question, and the substantial ques- tion between the parties is whether in the case of such an assumedi bad building (which I assume to be the case here for themoment, belore going into the detailed evidence) an urban sanitary authority has not imposed upon it by Parlia- ment the duty, and has not given to it the power to do the very thing which has been done in this case. Now, in the first place,' think, it is perfectly clear that in this Act of Parliament the different parts, as they are called, of the Ant are not intended to narrow the effect and force of each other, but they are independent for a great many pur- poses, and they are additional for other purposes or for pos- sibly the same purposes within the purview of th 3 Act, and, therefore, lam not at all impressed with the idea that because the 91st and these other sections to which reference hasbeen made, Ore a right to go to the magistrates for a par- ticular purpose,. that, therefore, the 156th and 157th and other olauses are net to be acted upon. On the contrary, I think they are M be acted upon in the fullest way, arid that the Urban Authority in the proper way may give effect to them, and I think it is irm3oesible when you deal with the Act of Parliament, to find words more express than what what are used hare:—" Every urban authority may make bye-laws withmespect to the following matters -:ater alia, the closing of buildings or. parts of buildinge- unfit for human habitation, and to prohibition of their use, for such habitation." Then the Act gives a number of details as to what must be done to make the bye-laws perfect ,i and when Caese different requirements which are laid down are com- plied with the bye-laws are complete and effective, subject always et eourse to that statement in the Innd section which says that no bye-law shall be of any effect if repug- nto say aleeve effective.ry str cat o th doubteto i tv town to the law of England or to the provisions of this Act, but byseltetwteor were made 'should be 200 yards wide, or if a bye-law said that if a per- son dol not comply with a particular order he should have his hand cut off, or any other thing which would reduce the bye-law to an absurdity, then it would be repugnant, but where the bye-law is really only to do that aakich is to give effect to the duty which is thrown upon the Corporation,, or the Urbax Au- 'therity, by the Act, the bye-law, when properly passed by the due authority becomes, and is, effective. Now, it it also I thiek a matter that one may take judicial notice of, that the bye-laws in the case are generally framed on express bye- laws sent by the office itself in London. I do not mean to say that it goes t. prove they are not. after 'all, bye-laws, but still it goes to show that thess bye-laws are carefully considered ; and the bye-law that M. Retch read out to me, appeared to me to be almost in words the bye-law which is issued by the office which has to do with the public health. Therefore, apart from any express effect to be given to it is I that way, it o a reasonable bye-law, and I confess it seems to me a very reasonable course to be adopted in a case of this kind. That brings me to the consideration of what is the evidence. Now, as I said before, lam sorry that the plaintiff went into the luestion about his case not being prc- perly considered, but the evidence here is simply overwhelm- ing. We have evidence that I cannot pass over, that the walls are only nine inches thick, and the foundations are on almost sludge. Mr. Norman says that there is no proper drainage in the cellars a the houses, the consequence being that the ground forming the site of the cellars is saturated with water emitting an offensive stench, and that the drains of the houses aro connected with a ditch v.Uch runs behind the house. There is all that evidence, and the evidence of Mr. Spinks, the doctor, as also of Mr. Gornall, who is also a medical mac and I think the evidence, as far as I can juege of it, is neither exaggerated not excessive in any way, trat it shows at far as I am able to form

an opinion upon it, that ,t a, yew come to by the local authority or the Urban anal 10. is quite correct thus far, that it calls on the plaintiff. show_ cause why an order should not be made. Ip,is not a peremptory order, but it is a notice to call on him lo show cause why the Act of , Par- liament should not be-entered, and after' having heard Mr. Hopkinson in full, X really cannot coma to the conclusion that there was any necessity for his application. When the matter comes before the tribunal which under the Act of Parliament has a right to decide this question, I cannot see why there should not be full and ample discussion, and why proper arrangements should not be made. If the plaintiff, Mr. Jeans, will within it certain time properly, -reasonably, and fairly, to the satisfaction of the district surveyor or who- ever is the person to. judge of , it; put this property into a proper state of 'repair, I cannt4 understand why any harm whatever should accrue to him. But be that as it may, lam clearly of opinion that there is no proper. ground here to make any order on this, motion, and I must refuse the motion with costa. _ Mr. Roteb : I may say, we always have intended, and we do intend still, to give • the plaintiff qvery opportunity of making his property habitable. The Vice-Chaacellor : If the plaintiff will apply for that purpose, I should be content to take these passages out of his affidavit, but at present this matter may not stop here. Mr. Botch: Practically this matter has been decided now, and I suggest that we should turn this motion by consent into a motion for judgment, and take an order dismissing the action with costs.- - The Vice-Chancellor: Turn this into the hearing of the action. . Mr. Hopkinson: I think that is a perfectly reasonable

course. The Vice-Chancellor: Set it downpro forma. Mr. Hopkinson : This will not be taken as a consent order. Mr. Botch: No. The Vice-Chancellor: I never knew a case where the Public Health Acts came in question where any consent was ever given. Ido not mean to say for a moment that if this matter were heard at the hearing I should not have gone more into the authorities; and if, therefore, this matter is carried elsewhere, I think the Court of Appeal should know that my judgment is only given on motion. Mr. Hopkinson: On that point I was prepared with a vast mass of authoilties to furnish to your Honour, and I should have quoted them; but I think my point wail Apedially under the Act of Parliament, and I did not think it was fair to your Honour to devote a long time in quoting authorities upon it. The Vice-Chancellor: I have only given judgment on an interlocutory application. The parties may choose to turn that into the bearing of the action. That I have nothing to do with. If it saves them expense I shall be glad. Mr. Hopkinson: It would be a reasonable course. The Vice-Chancellor: I am only speaking for myself. I say, if I had thought that this was to be the bearing of the action, I should probably have gone a little more into the authorities than I have done. Mr. Rotch : If it is carried elsewhere the Court of Appeal shall know fairly, Sir, that this was merely an interlocutory application, and decided as such. The Vice-Chancellor: Just so. There is a case which makes a Mb difficulty in that, Chambers v. The Midland Banking Company, where a particular point was not argued fully in the court below, and the parties were very much blamed in the Court of Appeal because they had not argued it fully in the court below, and the Appeal Court said, "It is aot a fair proceeding to bring a matter before us which was not argued fully in the court below." Mr. Hopkinson : There may be authorities cited which have not been cited to-day, but Ido not know that the point could be taken in a different way. The Vice-Chancellor: You must do as you like about it. My judgment is only given on an interlocutory application. Set this down as the hearing of the action, and dismiss the action with costs.

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND.

Mr. Parnell was at Cork, on Sunday. He congatulated a large assembly which he addressed on the magnificent pro- gress which the Irish cause was making, and said that if the organisation of the people was kept up they would after a year or two gain free land and afterwards the right to make their own laws. THE IRISH Arms AcT.—Arrangements are being rapidly made by the authorities for carrying into effect the provi- sions of the Arms Act. A circular has been issued to the constabulary, signed by the Inspector-General, containing instructions as to the manner in which arms are to be demanded and surrendered, and ibe means by which those from whom arms are taken are to receive compensation. The constabulary will furthef be supplied with a series of books containing registers of the arms surrendered, the stations at which the surrenders are made, and books of label receipts. The in- structions are detailed and elaborate. A Tralee telegram reports a sate of 16 head of cattle, seized for rent from a farmer named John Kellisher, of Knockbrack, at the suit of. the-Earl of Kenmore. Over 70 policemen surreunded the cattle and kept the crowd off with fixed bayonets. Eighty men of the 48th and 104th Regi- ments were also present. - Mr. Harrington, president of the Tralee Land League, bought the cattle for the owner for

£O3. THE BOYTON CASE.—The Irish World (New York) calls upon the trustc,es of the Skirmishing-• Fund to give an ac- count of moneys in their possession, now amounting to $90,000. It prints letters from several Congressmen remark- able for their subserviency to Irish voters. In regard to the Boyton case, they, of course, denounce the arrest as an act of tyranny, calling for government interference. Secretary Blaine is represented as saying to the correspondent of the Irish World that the matter is receiving his serious atten- tion, and that the State Department will perform its whole duty promptly. I have high official authority for the state- ment that the Government entertain doubts as to Boyton's citizenship. He has a passport 18 yeare old, and the name in it is not the same as is present name. He has been in business in Len4on many years, and his citizenship is pro- bably mythical. The Government will take no action until it has fully investigated his claim to Americanyrotection.

LIVERPOOL AND WARRINGTON POSTAL FACILITIES. A• deputation from the Iron and General Metal Trades Section of the Liverpool Chamber of Commerce had an interview on Monday with Mr. J. D. Rich, liostmaster, in regard to the insufficient postal arrangements between Liverpool and Warrington and South Wales. A report drawn up- by a sub-committee of th 3 section, and subse- quently adopted by the committee and submitted to Mr. Rich, sets forth that, although Warrington is so near Liver- pool, it is almost impossible to obtain an answer to letters on the same day,---9-45 from Liverpool is too early for general convenience, and it was suggested by the sub committee that the hour be made 11-15 (the same as the Manchester mail), and that arrangements be made at Warrington for an afternoon despatch, to enable letters posted by 11-15 to be swered, and'replies received in Liverpool before five o'clock. There are sir despatches during the day to Manchester, but only two to Warrington. With reference to South Wales, the report observes'that 3-15 lean inconvenient hour for the despatch of the early mail, as two to three is the principal 'Charge honr, It was accordingly suggested that four would be more convenient, or that it might be arranged fir the 5-30 mail to be delivered in South Wales early next morning. As letters posted in South Wales on the previous evening do not reach Liverpool until 12-30 p.m., it was sug- gested that these mails should be accelerated. In the course of the interview the- deputation referred to the magniieent series of trains which run every hour between Liverpool and Warrington, so that there could be no difficulty in accepting the proposal submitted. The deputation also urged upon the postmaster the desirability of making some arrangement by which the mails intended for Liverpool from Canada-and the United States should be brought into Liverpool direct by the mail steamers, instead of being landed at either Queenstown or L'ondonderry. This, we understand, is.a • subiect the Chamber of Commerce intends taking up.. Mr. ' Rich replied that there were serious difficulties in the way, but that the subject should have the earnest consideration ' of the department.

On Monday, an inquest was held at Blackforel'Bridge, before Mr. J. B. Edge, on the body of James Dewhurst, aged 23. Deceased was a joiner, and bad been leading a very tin- otetely and irregular life, Orr the previous Thursday he died from the effects of taking rat poison. A verdict to that effect was returned. A singular death is reported from Oldham On April 3rd Robert Bradshaw, a cotton operattve, went home late at night 'drunk, and sat down on the top of the kitchen fireplace. His wife, whmwas in bed, was awakined by his screams, and on coming down found him enveloped in flames. He was dreadfully-bsrnt, and was removed to the Oldham Infirm- ary, wqere he has since died from his injuries, A dreadful murder was committed at Slough on Monday evenings the victim. being Mrs. Riddle, the wife of -a. butcher. During the absence of her husband some, one entered the place where she was writing, and inflicted several frightful', wounds. upon her head and neck with a choper, the unfor--' tunate woman being dead when discovered, by a neighbour. A young man has been arrested on suspicion of having com- mitted the crime. A shocking sequel to a lover's quarrel was enacted, in Liverpool on Tuesday. A youag woman named Fitzpatrick, about 19, on Monday night quarrelled with her lover. She followed him to the hotel where he was Aaying, but, was refused admission. She, however, remained on the steps of the hotel all night, and on kis refusing to see her On Tues- day morning she went away, returning shortly afterwards saying "she bad‘done it." She had' taken carbolic acid, and died in an hour. A very distresslyg case of suicide occurred in Liverpool on Tuesday,when a young woman named Annie Kirkpatrick poisoned herself with carbolic acid. On the previous night the unhappy girl had called at an hotel in Vernon-streat, for the purpose of seeing a gentleman friend. She was refused admittance, and spent the night on the hotel steps, and in the morning committed suieide in the manner indicated. The deceased resided with her mother in the cit-y. • Mr. 11. Broadhurst, M.P., addressed a large meeting of working men on Tuesday night, in the Temperance Rail, Sheffield, and, referring to the Employers' Liability Mt, said they bad asked for the measure not forflte sake of gait), butte protect life. He sincerely hoped workmen would not heedlessly rush into mutual arrangements, whereby the proteition given by Parliament would be sold, as it were, like mess of pottage. He also spoke of the necessity 3 amending the patent laws and of lessening the olotroetictis tolhe return of working men to Parliament, •

div.p: BRITISH WOMEN'S TEMPERANCE • ASSOCIATION. • CONFERENCE AT WARRTNG-TON. The announcement of a conference to consider the position of the branch of the British Women's Temperance Associa- tion recently established here, and to devise means of deepening the interest and widening the sympathy of the ladies in the town and district of Warrington in the cause Of temperanne reform, brought together a large number of ladies in the ante-room at the Public Hall, on Monday afternoon. Mrs. Robert Garnett, of Penketh, was called to the chair, and she was supported by Mrs. Lucas, of London (vice-president of the Association, an sister to the Right Hon. John Bright); Mrs. Parker, of London, ex-president; Mrs. Burrows, of Atherton; and Mrs. Southworth, of Bolton. The CHAIRWOMAN stated that for some time past they bad had a branch of the British Women's Temperanoe Association in Warrington, but for want of help they had drooped considerably. Their meetings had been very poorly I attended, and they had failed to'secure the interest of other ladies in the town, and it had been thought well to hold that meeting that afternoon in order to awaken free sympathy;, and to induce fresh workers to join them. They would be very glad if the meeting resulted in obtaining the names of any ladies who would join with them in this move- ment. They had been trying to keep the movement afloat, but it had been so feeble they had almost felt ready to give it up. The movement, had just maintained an existence, and they wanted a new treasurer, and, particularly, visitors to carry on the work. When they began the movement they received in subscriptions £3; and, after paying for the I hire of a room at the British Workman Public House and a little printing, they had now in hand 11. 6s. She felt con- vinced that women could do a very great deal—perliap,s more than men—in the temperance movemerit, because as visitors they were much more efficacious; and concluded by reading an extract from a speech delivered a short time ago, in Exeter, by Mrs. Temple, wife of the Bishem of Exeter, showing the importance of ladies engaging in the work. • , Mrs. areas, president of the Association, then addressed the meeting. She said she dared say some of them would remember their visit to-Warrington' to farm thin branch of the British Women's Temperance Association, They had been very anXions that it, aladnici be thorOtlghly established here. They knew that it required a good deal of self denial with some to come out on this question, and there were others who were very willing to do so, but they were looking to others to help them. The address they had heard of Mrs. Temple's she thought would impress every one of them that they wanted to stir up public opinion on this question amongst women, and if women were silent at home, and would not take any part in the matter,then they must expect the country to be still more over-run than it is with this terrible drink. There Was no donbt that in towns like this, where she believed, there were breweries to a rather re- markable extent, they would find a great difficulty in moving. But let her beg of them just to think. This was'an impor- tant question and let every one of them think how they stood in the matter, and:whether there was anything for them to do. She was sure she had been greatly impressed herself, and she would notbe therelf she did not feel that it was an important duty for women to comeforward Mid defend their homes— (hear, hear,)—if it was in defence of home they were there that day. They knew how the home was ravished, how the house was stripped of all its comforts when one, whether it was father, or mother, or son, or daughter was overcome by this terrible fire water. Lately it bad been her experience to witness one or two instances which bad made a fearful impression on her mind. But she could not help thinking if women would just think what an awful thing it was to be overcome by drink, and if they eiaw anything of the kind they would make up their minds at once that they would have nothing at all to do with it. The British Women's Temperance Association was one that bad done a great deal of good. They had planted branches in various parts of the country, and they had lately planted five new branches in Lanesehire. They were very anxious that War- rington should take a prominent position amongst ' the branches at the annual meeting in May. They had between 150 and 200 branches, and Edinburgh was the stronghold. There they had done something remarkable. The ladies were a very' intelligent, energetic body, and they had pushed their way into the various religious denominations. They asked the ministers of those denominations to allow meetings to be held in their church or chapel or whatever building it was, and then addressed the ladies, of whom there were generally about 70 present, and she thought great good came out of it. It was astonishing what influence the ladies brought to bear, on the religious part of the community—when she said re- ligious she meant those who were good chapel or church goers; she did not say that those were not religieue out of these chapels—and it was a way of working 'which would be very advantageous in England if they could only accomplish it. But they found that the different denomina- tions in England were taking up the subject amongst them- selves. The Church of England Temperance Society were doing a great work, the Methodists and others were working in the same way, and they went on by slow degrees. Still, for all that there was a great body of people outside that they wanted to reach, and they had no other means than by calling the ladies together, as they had done that day, to ask them to think the matter over, and see if they could give up some of their spare time to help on this glorious cause. Some thought they required a little of these strong drinks— a little wine or a little brandy, or a little bitter beer, or some- I thing of that kind, and she did not wish to judge too harshly' of anyone, but she believed if they would only come up to I their faith—their religious faith—to the height that they I ought to do, that God would help them to abStain from these things. (Applause.) They wanted to feel that there was some help in that direction—that it was not entirely of themselves that they could do those things— that they wanted the help of their Lord. They had no idea, until they grasped their principles and began to look around them, of the sorrows and sufferings of not only the poor but every circle in life and they would be anxious-to work in every possible way. And it was astonishing how elastic time became to them under those impressions. She wassure there were many times when she left home she feltl as if it was impossible for her to leave. There were tied at home which she would gladly yield to, but it seemed she must leave things in confidence that all would go well, and her anxiety on this question was so great when she bad strength given her to ccme forward and speak to her sisters-. This branch,as their president had stated, was in a feeble state, and they wanted their assistance. They wanted them to become district visitors, and to come out to speak to the people. She did not say to come odt on the public plat. form, but to call their sisters together and see if they could not interest them. They had had a good deal of trouble-to get Peterborough to work, but they had persevered, and now they were, proceeding wonderfully. The secretary there wrote her not long ago that they had had a number of cot- tage meetings. She thought that they had had five cottage meetings sines the deputation were there, and 12 had signed the pledge. Now, the wives were most anxious to get up a public, meeting so that their husbands could come to hear- what they had to say. They had signed the pledge and *anted their husbands to sign. There were a great many women who if their husbands signed would not sign, but there could been comfort In these half-measures. They must go entirely the whole way to make the home what it should be. When they came to make the new appointments she hoped Mrs. Gar- nett would' remain as president and Miss A. Burgess as secretary, and that some of them would try what they could do, and not be too easily discouraged. Many times she had been inclined to turn` back and stay in her own home quietly, but she had fortunately had friends who said, "No, go on. and see what you can do," and she was very thankful they had been• able to do so much. Mrs. Parker was-the organiser of this association at Newcastle, and from there they moved their executive to London. They haetsince Worked the association from London, and she had had con.: siderable satisfaction in what they had done. (Applause.) Mrs. Brinnows, president of the Atherton branch, remarked that the-meeting was of a very different character to the one they came to about a year ago. They were few in numbers and lowain spirit, but she thought that afternoon, from see- ing so many, that they really were determined to work the VVarripgton branch, and. let it have a name of standing in the country.
