The opposition of manu- facturers to it, if persisted, cannot be justified on CENSUS TAKING AT RUNCORN, the ground that it is an innovation, inasmuch as it embodied in the Judicature Act (1875) (38 and 89 Vic., cap. 77), and has been successfully applied in at least one case, "Chorlton V. Russell and Sons, Hill and Sons, and Tenant and Co." when Mr. Justice Lush, in summing up, remarked that it was "a very wholesome and convenient practice." The only novelty in the present application of the principle is that offenders can be sued in County Courts instead of the Superior Courts, which is clearly most desirable, in order to avoid unnecessary expense. The proposed new clause (a) is also of great importance as a means of affording some redress to the public against works which have been omitted from the scope of the Bill, professedly on the ground that to in- spect them would necessitate an enormous increase of the staff of the Local Government Board. It is conceded that these works, which were specified in a schedule proposed in the House of Lords by Lord Broderick (Viscount Middleton), but rejected for the reason stated, ought to come under a different category to those dealt with in the Bill, there being, as yet, insufficient data respecting the injury caused by them; but that they do in some cases cause injury is manifest from the fact that they were included in the Bill of 1879, the power of proceeding against them being made contingent upon positive information being obtained, such as by the special investigation of an inspector provided for by this clause. As regards the "local objection clause (1), it only relates to new works, and if the welfare of the greatest number is to be the aim of the statute, it is obviously just to give the inhabitants of large towas the right of objection to the erec- tion of works intended for noxious manufactures within such a distance as will permit of their being a nuisance and a source of danger. As far as existing manufactures are con- cerned, it would appear that this clause would rather meet with their approval than otherwise. Beside submitting the above amendments for consideration in Committee, the Man- chester Noxious Vapours A.sseciation has petitioned Parlia- ment in general terms in favour of the bill. The Manchester Corporation has memorialised the Local Government Board in favour of the principle of the "local objection" clause suggestedby the association; and petitions to Parliament have been sent by the residents in theneighbourhood of Philips Park, and of Crumpsall, Blackley, Sm., praying for protec- tion from the particular kind of works by which they are respectively affected.

In a moment of weakness I consented to become one 0 the twelve enumerators to whom the work of counting the inhabitants of Runcorn was committed. The work turned out to be rather more formidable than at first sight it seemed. A great deal of time was taken up, and a larger amount of patience than I ever thought I possessed was expended; but if Sir Brydges Henniker receives any assistance in the de- sirable work of I " numbering the people," he is heartily wel- come to the humble efforts I have put forth. My first business vras the delivery of the schedules, and the'clubious looks I had to encounter when some doors were opened in response to my rather authoritative knock, would have made ' a man who was not on pretty good terms with himself feel I rather uncomfortable. But, thrice-armed in the justness of my work, I plodded on from house to house. It was a pleasing variation to the monotonous routine of question and answer, to be greeted by an intelligent housewife here and there with "0 yes, I know, master was reading about it in the paper last night. We expected you'd come some time this week." At some places I was invited in and treated to a family history by the members of that large class who carry their hearts in their sleeves. Their confidences are locked in my breast, or whatever the receptacle for such secrets, is called. One old woman, who had some unpleasant reminiscences of the last election of the Board of Guardians, when she was subpcenaed as a witness in a trial against someone, for tam- pering with the voting papers, in unmistakeable terms expressed her disinclination to have anything to do with the paper I was offering her. It took no little trouble to bring her to the belief that there was nothing of an electoral character about the harmless documents I It Ad in my hand; but after showing her the paper inside and out, and assuring I her in the language of legerdemain, there was "absolutely no deception,' she reluctantly accepted it. I found on going the following week to collect the papers that I had missed a court containing three houses, and the people felt slighted. "Why had they been overlooked ?" I apologised, which I had -no occasion to do, for the omission caused inconvenience to no one but myself, for I had to sit down and fill up the schedules, whereas if I had left them at the proper time, that extra work would not have fallen to my lot. The collection of the schedules was a difficult task in some portions of my district. Though there were cheering evidences that the "schoolmaster had been abroad," in the numerous neatly filled up papers I collected, yet there were melancholy proofs that he must have been very much "abroad "—in fact, not within fifty miles of the place. However, I found no more trouble than I expected, in consetmence of unfilled schedules. In some of these dens I felt bound to respectfully decline the proffered seat on a ricketty chair or a frousy-looking, apology for a sofa. After dodging down an entry I found myself before the door of an out-of-the-way cottage, and knocked loudly. The door was opened by an elderly man of not the clearest vision, who evidently took me for the rent collector, it being Monday morning; and, without giving me time to inform him as to my business, said, "1100 says yo mun come again next Monday." I thought I had fallen into the hands of a humourist, and so I replied, "That will be a week too late." 1 It then began to dawn on his dim intellect that the bogey he had conjured up was nothing more formidable than an enumerator, and gave me the paper at once. This notion of the rent day explained the problem that had puzzled me for some time that morning as to the where- abouts of some of the housewives when I called at their honses and found them absent. "Eufeka !"—" Rent-Mon- day !"—" My Uncle's!" The incidents were not all comic, there was a vein of sorrow and even of tragedy at times; as when a young mother, with quivering lip and tear-dimmed eve, told me they were one less than they were when I called last week—"a little one has gone;" or in that house where a widow was sobbing in incontrollable grief at the loss of one who had been cut off without a moment's warning two days ago. There is something to be learnt

from "The short and simple annals of the poor." There was some difficulty in fixing the relationship of some members of the families I called upon. A young man of thirty, who was the second husband of a woman of fifty, had to be made to appear a grandfather, because his step-daughter's child dwelt in the same house with him. He WAS some time before he took in the situation. Speaking of disparity in ages reminds me of one gay Lothario of 63 winters who had united his fortune with a dainty damsel of 28 summers, and two pledges of affection made what I should be inclined to call a nice quartette party. One patriarch set down his age at 601, and that of the partner of his joys and sorrows at 605. Ido not think I took too great a liberty when I set them down at the comparatively juvenile age of 61 and 65 respectively. The spelling On sonic of the papers would have rejoiced the heart of Pitman the inventor of phonetic spelling. Sound, and not sense, was the guide in many cases. The paper, how- ever, which gave me the greatest trouble to decipher wasfilled up by a gentleman in a public office in the town. Such carelessness is reprehensible. There were very few who came out strong in the column for "rank, profession," &c. One modest individual wanted to be " all there," and so he riehed to be known as a "Cabinet-maker, Insurance col- lector, and occasional Primitive Methodist local preacher." In the column for infirmities one genius set down himself as "blind of one eye." Another exact " Head of a family," described himself as " Wake in the chest," his "wife as " delecate," his son as " heithy." his daughter "strong" and his baby " delecate." I hope this candid customer will not be offended if these interesting perticulars are not thought of sufficient value to be tabulated by the Registrar General. One family, fresh from the Emerald Isle, wished it to be dis- tinctly understood that they were all Roman Catholics. I told them I was pleased they were something, but as far as the census was concerned it did not matter a jot whether they were Catholics or not. lam glad that we were not pestered with the religiousbeliefs of the people. In all conscience, it is sufficient to ask the age and business, the place of birth, and condition as to marriage' without getting into trouble over creeds and churches. What a godless people we should be made out to be, if everyone stated cor- rectly to which church they belonged, regular attendance being a sine qua non of membership. Lot us keep off dangerous ground. The only people who would be pleased with the result would be the Atheists and the Salvation Army. The first because of the vast amount of indifference to religions teaching that would be plainly manifested, and the second because it would strengthen their argument that church and chapel Chris- tianity is "played out." Very modest people these Salva - tionists are. The Surveyor had asked on several occasion., how he could com- plete the roads unless be had enough to do so from cipital account. The estimates presented by the committee had been too low to start with, and the roads had cost much more than was originally intended. The Cualleataar did not think that Mr. Carlile quite understood what he (Major Cross) meant. The great hard- ship was that the committee were calling upon the ratepayers to pay money at the present, the payment of which ought to be deferred. It was a great hardship to ask the ratepayers to pay in one year what ought to be spread over thirty years. Mr. KNIGHT again explained that instructions :had been given to have the accounts looked through. The CHAIRMAN: Yes, Mr. Knight, and the chairman of the Highway Committee was to see that the work was done. Mr. Canteen understood that it was arranged the mem- bers of the Highway Committee should do the work, but that the accountant was to give them every assistance he could.

YOTE OF THANKS TO THE CHAIRMAN. Mr. GOSSAGR, in moving a hearty vote of thanks to Major Cross for his services during the year, said he thought he might say with perfect safety that the Chairman had never bad such a twelvemonths' work as the last, since he -.7.ad occupied the position. Their warm thanks were due to him not only for the manner in which he had carried out the actual duties of Lis office, but for the many other matters to which he had given his attention whinh did not really come, within that sphere. Mr. HEYEs seconded the proposition, and said he con- sidered the ratepayers owed the Chairman of the Board a great debt of gratitude for the enormous amount of trouble he had taken in looking after their interests. The resolution having been carried with acclamation, the CHAIRMAN briefly acknowledged' the compliment. He remarked that he would cot deny that the past year had been an anxious one with regard to the finance of the Board. He was very glad to be able to say that, notvrithstandine• all the difficulties connected with the finances, the °Board had not lost one single penny beyond that caused by the disappearance of Mr. Pierce, the late accountant, which amounted'to about £2OO. For evety other shilling of expenditure they had, in reality, got good value for their money. (Hear, hear.) He was happy to say that the finances were in a first-rate state. Not only was their capital right, but the sinking fund was so also; and every quarter they were steadily getting into a better posi- tion. The banking account, about whieh so much had been said, and which was at one time up to £20,000, was now down at less than half that sum, and was steadily in- creasing. The gasworks were beginning to pay ;—so much was this the case, that he saw his way, and he hoped the Gas and Water Committee would soon see theirs, to a sinking fund, an before long, to a considerable reduction in the rate for gas. The waterworks were also in a satisfactory state, and would shortly begin to show a profit. The other committees were also in a satisfactory condition. Perhaps Mr. Knight would pardon him for having spoken so strongly that day about the Highway Committee. That gentleman had remarked that all the money to which reference had been made, had been spent. He (the speaker) had no doubt that this was really the case, and that the committee could show vouchers ; the only thing he wanted was to see the various items placed to their proper accounts. The business of the Board then terminated.

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. George Pilkington. BEGGlNG.—Bernard Lavelle, a tramp, was sent to prison for 14 days for begging in Wellington-street on Sunday
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. George Pilkington. BEGGlNG.—Bernard Lavelle, a tramp, was sent to prison for 14 days for begging in Wellington-street on Sunday

afternoon. TrESDAY.—Befors Mr. George Pilkington. ATTEMPT TO COMMIT SRlClDE.—Bridget Oates, aged about 40 years, the wife of a chemical labourer living in Midwood-street, Simons Cross, was charged with attempting te commit sificide.—A youth named Smith, the son of Mr.l Smith, ironfounder, Lngsdale-road, stated that on Monday evening, about seven o'clock, he was with a companion near the brook in Bradley-fields, when he heard an alarm raised. On going to the side of the brook he saw the prisoner in the water, with her head and part of her body covered: He went into the water and dragged out the woman, who was nearly dead. P.C. Strickland was sent for, and after her recovery ahe told that officer that if she could not be allowed to drown herself she would cut her own throat and those of her chil- dren. She was then taken to the police station.—Prisoner was remanded for a week to Walton gaol, in order that she might be examined as to her mental condition, and brought under the influence of the chaplain. Wanteasna.v.—Before Mr. F. W. Earle (chairman) and Mr. George Pilkington. THE ApPLETON PosTMAsTER FINED .£3 AND COSTS. John Young, postmaster, of Appleton, was summoned for keeping a dog without a license.—Defendant did not answer to the summons.—The evidence of P.C. Simpson was to the effect that at a quarter-past three o'clock on the afternoon ' of the 21st ult. he called at the defendant's, and seeing a , dog there he asked to speak to Mr. Young, but Mrs. Young told him he was not at home. He called again on the fol- lowing day. He saw Mr. Young, and asked him to let him see his dog license. He said, "All right," and called to his wife to fetch the license. She said," What license," and he replied, "The dog license." Mrs. Yonne. then went up- stairs, and was shortly afterwards followed "by her husband. In a few minutes they returned, but instead of showing him the document defendant asked him to call again, on the ground that he was busy with the letters, He went to the house again on the 23rd ult., and asked defendant's wife to permit him to see the dog license. She produced one numbered 29, and issued at Appleton post Office. He questioned her as to whether it had been issued on the date which it bore upon the face of it, and she said it had. The license stiown to him ap- peared to have been quite newly made out, and he therefore, requested them to let him see the register of dog licenses, but they refused on the ground that they had strict orders to show the register to no one but the excise officer. He re- ported the matter to sergeant Coutts' and on the following day, be and that officer, called at the defendant's and asked 'Mrs. Young to permit them to see the register. On examin- ing it, they found that there bad been no license taken out for any person of the name of Young on the 19th ult. There was a blank duplicate issued at 5 p.m., on the 21st, and • numbered 29. On asking for an explanation they were told by the defendant that it was a duplicate of his own license. —Sergeant Coutts corroborated, and also remarked that on calling at the defendant's office, on the sth inst.. he found the duplicate had been filled up for the 21st ult.—The chair- man said the Bench considered this about the worst case in respect to dog licehses which they had ever had before them The defendant and his wife were people whose duty it was to look after a post office, and there was no doubt they had taken advantage of their position to keep a dog without paying for any license. Their conduct won' dbe reported to the proper authorities, and, in order to show their sense of it, the magistrates would fine defendant £3 and costs.—At a later part of the proceedings, the defendant entered the I court, and uttered ono or two sentences apparently by way of extenuation, but they were utterly inaudible in the re- porters' box. He was then told by the chairman that the magistrates had decided the:case, and they could not re- open it. KEEPING DOGS WITHOUT LICENCE.—James Hy. Young was fined 20s. and 12s. costs; and Samuel Mercer 51. and costs (making 175.) for keeping dogs without license. In a -Can against John Stark, in which there were strong mitiga- ting circnmstanles, defendant was only ordered to pay costs. SCHOOL BOARD PROSECCTIONS.—The following were each summoned by the Widnes School Board, for whom Mr. Lanby, the clerk, appeared, charged with not sending their children to school :--James Peacock, Thomas McGridy, Isaac Sankey, and James Rathbone. Each of the defend- ants were ordered to pay 6d., and 45.6 d. costs. THE END OF A DEATNIEN SPREE.—A tall !young man, named John Wilkinson, was charged with assaulting Mrs. Daniel Davies, who keeps a butcher's shop in Waterloo - road, and her daughter, Mrs. Elizabeth Coupe, confectioner' carrying on business in the game street.—Mr. Swift appeared for the co ;n plainants.—Th ey were both widows, and at about eleven o'clock on the morning of the 31st ult. the defendant went to Mrs. Davies's shop and conducted himself in a manner indicating that he must either have been drunk or mad. He, first of dl, took possession of the milk cart which was standing at the door, and drove the horse and cart up and down the street. The complainants asked him to let the boy who had charge of the cart go about his busi- ness, on which he used very bad language. He next walked up and down the street in a maudlin drunken fashion, and then went to the door of Mrs. Davies's shop, wishing to obtain admission. She told him ,he would not have him there. He kicked the door in, and struck Mrs. Davies in the eye, which he discoloured. He also attempted to kick her. The daughter tried to pretert her mother, on on which defendant attacked her, and, as she was going for a policeman, struck her.--Defendant alleged that he was struck first by 'Aire. Davies. and he called a rough-looking young Man. named Wm. ROSCCW, and a bier, with the object of proving this.—The Chairman said lie supposed defendant must have visited the complainant's shop after he had been drinking heavily. He would have 10 and 7s. 6d. costs to pay in the one case and 10s. and Ss. ot I. costs in the other; 10e. 6d. would also be allowed toward the advocate's fee. THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY. APRIL 16, 1881.
RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday. Mr. S. Collier presided, and there were also present Messrs. T. Norman, P. Briscoe, W. Whittaker, H. Coleburn, James Handley, W. Littler, Geo. Marshall, and W. F. Salkeld (secretary).

_ INTBRIIENTS. The Secretary reported that there had been 19 interments in the cemetery during the month, making a total number since the opening of the cemetery of 5,410. Accounts amounting to £2B Bs. were passed for payment.

- The auditors, Mr. Geo. Moss and M. F. Fairhurst, reported L hat they had found the accounts of the Board correct.

THE BURIAL OF PAUPERS AND THE PAYMENT OF FEES. The SECRETARY laid before the Board the copy of a letter which he had written to the clerk of the Runcorn Board of Guardians, with reference to the burial of paupers. Mr. COLEBERN wished to know if Mr. Salkeld had received a further letter since the matter was brought before the Guardians. The SECRETARY said he had not; but he had a pri 'ate letter from Canon Barclay, to the effect that, if there was an interment in the Dissenting or Roman Catholic ground, he should claim the fee; and if it was paid to the Dissenting minister or Roman Catholic priest, he should object to the payment before the auditor. Mr. NORMAN: That is what Canon Barclay stated at the meeting of the Guardians. If Canon Barclay is not entitled to the fees, he did not want them; but let the question be thoroughly decided as he has suggested. Mr. HANDLEY said it was not the opinion of Mr. Glen, barrister to the Poor Law Board, that the fees belonged to the vicar. His comment on the Act was as follows :—The minister cannot, either by the caron or the common law, demand anything for the burial; but,, as a fee may be due by prescription of immemorial usage, the laity are compellable to observe the custom; and, though the minister may not refuse to bury because the custom is not observed, he may afterwards recover according to the custom of the particular parish. The custom must be immemorial and invariable, and where customary fees were allowed to be payable out of the poor rates, the custom was disproved, for the origin of poor rates being within legal memory, the custom could net be immemorial. Thus it was clearly stated that If any burial took place at the cost of the parish it could not be im- memorial, because the origin of poor rates was within legal memory. Mr. CoLvnunx wished to correct a statement made by Mr. Norman, as a member of the Runcorn Board of Guardians. He was reported to have said that the chairman would no doubt have seen that the matter had been before the Burial Board, and that a member—he presumed he meant Mr. Cole- burn—stated that several persons had spoken to him about the fees being paid to the • Vicar of the Parish." He would like Mr. Norman to say whether the report was correct. Mr. NORMAN said his 'remarks had been correctly re- ported. Mr. COLE/313RM said he did not mention anything about the fees when he fire brought forward the matter at the Board, so that Mr. Norman was wrong. Mr. NORMAN : Then, of course, I withdraw what I said. Mr. COLERIIRN said he was glad of it, because he had been totally misrepresented. Mr. NORMAN now stated that the secretary asked the question " What about the fees ?" and he had confused the observation. After some further conversation it was decided that Mr. Handley, Mr. Coleburn, and the secretary should prepare a letter to be sent to the Runcorn Board of Guardians. The other business was not of public interest.

TIITIESDAT.—Before Mr. Wm. Bankes (chairman) and Mr. S. B. Chadwick. THE SOCIAL Evit.—Eleanor Reynolds was sent to prison 14 days, with hard labour, for immoral conduct in Green- way-road, on the previous night.—Thomas Blakemore, a paramour of the same woman, was ordered to find two sureties in £lO, and be himself bound in a similar sum to keep the peace for six months, or, in default, be imprisoned one month, for assautting a man in Greenway-road. BRUTAL ASSAULT UPON A WOMAN. —Joseph Venables was charged with assaulting Agnes Ford, at Runcorn, on the 13th inst.—The evidence was to the effect that the com- plainant was a fallen woman, and that she kept the prisoner. On Wednesday night they had a dispute in Cooper-street, and he struck her several' times. She ran away, and he fol- lowed her into High-street, and kicked and struck her several times in a most brutal manner.—Superintendent Williamson happened to see the assault, and at once took the fellow into custody. He and Inspector Hollingworth took the man to the police station, and whilst they were putting the usual queations to him, he managed to make his escape into the street, and was only secured after a hot chase.—He was sent to gaol for three months, with hard labour. A GANG OF ROUGHS SENT 70 GAOL.—ABOMINABLE CON- DUCT.—Dominic Coleman, James Coleman, Patrick Towey, and Peter Gamow, Irishmen, were brought up under a warrant, charged with assaulting Thomas Forster, a brick- layer, of Wellington-street, at Rock Savage.—Prosecuter said that on the previous Sunday afternoon he went to Rock Savage in company with his wife and. a young woman named Neild, for a walk. Whilst passing along the road, I he saw the four prisoners and two other men, chasing somel lads who were in a field. Neither he nor the two women with him made any remark, but immediately afterwards the prisoners came to them in the road and surrounded them. Two of the men seized him, and swore by the Saviour that they would take his life. I) iring this proceeding the other men stood round about, with paving stones in their hands, and urging the two men to violence. With some difficulty he managed to get away from the men, but in con- sequence of their conduct he was prevented from pursuing his walk, and had to return home, where his wife had since been under the care of Dr. Mclaugall, and was that day unable to attend court.— Annie Nield gave corroborative evidence, and Sergeant Whalley said that he was in Halton on the Sunday after- noon and he saw the prisoners go in the direction where the assault was alleged to have been committed, after the clos- ing of the public-houses.—Superintendent Williamson said he had had a number of complaints as to the violeot con- duct of which the prisoners had frequently been guilty. Indeed, from all he heard, he was of opinion that when the I prisoners were turned out of the public-houses on Sunday' [afternoons, after closing time, they were fit for any kind of mischief.—The Chairman said it appeared that the pri- soners were a terror to the neighbourhood, but they would have to be taught that such conduct as that of which they [ had been guilty would on no account be tolerated in the district. The magistrates would use a very strong hand in putting down any such lawlessness, and, as a warning to any others who might be inclined to follow in a similar course, each of the prisoners would be sent to gaol for one month, with hard labour.

div.head: RUNCORN PARLIAMENTARY DEBATING SOCIETY.
div.p: RUNCORN PARLIAMENTARY DEBATING SOCIETY.

ANNUAL SOIREE. The very successful session of the RuncornParliamentary Debating Society was brought to a close on Tuesday even- ing, when a soirée was held in the Public Hall. The pro- ceedings began with an entertainment in the smaller hall, which was filled with members and their friends, including a goodly number of ladies. Mr. F. A. Lake (Nottingham) took the chair in the absence of the Speaker. Mr. J. R. Frith (Home Secretary) proposed a vote of thanks to the Speaker for hit services during the session. Mr. G. Rhodes (Stoke) seconded the proposition in a speech of some length and interest. The motion was carried by acclamation. Mr. Geo. Parr, of Warrington, then gave "Smiling Tom" in character, which created great amusement. Mr. W. J. Shore (Leader of the Opposition) read an amusing extract from Max Adeler's "Elbow Room," which was well re- ceived. Mr. W. Handley (Prime Minister) proposed pros- perity to the "Runcorn Parliamentary Debating Society," and took occasion to give a resunt of the work of the ses- sion. The Leader of the Opposition followed in fitting terms, and the motion was carried unanimously. Mr. J. Craig (Foreign Secretary), as one of the originators of the Society, responded and spoke of the- value of such institutions. Mr. W. White (Gloucester), a rising basso, sang with great taste and skill "The Yeoman's Wedding Song." Mr. Craig then read Franklin's lines on "-Paper," with his visual ability. •The Misses Jukes played a piano- forte duet entitled " Chilperic," which was loudly applauded and received a well-merited encore, and the last part was re- peated in response. Mr. F. Fairhurst sang the fine bass song "Safely follow him," in good style. Mr. E. Rhodes (Presi- dent of the Board of Trade), recited "Bernardo del Carpio in a highly creditable manner. Mr. Parr, followed with " Vilikins and his Dinah," in character, and being encored, responded with " Raspberry Jam," in the character of the " Handsome page boy." Mr. Parr's contributiona to the evening's entertainment gave great satisfaction. Miss Jukes was the accompanist, and it is needless to add that she ac- quitted herself admirably in that capacity. After votes of thanks to the ladies and gentlemen who had taken part in the entertainment, and to the chairman, had been passed, dancing was commenced in the large hall, and kept up with spirit until nearly two in the morning. The refreshments, which were first class were provided by Miss Parsons, of Bridge-street. The pleasant evening spent on Tuesday, augurs well for the succees of the next session, which will commence early in October.

RUNCORN POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. Charles Reynolds (ckairsnan) and Mr. James Reynolds. A " BLACKGIJARDLY " BROTTIER-Isr-LAw.—A young man, named Joseph Taylor, was summoned for assaulting his sister-in-law, Elizabeth' Taylor, on the sth inst. Com- plainant said she went to the defendant's house to complain to him about having beaten her little boy. She had not, however, got past the door step before be kicked her into the street, and followed her, and struck her twice.—Sarah Reece and Mary Riley were called for the complainant, and each stated they saw the defendant kick her.—Mr. Burton, who appeared for the defence' said. that after the evidence which had been offered, he could not make any defence on the part of his client, who must plead guilty. The case was a family dispute, and had the complainant not gone to the house, there would have been no disturbance. He certainly did use some violence, but be (Mr. Burton) did not consider she was injured.—The Chairman said the Bench thought the prisoner had behaved in a blackguardly manner, for if he had wanted to put the woman out of the house, be could have done so without using violence. He would be fined 205., and the costs, 178., or, in default of payment, one ' month's imprisonment. A WARNING co TRESPASSERS.—Sarah Houghton, a married woman, was summoned for trespassing on land near Messrs. Wig g Bros. and Steele's works, belonging to Joseph Ashley, and causing damage to the amount of ld.—Complainant, who has frequently had to summons people for trespassing on the land, said he was so much tormented by this conduct, that if the magistrates could not grant him any remedy, he should have to give the land up. On the 26th ult., his son I saw the defendant going seeress the field, and told her she was trespassing, hut she refused to return.—Defendant said she had a heavy baby and some goods in her arms at the tiros, and she could not think of going back after she had got so far.—The Chairman said it appeared a very difficult matter to conviace people they had no right to go upon the complainant's land. The statement of the defendant herself seemed to show very clearly that she knew that she bad no right there, and she would be fined /Os., and costs 105.6 d., or, in default of payment, be imprisoned 14 days. A TROUBLRSOME WOMAN—Catherine McCann was sum- moned for assaulting Ann Tonlkinson on the sth Complainant said the defendant had Pleaded with her very hard to withdraw the charge, and she should be glad if the Bench would allow her to daso. The magistrates consented. —Defendant was next charged with having been drunk and disorderly in High-street, on the 9th inst. The case was proved by P.C. Norden, and defendant was fined aos., and cos's 6s. 4d., or, in default of payment, one month's imprison-

HIGHWAY RATES FOR ST. HELENS. —At the Sb. Helens Police Court, on Monday, before Messrs. W. L. Evans and Willis, highway rates for the rural townships. of Eecleston and Win(lle at the rate of ICk.l in the pound were sanctioned, on the application of Mr. Ranson and Mr. Swift, surveyors for the respective townships.

CLAIM FOR TIM DRTFIITION OF A FLAT. -- At the Liverpool County Court, before Mr. T. P. E. Thompson, judge, and a jury, an' action was tried ia which a Mr. Whitehead, owner of the flat Safeguard,. claimed £ll Ils, from the Liverpool and St. Helens Lighterage Company, Limited, for eleven days' detention of the flat. Mr. Stewart, instructed by Messrs. J. W. Carr and Co., ap- peared for the plaintiff, and the defendants wererepresehted by Mr. Walton, instructed by Mr. H. W. gallins. The plaintiff's case was that he was engaged by the defendants to carry a cargo of phosphate manure tram Wist-bank, Widnes, to the Wellington Dock, Liverpool„ for the steamer Buenos Ayrean ; that he accordingly loaded the cargo, and proceeded to tha Wellington Dock. On arriving there c n the 16th February last, he duly notified the defendants, but at that time the Buenos Ayrean had not arrived, and did aot arrive until the 26th February, and consequently the fiat was not discharged until the let March. For the plairliff it was contended that the custom of the port is to allaw 48 hours after arrival for discharging, and after that tirna to pay detention at £1 Is. per day. In this case the plaintiff allowed 48. hours for discharging, and on the 19th February notified the defendants that he should claim detention, and it was from that date until the let March, a period of eleven days, for which the plaintiff claimed detention at £1 is. per I day. For the defendants it was contended that there was no.such custom, and that the plaintiff himself had caused the delay. They also disputed the plaintiff's right to charge detention for Sundays. Witnesses having been callod OD both sides, and counsel having addressed the court, the learned Judge summed up, and the jury gave a YordW. ov the plaintiff fq %nlonnt clzanled4 with costs,

LIBERAL AND CONSERVATIVE MEETINGS AT FRODSHAM. SPEECH BY SIR GILBERT GREENALL, BART. LETTER FROM MR. GLADSTONE. • On Thursday, the supporters of Mr. H. J. Tollemache, the Conservative candidate for West Cheshire, had a meeting at the Town Hall, Frodsham. There was a fair attendance. Mr. E. Abbott Wright, IF., of Castle Park, Frodsham, pre- sided; and there were also present the Hon. W. F. Tolle- mache, Mr. Henry J. Tollemache, the candidate; Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., of Walton Hall, Warrington; Cap- tain Park Yates, of Ince; Mr. James Reynold, J.P., of Fox Hill; Mr. Henry Churton, Chester; Mr. John Hieson, J.P., of Oakmere; Mr. Thomas Hignett, agent to the Marquis of Cholmondley ; and Mr. John Ashton, magistrates' clerk, Runcorn, the Conservative agent. The CRAIRMAIT opened the proceedings by a reference to the death of Mr. Egerton, and the great service he had ren- dered to that part of the county and the agricultural in- terest. As they had lost their late member, they must try to do their best to find a substitute. He believed they would do this in Mr. H. J. Tollemache, who was so well known for the able manner in which he had performed his duties in connection with the Quarter Sessions. He was very gratified that the present Conservative candidate had been constrained to give way to the wishes of the constituency and agree to stand, although he was associated in a family sense with the other representative of the division, the Hon. W. F. Tolletuache. Mr. HENRY J. TOLLEMICHE, the Conservative candidate, who was well received, expressed the pleasure it afforded hkn to see his good friend, Mr. Wright, who had been so I kind to him since the commencement of the coatest. in the I chair. Mr. Wright had been mainly instrumental in bring- ing together the very satisfactory meeting which he had the pleasure of seeing there that day. (Applause.) He hoped that he was, like all Cheshire men, a gallant man, and it afforded him great pleasure to see the faces of several ladies present that day. (Hear, hear.) He was sure that the services of those " ladies would be most valuable in the present Conservative candidature, and most kindly appreciated by himself. He should like to endorse most heartily and cordially every word which the chairman , had uttered in regard to their deceased representative. He felt it an extremely difficult matter to come forward for the purpose of succeeding ' such a kind, generous, able, and worthy gentleman. He next dwelt upon his political prin- cipals, avowed himself a Conservative, and said he would support any measures which would maintain and strengthen the constitution of the country. Speaking on the previous day, Sir Thomas Cualiffe, although he gave him (the speaker) credit for meaning what he said in his address, remarked that if ha were returned to the House of Commons he would have to be a dummy there, and be ordered about by the chiefs of his •party. Perhaps Sir Thomas Cunliffe spoke from personal experience, for about that time last year he was returned to Parliament, and he supposed that he found he was only a dummy and led about. (Laughter.) I He could assure Sir Thomas that lie had no intention of pledging himself to give a solid vote upon any question he might be ordered to, but he should exercise his discretion; and although he should give a steady, consistent support to the Conservative cause he would not bind himself to vote for one particular measure because it happened to be brought forward by Conservatives, or to oppose any measure because it was brought forward by Liberals. (Applause.) The speaker next condemned the policy of the pl.( sent Govern• ment as a peace-at-any-price policy in regard to our depend- encies; and condemned the proposed retirement from Candahar and the making of peace with the Boers under the peculiar circumstances of the case. He strongly condemned the way in whiok Her Majesty's Ministers had ruled Ireland since they had come into power. Mr. Tellemache next condemned the fearful incubus laid upon the country ow account of the cattle plague rats; and spoke in strong terms against extending the caunty franchise, and assimilating it to the borough. In conclusion, be said ho thought the con- test would not prove a bitter one, and sat down amidst applause. In answer to a question, Mr. Tollemache said he would not pledge himself absolutely to support the closing of pub- lic-houses on Sundays. Mr. JAMES REYNOLDS, J.P., proposed, and Mr. Ilrusote seconded, and the Hon. W. F. rToLt.ntaacap supported, a vote of confidence in the candidate. Sir GILBERT GREENALL, Bart. (late M.P. for Warrington), also spoke in support of the motion. Ile said he should have been very glad to have been, silent upon that occasion, Ibut there were times, when men of one mind were met to- gether for the accomplishment a one object, when they had a right to ask others to take come part. He did-so most willingly that day. He was present there in sorrow, for it was his. privilege to know Sir Philip Egerton well. (Hear, hear.) The late Sir Philip was a most able man ;. one who was of great assistance to him, and who used hisnbilities to the utmost in Jurthering the interests of the ccunty which he represented. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He did not speak without an extensive- knowledge of their late repre- sentative, for it had been- his privilege to sit- with him as Chairman of Committee3--1t was his good fortune to sit and receive instruction, from a man of Buell great expe- rience, (Hear, hear.) The county had truly sustained a gredLioss in the death of that gentleman, for he was one true in his friendshipsand opinions, and his primary object was to do that which ought to be the aim of all of , them—his duty. tHear, hear.) Sir Philip Egerton left an honoured name behind him, and ottembich the county would long hold in great esteem for what ho had done on account of the inhabitlnts. (Hear, hear.) He was plead to be present that morning, and to have the pleasure of making the acquaintance of the Conservative candidate, I an acquaintance which he felt sure would prove extensive, as he felt sure that Mr. Tollemacha would be returned as the parliamentary representative of that divisive. Some- thing had been already said during the contest :about silent members. Now, if there was one man in the world who re- gretted he hail said too much, it was their pl-Sent Prime Minister. div.head: WEST-CHESHIRE ELECTION.
div.p: THE WEST-CHESHIRE ELECTION.

Mr. James Tomkinson issued his address as the Liberal candidate for West-Cheshire, on Saturday. He says he is strongly in favour of a peaceful foreign policy, and of the good government of our present empire, as opposed to a constant extension. He will support a reform of the bank- ruptcy laws, the abolition of the law of entail, and any mea- sure empowering a majority of the ratepayers to regulate their own liquor traffic. Mr. Tomkinson arrived in Chester from London, on SaturAay, and addressed the farmers at the Corn Market. He was well received.
To-day (Saturday) is the day fixed by the High Sheriff of Cheshire for the nomination of a member for West Cheshire, and Friday next for the election.
n The proceedings terminated with a Tote of tha ics-to the chairman.

TO THE ELECTORS OF WEST CHESHIRE. GENTLEMEN,—A Vacancy having occurred in the Representation of your Constituency, through the lamented death of the late Sir Philip Egerton, I have the hmour to offer myself as a Candidate for your suffrages at the ap- proaching Election. My principles ars those of a firm and consistent Liberal; and should I be fortunate enough to be returned as your Represen- tative I shall be prepared to give a hearty support to Her Majesty's present Government, retaining only such liberty of action as I may feel conscientiously called upon to exercise. I am strongly in favour of a peaceful Foreign Policy and the Cultivation of friendly relations with other Powers, and of the consolidation and good government of our present Empire as opposed to its constant extension, and 1 strongly approve of the withdrawal from Candahar, and of the moral courage that has actuated the policy of the Government in Transvaal affairs. As regards Domestic Policy, I am fully convinced of the necessity of many important measures which are being, and will be, dealt with by a Liberal Government; of a thorough reform of the Law of Bankruptcy; of the further encourage- ment of thrift among the poorer classes, and of the readjust- ment of local burdens, the unequal pressure of which is felt by all classes. I should give a firm support to any measure empowering a majority of Ratepayers to regulate their own Liquor Traffic. lam also in favour of the abolition of the Law of Entail, and of any measure calculated to cheapen and simplify the transfer of land. In conclusion, I appeal with confidence to the fruits of the Policy and the Legislation of the last Liberal Administration to prove that the true welfare of this great Empire Is safe in Mr. Gladstone's hands; and I would point to the Legislation of last Session, and to the measures now before the country, as an earnest of the beneficial reforms which may be expected from his present Government. I have the h mour to be, Gentlemen, Teur.obedient Servant, JAMES TOMRINBON. Willington Hall, Tarporley, April 8, 1881.

TO THE ELECTORS Or WEST CHESHIRE. CIENTLEMEN,—Owing to the lamented death of our "I valued friend and representative, the late Sir Philip Egerton, a vacancy has occurred in the representation of this Division of the County, and having been requested by an in- fluential body of Electors to offer myself as a Candidate, I venture to solicit your suffrages. If you do me the honour to elect me as your representative I will carefully consider all measures that may be brought before Parliament, and as a Conservative will cordially sup,. port any that will tend to maintain and strengthen the Con- stitution of this country. I strongly condemn the policy which has directed the with- drawal of the British forces from Candahar, and still more the surrender of the Transvaal to the Boers, to the great loss and danger of the loyal Natives and British Colonists. The unfortunate condition of Ireland must continue to occupy the attention of Parliament, and while considering that more prompt measures by the Government weuld have prevented many of the present difficulties, I will give the proposed Land Bill my best attention, and render no factious opposition. I trust to the report of the Duke of Richmond's Commission on Agriculture for some practical suggestions tending to benefit this important interest which has so long suffered from de- pression, and direct attention at the same time to Local Taxa- tion: and any proposals that will bring about a more equi- table adjustment of rating shall receive my hearty support. The interval before the Election is extremely. short, but I shall endeavour as far as possible to make the acquaintance of those whom I hope shortly to call my constituents. I have the honour to be, Gentlemen, Your obedient Servant, HENRY J. TOLLEMACHE. Dorfold Hall, Nantwich, April 11th, 1881.

THE Lords of Her Majesty's Most Honourable Privy Council, by virtue and in exercise of the powers in them vested under The Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act. 1878, and of every ether power enabling them in this behalf, do order, and it is hereby ordered, as follows: This Order shall take effect from and immediately after the eleventh day of April, one thousand eight hundred and eighty-one. 2. The area declared, by Order of Council dated the eighth day of February, one thousand eight hundred and eighty-one, to be an area Infected with kot-and-mouth disease (namely)_ tire county of Lancaster. and the boroughs of Accrington, Ash- ton-under-Lyne, Barrow-in-Furness, Blackburn, Blackpool, Bolton, Burnley, Bury, Clitheroe, Lancaster, Manchester, Old- ham, Over Darwen, Preston, Rochdale, St. Helens, Salford, Southport. Stalybridge, Warrington, and Wigan. except as follows: The Petty Sessional Bivlsion of liiirkdale; and the foreign animals wharf at the Ramadan Dock, at Barrow-In- Firmness; and such landing-places in that county or in those boroughs as were at the date of that Order used for the landing of animals from Ireland.--is, except the townships of Barton- upon-Irwell, Stretford, Heaton Norris, the hamlet of Mossley, townships of Tongs, Royton, Chatterton, Tl3ornham, Butter- worth, the hamlet of Whitworth lower end, in the hundred of Salford; the townships of Eccles Hill, and Clayton-le-dale, in the hundred of Blackburn, and the township of Ditton, in the hundred of West Derby: in the county of Lancaster, and the boroughs of Accrington, Blackburn Bolton, Burnley, Bury. and Salford, hereby declared to be free from foot-and. mouth disease, end that area, except as aforesaid, shall, as from the commencement of this Order, cease to be an area or part of an area infected with foot-and-mouth disease. 3. The townships of Barton-upon-Ire, Stretford, Heaton Norris the hamlet of Mossley, the townships of Tonge, Royton, Chatterton, Thornbam, Butterworth, the hamlet of Whitworth lower end, in the hundred of Salford; the townships of Eccles Hill, and Clayton-le-dale, ta the hundred of Blackburn; and the township of Ditton, in the hundred of West Derby; in the county of Lancaster, and the boroughs of Accrington, Black- burn, Bolton, Burnley, Bury, and Salford, shall continue to be and are hereby declared to be an area or areas infected with foot-and-mouth disease. C. L. PEEL. The above Order is advertised in pursuance of the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act, 1878. WM. RT. BROOK, Town Clerk. Town Clerk's Office, Warrington, 13th April, 1881.

PRESCOT HIGHWAY BOARD. The monthly meeting of this Board for the current year was held on Tuesday, there were present Messrs. W. L. Evans, ..T.P. (chairman), Matthew Lowe (Rainhill), Robert Tyrer (Knowsley), Whitfield (Bold), and Henry Fogg (Whiston); Mr. Henry Cross (clerk,) and Mr. William Goldsworth (surveyor.) THE FOOTPATHS .LT RAINHILL. Jr. answer to the chairman, respecting the repairing of the footpaths in Rainhill village, Mr. Lows said a few of the owners of the adjoining property were willing to contribute one-half the cost of flagging and asphalting the footpaths in front of their respective properties, but the majority of the owners thought they should only be asked to contribute one- third of the cost. It was . accordingly resolved that the owners be asked to pay one-third only, instead of half the cost of putting the footpaths in Rainhill village into a thorough state of repair. SURVEYOR'S EXPENDITURE. The SURVEYOR submitted his monthly statement of ex- penditure from February 28th to March 24th, which was as follows :—Bold, £32 2s. 6d.; Knowsley, £l4 3s. id.; Rain- hill, £ll 13s. 20.; ' ,Whiston £8 175.; team labour, £55 Ils. od.; new materials, £10453. 9d. • incidental expenses, £ll Os. 90.; total, £237 13s. 9d. Deduct £lOO received on account, leaving a balance of £137 13s. 9d., for which a cheque was signed in favour of the Surveyor. I THE INCOME AND EXPENDITURE DURING THE PAST YEAR. I The SURVEYOR submitted a statement which he had prepared of the income and expenditure during the past year. The receipts up to March 25th, this year, amounted to £3,113 Bs. 4d., and-the expenditure to £3,462 25., leaving a balance due to the treasurer, the clerk, and the surveyor of £348 13s. Bd. The Board commenced the year with a balance of £678 12s. 7d. against them, but this had been reduced by one-half. NEW CALLS. The SURVEYOR submitted his estimate for the y ar ending 25th March, 1882, from which it appeared that t .e probable expenditure, including salaries, Sze., would be about £2,956. After some discussion, it was resolved the following calls be made :—Bold, £250; Kbowsley, £335; Rainh ill, £300; and Whiston, £4OO. VOTE OF THANKS TO THE 'CHAIRMAN. 'Mr. TYREE proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman for the courtesy and kindness he had shown towards them during the past year. Mr. LOWE seconded the motion which was unanimously agreed to. The CHAIRMAN, in response, said he was glad to find his services had been appreciated, and he begged to thank them for the assistance they had rendered him in the discharge of the duties of his office. He trusted that at the close of the coming year the finances would be in a better condition than they were at the present time.
